animal-and-plant-cells: Which structure is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall for support. Animal cells only have a cell membrane.
Where does aerobic respiration take place in a cell?
Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, releasing energy from glucose.
What is the function of ribosomes?
Ribosomes join amino acids together to make proteins.
Give two features of a sperm cell and explain how each helps it carry out its function.
Tail (flagellum) to swim to the egg; many mitochondria to release energy for swimming; acrosome containing enzymes to digest the egg's outer layer; haploid nucleus carrying genetic information.
Explain why root hair cells do not contain chloroplasts.
They are underground so receive no light, so they cannot photosynthesise. Chloroplasts would serve no purpose.
Which part of a plant cell contains cell sap and helps keep the cell turgid?
The permanent vacuole is filled with cell sap. It pushes against the cell wall, keeping the cell firm (turgid).
What is the cell wall of a plant cell made of?
Plant cell walls are made of cellulose, which strengthens the cell and supports the plant.
In which part of a cell do most enzyme-controlled chemical reactions take place?
The cytoplasm is where most chemical reactions happen, and it contains the enzymes that catalyse them.
Which structure controls which substances enter and leave an animal cell?
The cell membrane is partially permeable and controls the movement of substances in and out of the cell.
A muscle cell has many more mitochondria than a skin cell. Why?
It needs to make more protein for growth
It needs more energy released for contraction
Mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration. Muscle cells need lots of energy to contract.
Name the structure that contains chlorophyll and explain why palisade cells contain many of them. (2 marks)
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll; palisade cells contain many chloroplasts to absorb as much light as possible for photosynthesis.
Describe the function of the nucleus in a cell. (2 marks)
Contains the genetic material (DNA/chromosomes); controls the activities of the cell.
A root hair cell has a long, thin extension. Explain how this adaptation helps the cell carry out its function. (2 marks)
It increases the surface area of the cell; so more water and mineral ions can be absorbed from the soil.
A cell has a cell wall, ribosomes and a large permanent vacuole, but no chloroplasts. It is most likely:
Root hair cells are plant cells underground, so they have no chloroplasts. Bacteria have no permanent vacuole; sperm cells have no cell wall.
bacterial-cells: Where is the genetic material found in a bacterial cell?
In chromosomal DNA loop and plasmids in the cytoplasm
Bacteria are prokaryotes with no nucleus. Their DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm, plus small rings called plasmids.
Plasmids are small circular pieces of DNA. They often carry genes such as antibiotic resistance.
What is the function of a flagellum?
The flagellum rotates to move the bacterium.
State two differences between a bacterial cell and an animal cell.
Bacteria have no nucleus (DNA loop free in cytoplasm); bacteria have a cell wall; bacteria may have plasmids and a flagellum; bacteria have no mitochondria; bacterial cells are much smaller.
Bacteria are described as prokaryotes. What does this mean?
Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus. Their genetic material lies free in the cytoplasm.
Which feature do bacterial cells and plant cells both have?
Both have a cell wall, though the bacterial wall is not made of cellulose.
Roughly how large is a typical bacterial cell compared with a typical animal cell?
Bacteria are generally much smaller than eukaryotic cells, often around 1 to 10 µm long.
Which structure in a bacterium contains genes that may give resistance to antibiotics?
Plasmids are small rings of DNA that often carry extra genes such as antibiotic resistance.
Bacteria divide by binary fission, copying their DNA and then splitting into two cells.
Describe how a bacterial cell differs from a plant cell in the way its genetic material is arranged. (2 marks)
Bacterial DNA is a single loop free in the cytoplasm (plus plasmids) with no nucleus; plant cell DNA is in chromosomes enclosed in a nucleus.
Name the part of a bacterial cell where proteins are made. (1 mark)
A bacterial cell divides every 30 minutes. Assuming no cells die, how many bacteria will there be after 3 hours from one cell? Show your working. (2 marks)
Which pair of structures may be found in bacterial cells but never in animal cells?
Bacteria have no nucleus or mitochondria. Ribosomes, cytoplasm and a membrane are found in both.
microscopes-and-magnification: A microscope has a ×10 eyepiece lens and a ×40 objective lens. What is the total magnification?
An image of a cell is 5 mm wide. The real cell is 0.05 mm wide. What is the magnification?
How many micrometres (µm) are in 1 millimetre?
Why can electron microscopes show more detail than light microscopes?
Electron microscopes have higher resolution and magnification, so they can distinguish structures that are very close together.
A cell measures 0.02 mm. What is this in micrometres?
The image of a cell is 60 mm long and the magnification is ×300. What is the real length of the cell?
Real size = image size ÷ magnification = 60 ÷ 300 = 0.2 mm.
The ability to distinguish two points that are close together as separate
How many times bigger an image is than the object
Resolution is the smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as separate.
Which is an advantage of a light microscope over an electron microscope?
Light microscopes can be used on living cells; electron microscopes need specimens in a vacuum and so they are dead.
A student draws a cell 45 mm long. The real cell is 150 µm long. Calculate the magnification. (3 marks)
Describe how a student should prepare a slide of onion epidermis for a light microscope. (4 marks)
Peel a thin layer of epidermis; place it flat in a drop of water on a slide; add a drop of iodine (stain) to show structures; lower a coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles.
Give two reasons why electron microscopes have helped scientists understand sub-cellular structures better than light microscopes. (2 marks)
Higher magnification; higher resolution so small structures such as ribosomes and internal details of mitochondria can be seen.
A bacterium is 2 µm long. In a micrograph its image is 10 mm long. Calculate the magnification.
Convert to the same units: 10 mm = 10 000 µm. Magnification = image ÷ actual = 10 000 ÷ 2 = 5000.
enzymes-and-the-active-site: enz-1
What type of molecule is an enzyme?
Carbohydrate
Lipid
Protein
Nucleic acid
Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts.
enz-2
Why does an enzyme only work on one type of substrate?
The substrate must fit the shape of the active site
Enzymes are used up in the reaction
Enzymes only work at 37 °C
Each cell only contains one enzyme
In the lock and key model, only a substrate with a complementary shape fits the active site.
enz-3
Describe the lock and key model of enzyme action.

The substrate (key) has a shape complementary to the enzyme's active site (lock). It binds to form an enzyme-substrate complex, the reaction happens, and the products are released. The enzyme is unchanged and can be reused.
g01-enz-1
What is the name of the molecule that an enzyme acts on?
Substrate
Catalyst
Active site
Product
The substrate binds to the enzyme's active site and is converted into products.
g01-enz-2
Why are enzymes described as biological catalysts?
They provide energy for reactions
They are used up in the reaction
They are living cells
They speed up reactions and are not used up
A catalyst increases the rate of reaction without being changed or used up itself.
g01-enz-3
What is the active site of an enzyme?
The product of the reaction
The part of the enzyme where the substrate binds
The place where enzymes are made
The outer membrane of an enzyme
The active site is the region with a specific shape where the substrate binds and the reaction occurs.
g01-enz-4
Which statement about the enzyme-substrate complex is correct?
It forms after the products are released
It forms when the substrate fits into the active site
It forms when the enzyme is denatured
It contains no substrate
The enzyme-substrate complex forms when the substrate binds to the active site, before products are released.
g01-enz-5
Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide but not starch. This is because enzymes are
specific
denatured
living
fast
Each enzyme has an active site complementary to only one substrate, so it is specific.
g01-enz-6
Explain why an enzyme is unable to catalyse a reaction once its active site has changed shape. (2 marks)
The substrate no longer fits (is no longer complementary) the active site; so no enzyme-substrate complex can form.
g01-enz-7
State two ways in which enzymes are important in living organisms. (2 marks)
They speed up metabolic reactions so they happen fast enough to sustain life; they work at body temperature; they allow reactions to be controlled; they break down large molecules in digestion.
g01-enz-8
Explain why a protease enzyme cannot digest starch. (2 marks)
Starch does not have a shape complementary to the protease active site; so it cannot bind and no reaction occurs.
gcse-bio-enzymes-and-the-active-site-c1
Amylase cannot break down proteins because:
Protein molecules are too large to enter any enzyme's active site
Amylase works only at the low pH found in the stomach
Proteins denature amylase as soon as they bind to it
Its active site is not complementary in shape to protein molecules
Enzymes are specific: only a substrate with a complementary shape fits the active site.
factors-affecting-enzyme-activity: What happens to an enzyme when it is heated well above its optimum temperature?
Its active site changes shape and it denatures
High temperatures break bonds holding the enzyme's shape. The active site changes so the substrate no longer fits.
Why does increasing temperature (below the optimum) increase the rate of an enzyme reaction?
Molecules have more kinetic energy so collide more often
More kinetic energy means more frequent successful collisions between enzyme and substrate.
A reaction takes 20 s to complete. What is the rate in s⁻¹?
Explain why increasing substrate concentration eventually stops increasing the rate of reaction.
All the active sites become occupied (saturated), so enzyme concentration becomes the limiting factor.
Pepsin works best at pH 2 and amylase works best at pH 7. This shows that
all enzymes have the same optimum pH
different enzymes have different optimum pH values
Each enzyme has its own optimum pH, matched to where it works in the body.
What happens to the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction if the pH moves far from the optimum?
It decreases as the enzyme denatures
Extreme pH changes the shape of the active site so the enzyme denatures and the rate falls.
On a graph of rate against enzyme concentration (with excess substrate), what does the line show?
Rate rises and then falls sharply
With excess substrate, more enzyme means more active sites so the rate increases proportionally.
The rate of an enzyme reaction doubles when the temperature is raised from 20 °C to 30 °C. What is the most likely reason?
More frequent collisions with more energy
Particles have more kinetic energy so more frequent, more energetic collisions occur.
In an experiment 3 cm³ of oxygen is made in 12 s. What is the mean rate of oxygen production?
Describe how you would investigate the effect of pH on the rate at which amylase breaks down starch. (4 marks)

Mix amylase with starch solution and a buffer of a chosen pH; keep temperature constant in a water bath; take samples at intervals and test with iodine; record time for the iodine to stop turning blue-black; repeat with buffers of different pH.
A graph shows enzyme activity rising to 40 °C then dropping rapidly to zero by 60 °C. Explain the shape of the graph. (4 marks)

Rate increases up to 40 °C as particles have more kinetic energy and collide more often; 40 °C is the optimum; above it the bonds in the enzyme break and the active site changes shape; the enzyme denatures so substrate no longer fits and the rate falls to zero.
Explain why the rate of reaction levels off when the enzyme concentration is increased but the substrate concentration is low. (2 marks)
Substrate becomes the limiting factor; there are not enough substrate molecules to occupy all the active sites.
Starch was fully broken down by amylase in 120 s at pH 7 and in 300 s at pH 4. Calculate the rate (1/time) at each pH and explain the difference.
pH 7: 0.0083 s⁻¹; pH 4: 0.0033 s⁻¹. pH 4 is further from the optimum, so the active site's shape is altered and fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form.
Rate = 1 ÷ time. A longer time means a slower rate.
enzymes-in-synthesis-and-breakdown: Amylase (a carbohydrase) breaks starch into simple sugars such as maltose.
What are proteins broken down into?
Proteases break proteins into amino acids.
Lipids are broken down by lipase into:
Lipase breaks lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.
Give one example of an enzyme involved in synthesis and say what it makes.
Glycogen synthase joins glucose molecules to make glycogen (or DNA polymerase builds DNA, or enzymes building proteins from amino acids).
Which enzyme is found in saliva and begins the digestion of starch in the mouth?
Salivary amylase breaks starch down into maltose.
Where in the body is bile produced, and what is its role in lipid digestion?
Made in the pancreas; it neutralises stomach acid
Made in the stomach; it breaks lipids into fatty acids
Made in the gall bladder; it is an enzyme that digests lipids
Made in the liver; it emulsifies fats to give a larger surface area for lipase
Bile is made in the liver (stored in the gall bladder). It is not an enzyme: it emulsifies fat into small droplets, increasing surface area for lipase, and its alkalinity provides suitable pH.
Which row correctly matches an enzyme with its product(s)?
Carbohydrases break carbohydrates into simple sugars. Protease makes amino acids; lipase makes fatty acids and glycerol.
Why are large food molecules such as starch broken down during digestion?
They are too large to be absorbed into the blood
Large insoluble molecules cannot pass through the gut wall into the blood. Digestion makes small soluble molecules that can be absorbed.
Which of these is an example of an enzyme being used in synthesis?
Lipase digesting fat in the small intestine
Enzymes joining glucose molecules to make starch in a plant
Amylase producing maltose in the mouth
Protease breaking down a protein in the stomach
Synthesis builds large molecules from small ones. Plants use enzymes to join glucose molecules into starch (and animals into glycogen).
Explain why the stomach and the small intestine need different conditions for their digestive enzymes to work. (3 marks)

Stomach protease (pepsin) works best in acidic conditions (about pH 2) provided by hydrochloric acid; enzymes in the small intestine work best in alkaline conditions (about pH 8); bile (made in the liver) neutralises stomach acid and provides the alkaline conditions; each enzyme has an optimum pH and is denatured if the pH is wrong.
Describe the roles of the pancreas and the small intestine in the digestion of proteins. (3 marks)

Pancreas makes protease (and other digestive enzymes) and releases it into the small intestine; protease breaks proteins into amino acids; small intestine also makes protease and is where digestion is completed and the amino acids are absorbed into the blood.
Explain why bile increases the rate of lipid digestion even though it is not an enzyme. (3 marks)

Bile emulsifies lipids, breaking large droplets into smaller ones; this increases the surface area for lipase to work on; so lipids are broken down faster into fatty acids and glycerol; bile is also alkaline, giving the optimum pH for the lipase.
Which pairing of enzyme and reaction is correct?
Lipase: lipids → fatty acids and glycerol
Carbohydrases break down carbohydrates, proteases proteins and lipases lipids. Other enzymes build large molecules, such as glycogen from glucose.
testing-for-biological-molecules: Which reagent turns blue-black in the presence of starch?
Iodine solution changes from orange-brown to blue-black when starch is present.
A positive Biuret test for protein gives which colour?
Biuret reagent turns from blue to purple when protein is present.
Describe how to test a food sample for reducing sugars.
Add Benedict's reagent and heat in a water bath (about 80 °C) for a few minutes. A colour change from blue to green, yellow or brick red shows reducing sugar is present.
A food sample is tested with Benedict's reagent and heated. It stays blue. What can be concluded?
Reducing sugar is present in high concentration
Benedict's stays blue when no reducing sugar is present. It tells us nothing about starch or protein.
Which reagent is used to test for lipids, and what is a positive result?
Ethanol; a cloudy white emulsion forms
The emulsion test: shake the sample with ethanol, then pour into water. A cloudy white emulsion shows lipid is present.
Why must the Benedict's test mixture be heated in a water bath rather than held over a Bunsen flame?
A Bunsen flame would change the colour of the reagent
Water is needed in the reaction
The reagent only works when boiling violently
A water bath gives a controlled, safe temperature and avoids spitting
A water bath at about 80 °C heats gently and safely; direct heating can make the liquid spit out of the tube.
A student adds iodine solution to a food sample and then Biuret reagent to a second portion. The first stays orange-brown and the second turns purple. What does the food contain?
Orange-brown iodine means no starch. Purple Biuret means protein is present.
Which colour sequence shows increasing concentration of reducing sugar in the Benedict's test?
Brick red, orange, yellow, green, blue
Blue, green, yellow, orange, brick red
Blue (none) then green, yellow, orange and brick red as more reducing sugar is present.
Describe how you would test a sample of food to find out whether it contains protein. (3 marks)

Crush the food and mix it with water (shake/filter); add a few drops of Biuret reagent (or sodium hydroxide then copper sulfate) and mix; protein present if the colour changes from blue to purple/lilac; stays blue if no protein.
A student tests a sample for starch by adding iodine solution to it. Describe the positive result and explain how the student could make the test more reliable. (3 marks)
Positive result is orange-brown to blue-black; repeat the test and compare results; use a control (e.g. water or a known starch sample) for comparison; use the same volume of iodine each time.
Describe how you would test for lipids in a solid food sample, and state the result that shows lipid is present. (3 marks)
Grind the food and shake it with ethanol; filter or decant the liquid into a test tube of water; a cloudy white emulsion forms if lipid is present; the liquid stays clear if no lipid.
A food sample turns lilac with biuret reagent and stays blue when heated with Benedict's reagent. It contains:
Biuret detects protein (lilac or purple). A reducing sugar would turn Benedict's green, orange or brick red when heated.
calorimetry: A burning food sample raises the temperature of 20 g of water by 10 °C. Using 4.2 J/g/°C, how much energy was transferred?
Suggest one reason why calorimetry with a boiling tube underestimates the energy in food.
Heat is lost to the surroundings (air, the tube, the needle) rather than to the water; or the food does not burn completely.
A nut heats 25 g of water from 20 °C to 48 °C. Using 4.2 J/g/°C, how much energy was transferred to the water?
In calorimetry, which quantity is measured to calculate the energy released by a burning food sample?
The change in mass of the water
The change in temperature of the water
Energy transferred depends on the mass of water, its specific heat capacity and the temperature rise.
A 2.0 g sample of food transfers 8400 J to water. What is the energy content per gram?
Which change would make a calorimetry experiment more accurate?
Using a bigger piece of food each time
Using a larger volume of water
Placing a draught shield around the apparatus and the boiling tube
Insulation or a draught shield reduces heat loss to the surroundings, so more of the energy reaches the water.
Why is the same mass of water used when comparing different foods in a calorimetry experiment?
It is a control variable so the temperature rise can be fairly compared
It makes the food burn faster
It increases the energy in the food
Keeping the mass of water (and its starting temperature) the same ensures any difference in temperature rise is caused by the food.
A 1.5 g piece of food heats 30 g of water by 25 °C. Calculate the energy released per gram of food. Use 4.2 J/g/°C. Show your working. (3 marks)
Explain why the value for energy in a food sample found using a simple calorimeter is lower than the value on the food label. (2 marks)
Heat is lost to the surroundings/air/apparatus so not all energy transfers to the water; the food may not burn completely, so not all its energy is released.
Describe how you would investigate which of two foods releases more energy when burned. (4 marks)

Measure a fixed volume/mass of water in a boiling tube and record starting temperature; weigh a sample of each food (same mass); set the food alight and hold under the tube until it stops burning; record the highest temperature and calculate the temperature rise (then energy = mass of water × 4.2 × rise); repeat with the other food using the same water volume; compare energy per gram.
Burning 1.0 g of a crisp raises the temperature of 25 g of water by 12 °C. Calculate the energy released per gram (c = 4.2 J/g/°C), and give one reason it is lower than the true value.
1260 J/g; heat is lost to the surroundings (or the crisp does not burn completely).
Energy = mass of water × 4.2 × temperature rise = 25 × 4.2 × 12 = 1260 J.
diffusion: dif-1
What is diffusion?
Net movement of particles from low to high concentration using energy
Net movement of particles from high to low concentration
Movement of water across a membrane only
Movement of particles against a gradient
Diffusion is the net movement of particles down a concentration gradient. It is passive.
dif-2
Which change would increase the rate of diffusion?
Lower temperature
Smaller surface area
Steeper concentration gradient
Thicker membrane
A steeper gradient, higher temperature, larger surface area and shorter distance all increase rate.
dif-3
A cube has sides of 2 cm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?
Surface area = 6 × 4 = 24 cm². Volume = 8 cm³. 24:8 = 3:1.
g02-dif-1
Which substance moves by diffusion from the air into the blood in the lungs?
Oxygen
Glucose
Carbon dioxide
Urea
Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli (high concentration) into the blood (low concentration).
g02-dif-2
How are alveoli adapted for efficient gas exchange?
A dry lining and few capillaries
Thick walls and a small surface area
Thin walls, a large surface area and a good blood supply
Thick walls and no blood supply
Thin walls shorten the diffusion distance, a large surface area increases the rate, and a rich blood supply maintains a steep concentration gradient.
g02-dif-3
A cube has sides of 4 cm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?
Surface area = 6 × 16 = 96 cm². Volume = 64 cm³. 96 ÷ 64 = 1.5, so 1.5 : 1.
g02-dif-4
Why do large multicellular organisms need specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems?
They have a lower rate of respiration
They have thinner cell membranes
Diffusion does not occur in large organisms
Their surface area to volume ratio is small, so diffusion alone is too slow
As organisms get bigger, surface area to volume ratio falls, so diffusion alone cannot supply every cell quickly enough.
g02-dif-5
A drop of purple dye is placed in a beaker of water. Which description of its movement is correct?
The dye moves only downwards due to gravity
The dye moves only if the water is heated
The dye moves from low to high concentration using energy
The dye particles move from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated
Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher to lower concentration, without needing energy.
g02-dif-6
Explain how the structure of the small intestine villi makes diffusion of digested food into the blood efficient. (3 marks)
Villi give a large surface area; thin walls (one cell thick) give a short diffusion distance; a rich blood supply (capillaries) removes absorbed molecules, maintaining a steep concentration gradient.
g02-dif-7
Explain why a single-celled organism does not need a transport system, but a large animal does. (3 marks)

A single-celled organism has a large surface area to volume ratio; diffusion distances are short so substances reach all parts quickly by diffusion; a large animal has a small surface area to volume ratio and long diffusion distances, so diffusion alone is too slow and a transport system is needed.
g02-dif-8
Cube A has sides of 1 cm and cube B has sides of 3 cm. Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of each cube and state which would allow faster diffusion into its centre. (4 marks)

A: surface area 6 cm², volume 1 cm³, ratio 6:1; B: surface area 54 cm², volume 27 cm³, ratio 2:1; cube A has the larger ratio; so diffusion into the centre is faster for A (shorter distance relative to volume).
gcse-bio-diffusion-c1
Which change would double the rate of diffusion across an exchange surface?
Doubling the thickness of the membrane
Halving the surface area
Halving the thickness of the membrane
Halving the concentration difference
Rate ∝ (surface area × concentration difference) ÷ thickness.
osmosis: osm-1
Osmosis is the movement of water across a partially permeable membrane from:
a concentrated solution to a dilute solution
a dilute solution to a concentrated solution
any solution using energy
a cell to its cell wall
Water moves from a dilute solution (high water concentration) to a more concentrated solution.
osm-2
A potato cylinder goes from 2.0 g to 2.5 g after soaking. What is the percentage change in mass?
osm-3
Explain what happens to a plant cell placed in pure water.
Water enters by osmosis because the cell contents are more concentrated. The vacuole swells and pushes against the cell wall, so the cell becomes turgid. The cell wall stops it bursting.
g02-osm-1
A plant cell is placed in a concentrated sugar solution. What happens?
Water leaves by osmosis and the cell becomes flaccid or plasmolysed
Sugar enters by osmosis
It becomes turgid
It bursts
Water moves out of the cell down its concentration gradient. The cell loses turgor and the membrane may pull away from the cell wall (plasmolysis).
g02-osm-2
Why does an animal cell burst when placed in pure water, while a plant cell does not?
Plant cells are not permeable to water
Animal cells absorb solutes faster
Plant cells have a cell wall that resists expansion
Plant cells do not have a membrane
The cell wall of a plant cell stops it from bursting as it becomes turgid. Animal cells have no wall.
g02-osm-3
A potato cylinder has an initial mass of 4.0 g and a final mass of 3.4 g after soaking in a solution. What is the percentage change in mass?
g02-osm-4
Potato cylinders are placed in sucrose solutions of different concentrations. The cylinder in 0.4 mol/dm³ shows no change in mass. What does this show?
The solution has the same water concentration as the potato cells
Osmosis has stopped permanently
The cylinders are dead
The potato cells have no water
No net movement of water means the solution is isotonic to the potato cell contents, so the concentrations are equal.
g02-osm-5
Which of these is NOT a control variable in an investigation of osmosis using potato cylinders in sugar solutions?
Size and surface area of the cylinders
Time left in the solution
Volume of solution
Concentration of the solution
Concentration is the independent variable being changed; the others should be kept constant.
g02-osm-6
Describe how you would find the concentration of the potato cell contents using a set of sucrose solutions. (4 marks)

Cut identical potato cylinders and measure initial mass; place one in each of several sucrose concentrations for the same time; remove, blot dry and reweigh; calculate percentage change in mass and plot against concentration; the concentration where the line crosses zero (no change) equals the concentration of the potato cell contents.
g02-osm-7
A potato cylinder gains mass in a dilute solution. Explain why. (3 marks)
The solution has a higher water concentration than the potato cells; water moves into the cells by osmosis through the partially permeable membrane; so the mass of the cylinder increases.
g02-osm-8
Explain why a plant that is not watered wilts, using the term turgor. (3 marks)

Less water enters the plant cells by osmosis; the cells lose turgor as the vacuole shrinks and the cell contents press less on the cell walls; so the cells become flaccid and the plant loses support and wilts.
gcse-bio-osmosis-c1
A potato cylinder's mass falls from 2.50 g to 2.20 g in a sugar solution. Calculate the percentage change in mass and explain it.
−12%; the solution was more concentrated than the cell sap, so water left the cells by osmosis.
Percentage change = (2.20 − 2.50) ÷ 2.50 × 100 = −12%. Use the starting mass as the denominator.
active-transport: act-1
How is active transport different from diffusion?
It moves substances down a concentration gradient
It needs energy from respiration and moves substances against a gradient
It only moves water
It only happens in animal cells
Active transport uses energy from respiration to move substances from low to high concentration.
act-2
Explain why root hair cells need many mitochondria.
They absorb mineral ions from the soil by active transport, which needs energy released by respiration in mitochondria.
g03-act-1
Root hair cells absorb mineral ions from soil water by active transport. Why can they not rely on diffusion alone?
The soil has a higher ion concentration than the cell
The cell has a higher ion concentration than the soil water, so ions must move against the gradient
Ions are too large to pass through the cell wall
Diffusion only works for gases
Mineral ion concentration is usually higher inside the root hair cell than in the soil, so uptake is against the concentration gradient and needs energy.
g03-act-2
Which organelle supplies the energy for active transport?
Mitochondrion
Vacuole
Nucleus
Ribosome
Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, releasing the energy needed to drive active transport.
g03-act-3
Root hair cells contain many mitochondria. What is the advantage of this?
They give the cell a larger surface area
They make the cell wall stronger
They absorb more water by osmosis
They release more energy for active uptake of ions
More mitochondria means more respiration, so more energy is available for active transport of mineral ions.
g03-act-4
A plant is placed in water with no oxygen. What would happen to its uptake of mineral ions, and why?
It would increase because the cells make more carrier proteins
It would increase because diffusion speeds up
It would stay the same because ions move by osmosis
It would decrease because aerobic respiration stops, so less energy is released
Without oxygen aerobic respiration is reduced, so less energy is available for active transport and ion uptake falls.
g03-act-5
Glucose is absorbed from the small intestine into the blood by active transport in some situations. When is this most needed?
When glucose concentration in the gut is higher than in the blood
When glucose concentration in the gut is lower than in the blood
When there is no glucose in the blood
When the gut has too much water
When gut glucose is lower than blood glucose, diffusion cannot work, so active transport moves glucose against the gradient into the blood.
g03-act-6
Explain two differences between active transport and diffusion. (2 marks)

Active transport needs energy from respiration, diffusion does not; active transport moves substances against (up) the concentration gradient, diffusion moves them down it; active transport uses carrier proteins.
g03-act-7
A student measures mineral ion uptake by roots at 5 °C and at 25 °C. Uptake is much greater at 25 °C. Explain why. (3 marks)
Higher temperature increases the rate of respiration (enzyme activity); more energy is released; more energy is available for active transport so more ions are taken up.
g03-act-8
Explain why active transport is important in the small intestine and in plant roots. (4 marks)

In the small intestine it absorbs glucose/amino acids into the blood when their concentration in the gut is lower than in the blood; this means all useful nutrients are absorbed; in roots it absorbs mineral ions (e.g. nitrate) from soil where concentration is lower than in the root cell; the ions are needed for healthy growth, e.g. to make proteins.
gcse-bio-active-transport-c1
Root hair cells in waterlogged soil absorb fewer mineral ions. The best explanation is that:
The extra water dilutes the minerals, so they diffuse out of the root hair cells instead
Waterlogged soil contains no mineral ions at all for the roots to absorb
Less oxygen reaches the roots, so less respiration provides less energy for active transport
Osmosis stops, so mineral ions can no longer be carried into the root hair cells
Minerals are absorbed against their concentration gradient, which needs energy from aerobic respiration.
mitosis-and-the-cell-cycle: How many daughter cells are produced by one round of mitosis?
Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
In which stage of mitosis do chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell?
In metaphase chromosomes line up at the equator, attached to spindle fibres.
DNA is replicated and organelles are copied
During interphase the cell grows, copies its DNA and makes more organelles such as mitochondria and ribosomes.
Uncontrolled cell division caused by changes in cells
Mutations can cause cells to divide uncontrollably, forming a tumour.
Give two reasons why organisms use mitosis.
Growth; repair of damaged tissue; asexual reproduction.
What is the correct order of the stages of mitosis?
The order is prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase (PMAT), followed by cytokinesis.
Chromosomes line up at the equator
Spindle fibres pull chromatids to opposite poles
In anaphase the spindle fibres shorten and pull the sister chromatids apart to opposite ends of the cell.
A human skin cell has 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in each daughter cell after mitosis?
Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes (46) as the parent.
Why must DNA be replicated before mitosis begins?
So the cell can become specialised
So the cell wall can form
So the number of chromosomes doubles in each daughter cell
So each daughter cell receives a full set of genetic information
DNA is copied in interphase so that each daughter cell gets a complete copy of the genome.
A cell spends 18 hours in interphase and 2 hours in mitosis. What percentage of the cell cycle is spent in mitosis?
Describe what happens to the chromosomes during prophase and metaphase. (3 marks)
Prophase: chromosomes condense and become visible, each made of two identical chromatids; nuclear membrane breaks down; Metaphase: chromosomes line up along the equator and attach to spindle fibres.
A tissue sample contains 200 cells. 30 are seen in mitosis. A full cell cycle takes 24 hours. Estimate how long mitosis lasts. (2 marks)
Explain how mutations in genes that control cell division can lead to cancer. (3 marks)
Mutation changes the genes controlling the cell cycle; cells divide uncontrollably by mitosis; this forms a tumour / mass of abnormal cells, which may spread (malignant).
A cell cycle lasts 20 hours. In a sample, 5% of cells are in mitosis. About how long does mitosis take?
The proportion of cells in a stage reflects the proportion of time spent in it: 5% of 20 hours = 1 hour. Most of the cycle is interphase.
growth-and-percentile-charts: gpc-1
In animals, cell differentiation mostly happens:
Throughout life equally
At an early stage of development
Only in old age
Only in the brain
Most animal cells differentiate early on. Many plant cells keep the ability to differentiate throughout life.
gpc-2
Plants grow mainly by cell division at:
Meristems at shoot and root tips
The leaves only
The xylem
The flowers
Meristem tissue at root and shoot tips divides by mitosis. Plants also grow by cell elongation.
gpc-3
A baby's mass is on the 75th percentile. This means:
75% of babies are heavier
75% of babies the same age are lighter
The baby is 75% of normal mass
The baby is underweight
On the 75th percentile, 75 out of 100 babies of that age have a lower mass.
gpc-4
Why do doctors track a baby's growth on percentile charts?
To check the baby is growing at a normal, consistent rate and spot problems early, e.g. if the baby moves across percentile lines or is far above/below others.
g03-gpc-1
A baby girl's length is on the 25th percentile at 6 months and the 50th percentile at 12 months. What does this show?
She is shrinking
She has grown faster than the average for her age over this time
She is unhealthy
Her measurements were wrong
Moving up percentile lines means her growth was faster than most babies of the same age.
g03-gpc-2
Which measurement is NOT usually plotted on a baby's percentile chart?
Length or height
Head circumference
Blood pressure
Mass
Percentile charts typically record mass, length/height and head circumference.
g03-gpc-3
A baby's mass falls from the 75th percentile to the 10th percentile in a few months. What is the best action?
Stop feeding the baby
Use the average value instead
Nothing, percentiles do not matter
Investigate for a possible health or feeding problem
A large fall across percentile lines may indicate a problem, so a doctor should check the baby.
g03-gpc-4
Why is a percentile chart more useful than comparing a baby with the mean mass for its age?
It only includes healthy babies
It shows the range of normal values in the population
It gives the exact mass the baby should be
It removes the need to weigh the baby
Percentiles show the spread of values so doctors can see whether a baby is within the normal range, not just above or below an average.
g03-gpc-5
A baby is on the 50th percentile for length. In a group of 200 babies of the same age, about how many are expected to be shorter?
50% are shorter, so 0.5 × 200 = 100 babies.
g03-gpc-6
A baby's head circumference is on the 97th percentile. What does this mean? (1 mark)
97% of babies of the same age have a smaller head circumference (only 3% have a larger one).
g03-gpc-7
Explain why a baby on the 5th percentile for mass is not necessarily unhealthy. (2 marks)
5th percentile is within the normal range for the population; if the baby follows a steady growth curve along that line it is growing consistently/normally.
g03-gpc-8
Describe two factors other than genes that can affect a child's growth. (2 marks)
Diet / nutrition (lack of protein or energy slows growth); illness or disease; hormones such as growth hormone; exercise or environment.
gcse-bio-growth-and-percentile-charts-c1
A baby's mass is on the 25th percentile. This means:
The baby is 25% below the mass it should be for its age
The baby is heavier than 75% of babies of the same age
The baby's mass has increased by 25% since it was born
25% of babies of the same age are lighter and 75% are heavier
Percentile charts compare a child with others of the same age. A sudden change in percentile matters more than the value itself.
stem-cells: stc-1
What is a stem cell?
A fully specialised cell
An undifferentiated cell that can divide and become specialised
A cell found only in plant stems
A cell with no nucleus
Stem cells are undifferentiated and can differentiate into other cell types.
stc-2
Where are plant stem cells found?
Xylem
Meristems
Guard cells
Phloem
Meristems in root and shoot tips contain plant stem cells.
stc-3
Why are embryonic stem cells more useful than adult stem cells for treatments?
They are cheaper
They can become almost any type of cell
They never cause rejection
They divide slower
Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into almost any cell type. Adult stem cells are more limited.
stc-4
Give one advantage and one risk of using stem cells in medicine.

Advantage: could replace damaged cells, e.g. to treat paralysis or type 1 diabetes. Risks: rejection by the immune system; cells may divide uncontrollably and form tumours; ethical objections to using embryos.
g03-stc-1
What is meant by differentiation?
Cell division by mitosis
A cell changing to become specialised for a particular function
A cell dying
Copying of DNA
Differentiation is the process by which an unspecialised cell develops the structures needed for a specific job.
g03-stc-2
Bone marrow transplants can treat some blood diseases because bone marrow contains:
Adult stem cells that can become blood cells
Meristem cells
Nerve cells
Embryonic stem cells
Bone marrow contains adult stem cells that can differentiate into the various types of blood cell.
g03-stc-3
Which is a source of embryonic stem cells?
Plant roots
Red blood cells
Skin from an adult
Embryos in the early stage of development
Embryonic stem cells come from early embryos, for example those created by IVF.
g03-stc-4
Therapeutic cloning is used to produce stem cells that are genetically identical to the patient. What is the main advantage?
The cells never differentiate
The cells divide faster
The cells are less likely to be rejected by the patient's immune system
The cells are cheaper to produce
Cells with the patient's own genes have the same antigens, so the immune system does not attack them.
g03-stc-5
Why can cloned plants be produced from meristem tissue?
Meristem cells are specialised for photosynthesis
Meristem cells can differentiate into any type of plant cell
Meristems contain xylem
Meristem cells have no cell walls
Plant meristems contain stem cells that can become any plant cell type, allowing rapid production of identical plants.
g03-stc-6
Give two reasons why stem cells from meristems are used to clone rare plants. (2 marks)
To save species from extinction; to produce many identical plants quickly / cheaply; to produce disease-resistant crops with desired features.
g03-stc-7
Some people object to using embryonic stem cells for research. Give two arguments for and against. (4 marks)

For: could cure diseases / paralysis; embryos left over from IVF would be destroyed anyway. Against: the embryo is a potential human life; destroying embryos is wrong; risk of tumours or viral infection being transferred.
g03-stc-8
Explain why stem cells could be used to treat a person with type 1 diabetes. (2 marks)
Stem cells could be made to differentiate into insulin-producing (pancreas) cells; these would replace damaged cells so the patient makes insulin.
gcse-bio-stem-cells-c1
Why might adult stem cells from a patient's own bone marrow be used instead of embryonic stem cells?
They will not be rejected, although they can form fewer cell types
They can form any type of cell, so they are more versatile
They divide faster than embryonic cells, so treatment is quicker
They carry no risk of infection or of forming tumours
The patient's own cells match their immune system. Embryonic stem cells can form almost any cell but raise ethical and rejection issues.
neurones-and-the-nervous-system: Which part of a neurone is insulating and speeds up impulses?
The fatty myelin sheath insulates the axon so impulses jump between gaps and travel faster.
Which neurone carries impulses from receptors to the central nervous system?
Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS.
The central nervous system is made up of:
The CNS is the brain and spinal cord.
Describe the function of dendrites and of the axon.
Dendrites receive impulses from other neurones; the axon carries impulses away from the cell body over long distances.
Which of these is an effector?
Effectors are muscles or glands that respond to a stimulus. Receptors detect stimuli.
What is the function of a relay neurone?
Connect sensory and motor neurones within the CNS
Carry impulses from receptor to CNS
Relay neurones are found in the CNS and connect sensory neurones to motor neurones.
Why is a motor neurone's axon often very long?
To receive signals from many neurones
To carry impulses over long distances from the CNS to an effector
The long axon carries impulses from the CNS (e.g. spinal cord) to effectors such as leg muscles.
Which sequence shows the path of an impulse in a nervous response?
A stimulus is detected by a receptor, passed to a coordinator (CNS), then to an effector, producing a response.
Which feature of a neurone allows it to carry impulses rapidly along the axon?
The myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds up transmission of electrical impulses.
Give two differences in the structure or function of sensory and motor neurones. (2 marks)

Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS, motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors; sensory neurones have the cell body off to the side of the axon, motor neurones have the cell body at the end.
Explain how the structure of a neurone is adapted to its function. (3 marks)

Long axon carries impulses over long distances; myelin sheath insulates and speeds up impulses; dendrites branch to connect with many other neurones / receive impulses; many mitochondria provide energy.
Describe the pathway taken by a nervous impulse when you touch a hot object and pull your hand away. (4 marks)

Temperature receptors in the skin detect the stimulus; sensory neurone carries the impulse to the CNS; relay neurone in the spinal cord passes it on; motor neurone carries the impulse to the effector (muscle) which contracts to pull the hand away.
In multiple sclerosis, the myelin sheath around some neurones is damaged. The main effect is that:
Nerve impulses travel more slowly or are disrupted
Myelin insulates the axon and speeds up impulses.
synapses-and-reflex-arcs: syn-1
How is an impulse passed across a synapse?
Electrical current jumps the gap
Neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap
The axons touch
Hormones in the blood
Neurotransmitter is released, diffuses across the gap and binds to receptors on the next neurone, triggering a new impulse.
syn-2
What is the correct order of a reflex arc?
Stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector → response
Stimulus → motor neurone → receptor → relay neurone → effector
Receptor → brain → effector → stimulus
Stimulus → effector → motor neurone → receptor
Impulses travel receptor → sensory → relay (in spinal cord) → motor → effector.
syn-3
Why are reflexes fast?
They involve the conscious brain
They bypass the conscious part of the brain
They use hormones
They involve many synapses
Reflexes are automatic. The relay neurone in the spinal cord means conscious thought is not involved.
syn-4
Explain why reflex actions are important.
They are rapid and automatic, so they protect the body from harm, e.g. pulling a hand away from a hot object.
g04-syn-1
What is a synapse?
A receptor that detects stimuli
A type of effector that releases hormones
A junction between two neurones where there is a small gap
The fatty sheath around an axon
A synapse is the junction between two neurones. The gap is crossed by chemicals, not electrical impulses.
g04-syn-2
In a reflex arc, which structure carries impulses from the spinal cord to an effector?
Sensory neurone
Relay neurone
Motor neurone
Receptor
Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands).
g04-syn-3
Why do nerve impulses travel in only one direction across a synapse?
The gap is too wide for impulses to go backwards
Hormones block the return signal
The impulse changes into an electrical signal
Neurotransmitter is released from only one side and receptors are only on the other side
Vesicles releasing neurotransmitter are only in the first neurone and receptors are only on the membrane of the next neurone.
g04-syn-4
A person touches a hot pan and pulls their hand away before feeling pain. Which is the effector?
The relay neurone in the spinal cord
The muscle in the arm
Temperature receptors in the skin
The sensory neurone
The muscle contracts to move the hand away, so it is the effector. The receptors detect the stimulus.
g04-syn-5
Which statement about reflex actions is correct?
They only involve the brain
They are slow because they need conscious decisions
They are automatic and rapid
They are learned through practice
Reflexes are automatic and rapid because the impulse does not have to pass through the conscious part of the brain.
g04-syn-6
Describe how an impulse is transmitted across a synapse. (3 marks)
Neurotransmitter is released from the first neurone (vesicles at the end of the axon); it diffuses across the gap; it binds to receptors on the next neurone, which triggers a new electrical impulse.
g04-syn-7
A knee-jerk reflex test is used by doctors. Explain why a reflex response is faster than a voluntary response. (2 marks)

The reflex pathway is short and uses few neurones/synapses; the impulse goes via a relay neurone in the spinal cord and does not pass through the conscious part of the brain, so no time is spent deciding.
g04-syn-8
Give the sequence of structures an impulse passes through in a reflex arc, starting with the stimulus. (3 marks)
Stimulus; receptor; sensory neurone; (synapse); relay neurone in the CNS/spinal cord; (synapse); motor neurone; effector (muscle or gland); response.
gcse-bio-synapses-and-reflex-arcs-c1
Nerve impulses can cross a synapse in only one direction because:
The synaptic gap is too wide for impulses to travel back towards the first neurone
Neurotransmitter is released only from the first neurone and receptors are only on the next one
Electrical impulses jump the gap, and the myelin sheath blocks them from returning
Neurotransmitter is destroyed as soon as it reaches the first neurone's membrane
The chemical neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap to receptors on the next neurone.
structure-of-the-brain: Which part of the brain controls balance and coordinates movement?
The cerebellum coordinates muscle movement and balance.
Which part of the brain controls breathing and heart rate?
The medulla oblongata controls unconscious activities like breathing and heart rate.
Which technique uses a strong magnetic field to produce detailed images of the brain?
MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) uses magnetic fields and radio waves.
Give two reasons why treating brain damage is difficult.
Neurones do not regenerate easily; the brain is complex and well protected by the skull; treatments can damage other areas; drugs struggle to cross the blood-brain barrier.
Which part of the brain is responsible for memory, language and consciousness?
The cerebral cortex is the folded outer layer of the cerebrum and controls higher functions such as memory, language and consciousness.
Why is the surface of the cerebral cortex highly folded?
To protect it from the skull
To increase the surface area so there is more room for neurones
Folding increases surface area, allowing a greater number of neurones and more complex processing.
A patient has a stroke that damages the cerebellum. Which symptom is most likely?
Loss of the ability to see colour
Loss of the ability to speak
The cerebellum coordinates muscle movement and balance.
Which method of studying the brain shows which areas are active during a task?
Studying patients with brain damage only
Stimulating the brain with electricity only
A PET scan shows active areas of the brain. MRI and CT scans show structure, and the other methods give less direct information.
Which part of the brain is damaged if a person can no longer control their heart rate or breathing?
The medulla oblongata controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing.
Describe how scientists have used evidence from patients with brain damage to find out about brain function. (3 marks)
Damage to a specific area causes loss of a specific function; this suggests the damaged area controls that function; observing which abilities are lost allows areas to be mapped to functions.
Give two advantages of using an MRI scan to study the brain compared with exploring it with electrical stimulation during surgery. (2 marks)
Non-invasive/no surgery needed; no risk of damaging brain tissue; gives detailed images of the structure; can be repeated safely.
Explain why it is difficult to treat brain tumours with surgery. (2 marks)

The brain is complex and each area has important functions; surgery risks damaging healthy tissue and causing loss of function; neurones do not regenerate easily; tumours may be in places that are hard to reach.
After a head injury, a patient's heart rate and breathing are irregular. The region most likely damaged is the:
The medulla controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing. The cerebellum coordinates balance and movement.
the-eye-and-its-defects: Which part of the eye controls how much light enters?
Muscles in the iris change the size of the pupil.
Which receptor cells in the retina detect colour?
Cones detect colour and work in bright light. Rods work in dim light.
In short sight light focuses in front of the retina, so a diverging lens spreads rays out first.
Cataracts make the lens cloudy. It can be replaced with an artificial lens.
Explain what happens to the lens when you look at a near object.
Ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments slacken, the lens becomes fatter (more convex) and refracts light more strongly.
Which part of the eye does most of the refraction (bending) of light?
The cornea refracts light the most. The lens makes fine adjustments to focus.
What happens to the pupil in bright light?
It gets smaller because circular muscles contract
It gets smaller because radial muscles contract
It gets larger because radial muscles contract
Circular muscles in the iris contract and radial muscles relax, making the pupil smaller to protect the retina.
In long-sightedness (hyperopia), light from near objects is focused:
The lens is too thin or the eyeball too short, so near objects focus behind the retina. A convex lens corrects this.
Which row correctly describes the lens when focusing on a distant object?
Ciliary muscles contracted, suspensory ligaments tight, lens thin
Ciliary muscles relaxed, suspensory ligaments tight, lens thin
Ciliary muscles contracted, suspensory ligaments slack, lens thick
Ciliary muscles relaxed, suspensory ligaments slack, lens thick
For distant objects the ciliary muscles relax, ligaments tighten and pull the lens thin, so it refracts light less.
Which is NOT a treatment for short-sightedness?
Laser eye surgery to reshape the cornea
Wearing a converging lens in glasses
Short sight is corrected with a diverging (concave) lens. A converging lens would make it worse.
Explain how the eye adjusts to focus on a near object. (4 marks)
Ciliary muscles contract; suspensory ligaments slacken/loosen; the lens becomes thicker/more curved; so light is refracted more strongly and focused on the retina.
Explain what causes short-sightedness and how glasses correct it. (3 marks)

The lens is too curved or the eyeball is too long, so light focuses in front of the retina; a diverging (concave) lens spreads the rays slightly before they enter the eye; so light then focuses on the retina.
Describe the pupil reflex in dim light and explain why it is useful. (3 marks)
Radial muscles in the iris contract and circular muscles relax; the pupil gets larger; more light enters the eye so that the receptors (rods) can detect enough light to see.
In short-sightedness (myopia), light from distant objects focuses:
Behind the retina, so a convex (converging) lens is used to correct it
On the retina but blurred, so a convex lens is used to sharpen the image
In front of the retina, so a concave (diverging) lens is used to correct it
In front of the retina, so a convex (converging) lens is used to correct it
The eyeball is too long or the lens too strong. A concave lens spreads the rays so they focus further back.
sexual-and-asexual-reproduction: sar-1
Which is a feature of asexual reproduction?
Two parents
Gametes fuse
Offspring are genetically identical
Produces lots of variation
Asexual reproduction involves one parent and mitosis, giving clones.
sar-2
An advantage of sexual reproduction is:
It is faster
Only one parent needed
Variation helps a species survive environmental change
No energy is needed to find a mate
Variation means some individuals may survive new conditions or diseases.
sar-3
Which organism can reproduce asexually?
Strawberry plant using runners
Humans
Birds
Dogs
Strawberries send out runners that grow into new identical plants.
sar-4
Give two advantages of asexual reproduction.
Only one parent needed; faster, so many offspring quickly; no energy spent finding a mate; good genes for the environment are passed on.
g04-sar-1
What are gametes?
Cells that contain two copies of every gene
Cells produced by mitosis that are identical to the parent
Sex cells with half the normal number of chromosomes
Fertilised egg cells
Gametes (sperm, egg, pollen, ovum) are haploid sex cells produced by meiosis.
g04-sar-2
Which type of cell division is involved in asexual reproduction?
Mitosis
Meiosis
Fertilisation
Binary fission only
Asexual reproduction involves mitosis only, giving genetically identical offspring.
g04-sar-3
Why does sexual reproduction produce variation in offspring?
Mitosis copies DNA with mistakes
Gametes from two parents carry different alleles and fuse randomly
The parents are always different species
The offspring are produced from a single parent
Mixing genetic information from two parents, with random fertilisation, produces genetically different offspring.
g04-sar-4
Which organism can reproduce both sexually and asexually?
Dogs
Birds
Humans
Malarial parasite
The malarial parasite reproduces asexually in the human host and sexually in the mosquito. Some fungi and plants also do both.
g04-sar-5
A farmer has one wheat variety that is well suited to local conditions. A new fungal disease appears. Why might a field of identical clones be at risk?
Clones always mutate quickly
Clones all have the same alleles so all may be susceptible to the disease
Clones cannot photosynthesise
Clones grow too slowly to produce a crop
Genetic identity means there is no variation, so if one plant is susceptible, all of them are.
g04-sar-6
Compare sexual and asexual reproduction. Give two differences. (2 marks)

Sexual involves two parents and fusion of gametes; asexual involves one parent; sexual offspring are genetically different, asexual offspring are clones; sexual involves meiosis, asexual mitosis only.
g04-sar-7
Explain why variation is an advantage to a species when the environment changes. (3 marks)

Variation means individuals have different alleles/characteristics; some may be better adapted to the new conditions (e.g. disease or climate); these survive and reproduce, so the species is less likely to become extinct.
g04-sar-8
Give two disadvantages of sexual reproduction compared with asexual reproduction. (2 marks)
Needs two parents/must find a mate; takes more time and energy; slower to produce many offspring; successful characteristics may not be passed on.
gcse-bio-sexual-and-asexual-reproduction-c1
Aphids reproduce asexually in summer and sexually in autumn. The best explanation is:
Sexual reproduction is faster in autumn, so it builds up numbers quickly before winter arrives
Asexual reproduction gives more variation, which is most useful in warm summer conditions
Sexual reproduction makes identical offspring that are already well adapted to the cold
Asexual reproduction builds numbers fast in good conditions; sexual reproduction gives variation for change
Each method's advantages suit different conditions.
meiosis: Meiosis involves two divisions and gives four genetically different haploid gametes.
How many chromosomes are in a human gamete?
Gametes are haploid with 23 chromosomes. Fertilisation restores 46.
Where does meiosis happen in humans?
Meiosis happens in the reproductive organs to make gametes.
Explain why gametes need to be haploid.
So when two gametes fuse at fertilisation the zygote has the normal diploid number of chromosomes (46 in humans).
How many times does the cell divide in meiosis?
Meiosis involves two divisions, producing four haploid cells.
What happens to the genetic material before meiosis begins?
It is moved out of the nucleus
The DNA is copied (replicated) first, so there is enough for four cells.
A human cell in the testis has 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes will each sperm cell have?
Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so each sperm has 23.
Why are the gametes produced by meiosis genetically different from each other?
Gametes absorb DNA from nearby cells
The DNA is copied incorrectly each time
Chromosomes are shuffled and distributed randomly between the cells
Chromosomes (and alleles) are mixed and shared out randomly, so each gamete is unique.
Which statement correctly compares mitosis and meiosis?
Mitosis produces 2 identical cells, meiosis produces 4 different cells
Mitosis happens only in the ovaries
Meiosis is used for growth and repair
Mitosis gives 2 genetically identical diploid cells for growth and repair; meiosis gives 4 genetically different haploid gametes.
Describe what happens during meiosis. (4 marks)
DNA/chromosomes are copied; the cell divides twice; four cells are produced; each has half the number of chromosomes (haploid) and the cells are genetically different.
A zebrafish body cell has 50 chromosomes. State the number of chromosomes in a gamete and in the zygote, and explain why. (3 marks)
Gamete 25; zygote 50; meiosis halves the number, and fertilisation fuses two gametes to restore the full diploid number.
Explain how meiosis and fertilisation together lead to genetic variation in a population. (3 marks)

Meiosis produces gametes that each have a different mix of chromosomes/alleles; fertilisation is random, so any sperm can fuse with any egg; so the offspring have new combinations of alleles from both parents.
A species has 16 chromosomes in its body cells. One cell divides by meiosis. The result is:
Four genetically different cells, each with 8 chromosomes
Meiosis halves the chromosome number and produces variation in the gametes.
structure-of-dna: DNA is two strands wound together in a double helix.
A pairs with T and C pairs with G (complementary base pairing).
A short section of DNA coding for a protein
A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a sequence of amino acids to make a specific protein.
The strands of DNA are held together by:
Weak hydrogen bonds between complementary bases hold the two strands together.
Outline how DNA can be extracted from fruit.
Mash fruit with detergent (breaks membranes) and salt (clumps DNA), filter, then gently pour ice-cold ethanol on top. DNA precipitates as white strands at the boundary.
A DNA strand has the base sequence ATGCCA. What is the sequence of the complementary strand?
A pairs with T and G pairs with C, so ATGCCA is paired with TACGGT. U is only found in RNA.
In a sample of DNA, 30% of the bases are adenine. What percentage are guanine?
A = T = 30%, so A + T = 60%. The remaining 40% is split equally between C and G, so G = 20%.
What is a nucleotide made of?
An amino acid, a phosphate group and a base
Two bases joined by hydrogen bonds
A sugar and two phosphate groups
A sugar, a phosphate group and a base
A DNA nucleotide has one sugar, one phosphate group and one base. Many nucleotides join to form a polymer.
Which part of DNA forms the sugar-phosphate backbone and which part carries the genetic code?
Backbone: sugar and phosphate; code: bases
The sugar and phosphate groups alternate to form the backbone. The order of the bases forms the code.
Why is ice-cold ethanol added in the DNA extraction method?
To separate the two DNA strands
To break open the cell membranes
To make DNA insoluble so it comes out of solution
DNA is not soluble in cold ethanol, so it precipitates and can be seen as white strands.
State the roles of detergent and salt in extracting DNA from fruit. (2 marks)
Detergent breaks down the cell membranes (and nuclear membrane) to release DNA; salt makes the DNA clump together.
Explain why DNA from different species has the same structure but different genetic codes. (3 marks)

All DNA is made of the same four bases, sugar and phosphate in a double helix; the order (sequence) of bases differs between species; different sequences code for different amino acid sequences and so different proteins.
Describe how complementary base pairing allows a DNA molecule to be copied accurately. (2 marks)
Each base can only pair with its complementary base (A with T, C with G); so each old strand acts as a template and the new strand has an identical sequence.
In a DNA molecule, 20% of the bases are adenine. What percentage are cytosine?
A pairs with T, so T = 20% and A + T = 40%. The remaining 60% is split equally between C and G: 30% each.
protein-synthesis: During transcription mRNA is made from DNA in the nucleus.
How many bases code for one amino acid?
A triplet of three bases (a codon) codes for one amino acid.
What brings amino acids to the ribosome?
tRNA molecules carry specific amino acids. Their anticodons pair with mRNA codons.
Which enzyme binds to the non-coding region in front of a gene to start transcription?
RNA polymerase binds to the promoter region and makes mRNA.
mRNA attaches to a ribosome; tRNA brings specific amino acids; tRNA anticodons pair with complementary mRNA codons; amino acids are joined into a polypeptide chain in the order coded by the mRNA.
The DNA template strand reads TAC GGA. What is the sequence of the mRNA made from it?
mRNA is complementary to the template: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C. RNA contains uracil, not thymine.
Which of these is a difference between mRNA and DNA?
mRNA is found only in the ribosome
mRNA is much longer than DNA
mRNA contains uracil instead of thymine
mRNA is single stranded, shorter, and contains the base uracil in place of thymine.
Why must mRNA be made rather than the ribosome reading DNA directly?
mRNA is made of amino acids
DNA cannot leave the nucleus but ribosomes are in the cytoplasm
Ribosomes can only read RNA bases A and T
DNA is too large to leave the nucleus. mRNA carries a copy of the gene to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
An mRNA strand has 90 bases in its coding region. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide (ignoring any stop codon)?
Three bases code for one amino acid, so 90 ÷ 3 = 30 amino acids.
What determines the final shape and function of a protein?
The number of ribosomes in the cell
The length of the mRNA only
The type of cell it is made in
The order of amino acids in the polypeptide, which folds up
The amino acid sequence determines how the chain folds into a specific 3D shape, which gives the protein its function.
Describe what happens during transcription. (3 marks)

RNA polymerase attaches to DNA at the start of a gene; the DNA strands unwind/separate; complementary RNA nucleotides pair with the template strand to make mRNA; the mRNA leaves the nucleus through a pore.
Explain how the order of bases in a gene determines the order of amino acids in a protein. (3 marks)
Each triplet of bases (codon) codes for one amino acid; the mRNA codon sequence is copied from the gene; tRNA anticodons pair with the codons so the amino acids are joined in that order.
Explain why a protein made of the same amino acids in a different order would have a different function. (2 marks)
Different order gives different bonds/interactions between amino acids, so it folds into a different 3D shape; the shape (e.g. active site) determines function.
A DNA template strand triplet is TAC. The mRNA codon and the tRNA anticodon are:
mRNA is complementary to the template (U instead of T). The tRNA anticodon is complementary to the codon.
mutations-and-protein-function: A change in the DNA base sequence
Mutations are random changes in the DNA sequence.
Have no effect or little effect on the phenotype
Most mutations have no effect. A few change protein shape or function.
A mutation in the non-coding region before a gene might:
Affect how much of the protein is made
It can stop RNA polymerase binding well, changing how much mRNA, and so protein, is made.
Explain how a mutation could stop an enzyme working.
A changed base sequence can change the amino acid sequence, so the protein folds differently. The active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits.
Which of these is a cause of mutations?
Ionising radiation such as UV, X-rays and gamma rays, and some chemicals, can damage DNA and increase mutation rate.
A mutation changes the DNA triplet CAA to CAG. Both code for the same amino acid. This is likely to have:
The genetic code is degenerate: several triplets code for the same amino acid, so the protein stays the same.
A single base is deleted near the start of a gene. Why is this often more damaging than a substitution?
It stops mRNA being made at all
It changes every triplet after the deletion
A deletion shifts the reading frame so all following codons change, altering many amino acids. A substitution usually changes one.
A mutation changes one amino acid in a structural protein but its shape is hardly altered. The most likely result is:
If the shape and function are not changed, the phenotype is unaffected.
A gene mutation occurs in a body cell. Why is it not passed on to offspring?
Body cells do not contain DNA
Only mutations in gametes are inherited
Body cell mutations are always repaired
Only mutations in gametes (or the cells that make them) can be passed to offspring.
A mutation changes one amino acid in an enzyme. Explain how this could change the rate of the reaction it catalyses. (3 marks)
The amino acid sequence changes so the protein folds into a different shape; the active site changes shape; the substrate no longer fits as well (or not at all) so the rate is lower.
Explain how a mutation in a non-coding region next to a gene could change the amount of protein made. (2 marks)
RNA polymerase may bind less well (or better) to the region; so less (or more) mRNA is transcribed and less (or more) protein is made.
Describe how a mutation can lead to a change in phenotype. (3 marks)
The mutation changes the DNA base sequence; this may change the amino acid sequence of the protein; the protein folds differently so its function changes, giving a different characteristic.
A mutation occurs in a non-coding region of DNA just before a gene. It could still change the phenotype because it may:
Change the amino acid sequence of the protein
Change how well RNA polymerase binds, altering how much of the protein is made
Remove the gene from the chromosome
Have no possible effect, because the region is non-coding
Non-coding regions can control gene expression; less or more protein can change the phenotype.
mendel-s-work: men-1
Mendel carried out his experiments using:
Fruit flies
Pea plants
Mice
Bacteria
Mendel crossed pea plants with different characteristics, e.g. tall and dwarf.
men-2
Why was Mendel's work not recognised in his lifetime?
He made errors
Genes and chromosomes had not been discovered
He used computers
He published in English
Scientists did not yet know about chromosomes, genes or DNA, so his 'inherited factors' were not understood.
men-3
State one conclusion Mendel drew from his pea plant experiments.
Characteristics are passed on by inherited 'factors' (genes); these factors come in pairs; some factors are dominant over others; factors are not blended.
g05-men-1
Why did Mendel's pea plants make good subjects for his experiments?
They contain no genes
They have only one chromosome
They have short life cycles and obvious contrasting characteristics
They reproduce asexually only
Peas grow quickly, produce many seeds and show clear alternative traits such as tall or dwarf, and he could control pollination.
g05-men-2
Mendel crossed pure-breeding tall and pure-breeding dwarf plants. All the offspring were tall. What did this show?
The offspring were mutants
Tall is the dominant characteristic
Dwarf is the dominant characteristic
Height is not inherited
Only one characteristic appeared in the first generation, so it is dominant and the other is recessive (hidden).
g05-men-3
When Mendel crossed the tall offspring with each other, about 3 in 4 were tall and 1 in 4 dwarf. What did this suggest?
The dwarf factor had been lost then reappeared by mutation
The dwarf factor was hidden in the first generation and passed on
Dwarf plants have no factors
Tall plants had no factors
The recessive factor was still present in the tall F1 plants and reappeared in the next generation in a 3:1 ratio.
g05-men-4
Which discovery, after Mendel's death, helped scientists to explain his 'inherited factors'?
The microscope being invented
Photosynthesis being understood
Antibiotics being discovered
Chromosomes behaving in a way that matched his factors during meiosis
In the 1900s scientists observed chromosomes and meiosis, which matched Mendel's ideas. Later, genes were identified as sections of DNA.
g05-men-5
Which statement about Mendel's 'factors' matches the modern idea of genes?
Factors blend together permanently
Factors are made of protein only
Each characteristic is controlled by a pair of factors, one from each parent
Factors are passed on only by the mother
Mendel proposed that characteristics are controlled by pairs of factors (alleles), one inherited from each parent, and these do not blend.
g05-men-6
Explain why Mendel's work was only accepted after his death. (2 marks)
Chromosomes, genes and meiosis had not been discovered at the time, so there was no mechanism to explain his factors; later observations of chromosomes supported his conclusions.
g05-men-7
Describe how Mendel's results supported the idea that inheritance is not a blending process. (2 marks)
Crossing tall and dwarf plants did not give medium plants; the dwarf characteristic reappeared unchanged in the next generation so the factors stayed separate.
g05-men-8
Suggest why Mendel's conclusions were reliable. (2 marks)
He used large numbers of plants/repeated the crosses many times; he counted offspring and looked at the ratios; he used pure-breeding plants and controlled pollination.
gcse-bio-mendel-s-work-c1
Why was Mendel's work not widely accepted during his lifetime?
His experiments were carried out on humans, so other scientists could not repeat them
He never published his results, so very few scientists ever learned about his work
His results contradicted Darwin's theory, which most scientists had already accepted
Genes and chromosomes had not been discovered, so there was no mechanism for his results
His idea of inherited 'units' was only explained decades later.
genetic-terms: A different version of a gene
A section of a cell membrane
Alleles are different forms of the same gene.
An organism with alleles Bb is:
Phenotype is the characteristic shown; genotype is the alleles present.
A recessive allele is only expressed when:
It is on the Y chromosome
Recessive alleles are only expressed in homozygous recessive individuals.
The entire genetic material (all the DNA) of an organism.
A plant has the genotype tt, where T is tall and t is dwarf. Which describes it?
Two identical recessive alleles = homozygous recessive. With no dominant allele the plant is dwarf.
Which is an example of a genotype?
A genotype is the combination of alleles, written as letters such as Ff. The others are phenotypes.
A gamete from an individual with the genotype Aa could carry:
Gametes are haploid and carry one allele of each gene, so a gamete from Aa carries A or a.
Which statement about the genome is correct?
It is one pair of alleles
It is all the genetic material in an organism
It is only the genes that are expressed
The genome is the entire DNA of an organism. Understanding it helps with finding genes linked to diseases.
A person with the genotype Dd shows the dominant phenotype. What does this show?
The dominant allele is expressed when present with a recessive allele
The recessive allele has been deleted
In a heterozygote, the dominant allele masks the recessive allele so only the dominant phenotype is seen.
Explain the difference between a gene and an allele. (2 marks)
A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein / controls a characteristic; alleles are different versions of the same gene.
Two parents with the dominant phenotype have a child with the recessive phenotype. Explain how this is possible. (3 marks)
Both parents must be heterozygous carriers; each passes on a recessive allele in their gamete; the child inherits two recessive alleles (homozygous recessive) so shows the recessive phenotype.
State why two organisms with the same genotype may not have identical phenotypes. (1 mark)
The environment also affects phenotype (e.g. diet, sunlight, climate).
A plant has the genotype Rr, where R (red) is dominant to r (white). Which description is correct?
Homozygous dominant, with a red phenotype
Homozygous recessive, with a white phenotype
Two different alleles make it heterozygous; one dominant allele is enough to show red.
monohybrid-crosses: mon-1
Two heterozygous parents (Tt × Tt) are crossed. What ratio of tall:short offspring is expected? (T = tall, dominant)
All tall
Offspring: TT, Tt, Tt, tt → 3 tall : 1 short.
mon-2
A cross Tt × tt gives what probability of short offspring?
Offspring: Tt, Tt, tt, tt → 50% short.
mon-3
Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele. Two carrier parents have a child. What is the probability the child has cystic fibrosis?
Ff × Ff gives 1 in 4 ff.
mon-4
A brown-eyed (dominant) parent has a blue-eyed child with a blue-eyed partner. What is the brown-eyed parent's genotype? Explain.
Bb (heterozygous). The child is bb so must have received a b allele from each parent.
g06-mono-1
Pea plants Tt × Tt produce 200 offspring. How many are expected to be short (tt)?
The cross gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so one quarter are tt. One quarter of 200 = 50.
g06-mono-2
Which statement correctly describes an organism's phenotype?
The combination of its gametes
The alleles it carries, such as Tt
The observable characteristic produced by its genotype and environment
The number of chromosomes in its cells
Phenotype is the observable characteristic. The alleles carried make up the genotype.
g06-mono-3
A homozygous dominant parent (RR) is crossed with a homozygous recessive parent (rr). What are the offspring?
All Rr, showing the dominant trait
Half Rr and half rr
All rr
3 RR : 1 rr
RR can only give R and rr can only give r, so every offspring is Rr and shows the dominant phenotype.
g06-mono-4
A cross gives offspring in a 1:1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotype. What are the parents' genotypes?
AA × aa
Aa × aa
AA × Aa
Aa × Aa
A heterozygous parent crossed with a homozygous recessive gives 50% Aa and 50% aa, a 1:1 ratio.
g06-mono-5
Two parents are both Aa for a recessive condition. What is the probability that their first two children both have the condition (aa)?
