Each child has a 1/4 chance of aa. For two independent children: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.
g06-mono-6
Black fur (B) is dominant to brown fur (b) in guinea pigs. Show the cross between two heterozygous guinea pigs and state the expected ratio of black to brown offspring. (4 marks)
Parents Bb × Bb; gametes B or b from each parent; offspring BB, Bb, Bb, bb; ratio 3 black : 1 brown.
g06-mono-7
A couple have four children and all four show the recessive trait. The parents are both carriers. Explain why this does not disprove the expected 3:1 ratio. (2 marks)
Fertilisation is random so each child has an independent 25% chance of showing the trait; ratios are only seen reliably in large numbers of offspring, not in a small family.
g06-mono-8
Explain what is meant by a heterozygous genotype and why a heterozygous individual may show the dominant phenotype. (2 marks)
Heterozygous means two different alleles for a gene, one dominant and one recessive; the dominant allele is expressed so the phenotype is dominant, with the recessive allele masked.
gcse-bio-monohybrid-crosses-c1
Two parents are both heterozygous for a recessive condition. What is the probability that their first two children both have the condition?
Each child independently has a 1/4 chance: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.
sex-determination: Which pair of sex chromosomes does a human male have?
Males are XY and females are XX.
What is the probability that a baby will be female?
XX × XY gives 2 XX : 2 XY, so 50%.
Which parent's gamete determines the sex of the child?
All eggs carry X. Sperm carry X or Y.
How many chromosomes are in a human body cell and how many of these are sex chromosomes?
Which gametes can a human mother produce with respect to sex chromosomes?
A woman is XX so every egg contains one X chromosome.
A couple have three girls. What is the probability that their fourth child is a boy?
Each fertilisation is independent. A Y-sperm and X-sperm are equally likely, so the chance is always 50%.
Which sex chromosome in a sperm cell results in a male child?
A Y-carrying sperm fertilising an X egg gives XY, which is male.
How many chromosomes are in a normal human sperm cell, and how many of these are sex chromosomes?
Gametes are haploid: 23 chromosomes, including one sex chromosome (X or Y).
In a Punnett square for XX × XY, what is the ratio of female to male offspring?
Offspring are XX, XX, XY, XY, so 2 female : 2 male, which is 1:1.
Use a genetic diagram to show how the sex of a child is determined. (3 marks)
Mother XX produces eggs carrying X; father XY produces sperm carrying X or Y; offspring XX, XX, XY, XY so 50% female and 50% male.
Explain why the numbers of boys and girls born are approximately equal. (2 marks)
Equal numbers of X and Y sperm are produced; either type is equally likely to fertilise the egg, so there is a 50% chance of each sex.
A man says his wife is responsible for them having no sons. Explain why he is wrong. (2 marks)
The mother's eggs all carry an X; the sex of the child depends on whether the father's sperm carries X or Y, so the father's sperm determines sex.
A couple has three daughters. What is the probability that their next child is a son?
Each fertilisation is independent: half of sperm carry X and half carry Y.
codominance-and-blood-groups: How many alleles control the ABO blood group?
Three alleles: Iᴬ, Iᴮ and Iᴼ (multiple alleles).
A person with genotype IᴬIᴮ has blood group:
Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant, so both are expressed.
Iᴼ is recessive, so group O must be IᴼIᴼ.
Can parents with blood groups A (IᴬIᴼ) and B (IᴮIᴼ) have a child with group O? Explain.
Yes. Each parent can pass on Iᴼ, giving IᴼIᴼ, with a probability of 1 in 4.
Both alleles are expressed in the phenotype of a heterozygote
The alleles blend to form an intermediate
One allele completely hides the other
In codominance both alleles are fully expressed, as with Iᴬ and Iᴮ giving blood group AB.
A man with blood group AB and a woman with blood group O have a child. Which blood groups are possible for the child?
AB gives Iᴬ or Iᴮ, and O gives Iᴼ. Offspring are IᴬIᴼ (A) or IᴮIᴼ (B).
A child has blood group O. Their mother is group A and their father is group B. What are the parents' genotypes?
The child IᴼIᴼ must have received Iᴼ from each parent, so both parents carry an Iᴼ allele: IᴬIᴼ and IᴮIᴼ.
Parents with genotypes IᴬIᴼ and IᴮIᴼ have a child. What is the probability the child has blood group AB?
Offspring: IᴬIᴮ, IᴬIᴼ, IᴮIᴼ, IᴼIᴼ, so 1 in 4 is AB.
Which genotypes can produce blood group A?
Iᴬ is dominant to Iᴼ, so both IᴬIᴬ and IᴬIᴼ give group A.
Explain why a person with blood group A could have genotype IᴬIᴬ or IᴬIᴼ. (2 marks)
Iᴬ is dominant to Iᴼ; Iᴼ is recessive so is masked when present with Iᴬ; so both genotypes give the same phenotype of group A.
A woman with blood group AB has a child with a man of blood group AB. State the possible blood groups of the child and explain why none can be group O. (3 marks)
Child can be A, B or AB; both parents only have Iᴬ and Iᴮ alleles; group O needs two Iᴼ alleles, which neither parent carries.
Describe how codominance is shown by the inheritance of blood group AB. (2 marks)
Alleles Iᴬ and Iᴮ are both present; neither is dominant so both antigens are produced and both are expressed in the phenotype.
Which pair of parents could have children with blood group O and with blood group AB?
Each parent must carry Iᴼ (for O) and the two must carry Iᴬ and Iᴮ between them (for AB). This cross gives A, B, AB and O, each 25%.
sex-linked-inheritance: Why are sex-linked disorders like haemophilia more common in males?
Males have only one X, so one recessive allele causes the disorder
The Y chromosome carries the allele
Males have no second X carrying a dominant allele to mask the recessive one.
A carrier female for colour blindness has genotype:
She has one normal and one recessive allele, so she is unaffected but carries it.
A carrier mother (XᴴXʰ) and unaffected father (XᴴY) have a son. Probability the son has haemophilia?
Sons get Y from father and either Xᴴ or Xʰ from mother: 1 in 2.
Explain why a father cannot pass an X-linked disorder to his son.
The father passes his Y chromosome to his son, not his X. The son's X comes from his mother.
A colour-blind man (XᵇY) and a woman with normal vision who is not a carrier (XᴮXᴮ) have children. What are the daughters' genotypes?
Each daughter gets Xᵇ from her father and Xᴮ from her mother, so all are carriers.
A colour-blind woman (XᵇXᵇ) has children with a man with normal vision (XᴮY). What is expected for their sons?
Sons get Y from the father and an Xᵇ from the mother, so all sons are XᵇY and colour-blind.
Why are females far less likely than males to have an X-linked recessive disorder?
A female needs two copies of the recessive allele, whereas a male needs only one
Females have a Y chromosome that masks the allele
The allele only occurs on the Y chromosome
Females have two X chromosomes so a second, normal allele usually masks the recessive one. Males have one X and no matching allele on the Y.
A boy has haemophilia, but both his parents are unaffected. What must be true of his mother?
The boy's Xʰ came from his mother, who is unaffected, so she must be a carrier (XᴴXʰ).
A carrier woman (XᴴXʰ) and an unaffected man (XᴴY) have a child. What is the probability the child is a carrier daughter?
Offspring: XᴴXᴴ, XᴴXʰ, XᴴY, XʰY. Only XᴴXʰ is a carrier daughter, so 1 in 4.
Complete a genetic diagram for a carrier mother (XᴴXʰ) and an unaffected father (XᴴY) and state the proportion of sons with haemophilia. (4 marks)
Mother's gametes Xᴴ and Xʰ; father's gametes Xᴴ and Y; offspring XᴴXᴴ, XᴴXʰ, XᴴY, XʰY; half of the sons have haemophilia.
Explain why a woman with an X-linked recessive disorder must have inherited the allele from both parents. (2 marks)
She has genotype XʰXʰ so needs two recessive alleles; one X comes from each parent, so her father must be affected and her mother affected or a carrier.
A colour-blind man and a carrier woman have a daughter. Calculate the probability that she is colour-blind and explain your answer. (3 marks)
50% (0.5); father XᵇY always passes Xᵇ to daughters; mother XᴮXᵇ passes Xᵇ half the time, giving XᵇXᵇ.
A woman who carries haemophilia (XᴴXʰ) and an unaffected man have a son. The probability that he has haemophilia is:
Sons get their X from their mother, and half of her X chromosomes carry Xʰ. Of all children, the probability is 1/4.
variation: Which is an example of continuous variation?
Height can take any value in a range, so it is continuous.
Variation caused by the environment is:
E.g. scars, language spoken, or plant height due to light.
Most characteristics, such as body mass, are caused by:
A combination of genes and environment
Most features are influenced by both genetic and environmental factors.
Identical twins grow up in different countries and have different masses. What does this show?
Since they have identical genes, differences in mass must be caused by the environment, e.g. diet and exercise.
Tongue rolling falls into distinct categories (roller or non-roller) with no intermediates.
What is the original source of new alleles?
Mutations change DNA and can create new alleles. Meiosis and fertilisation only shuffle existing ones.
A person has a scar on their knee. This is an example of:
A scar is caused by injury, an environmental factor, and is not inherited.
Which process in sexual reproduction increases genetic variation?
Any sperm can fuse with any egg, so random fertilisation gives many new combinations of alleles.
A graph of the heights of 500 students gives a bell-shaped curve. This suggests that height is:
A continuous characteristic influenced by many genes and the environment
A bell-shaped distribution of a measurable range of values is typical of continuous variation.
Explain how sexual reproduction leads to genetic variation between offspring of the same parents. (3 marks)
Gametes are produced by meiosis, so each has a different mix of alleles; fertilisation is random so any sperm can fuse with any egg; this gives many different combinations of alleles.
Plants of the same species with identical genes are grown in different soils and differ in height. Explain what this shows. (2 marks)
Identical genes mean genetic variation is not the cause; the differences are due to environmental factors such as mineral content or water in the soil.
Describe the difference between continuous and discontinuous variation, giving one example of each. (4 marks)

Continuous variation has a range of values with no distinct categories, e.g. height; discontinuous variation has distinct categories with no intermediates, e.g. blood group; continuous is often affected by genes and environment, discontinuous mainly by genes.
Human height shows continuous variation mainly because it is:
Controlled by a single gene that has just two alleles
Controlled by many genes and also affected by the environment
Determined only by diet and not by any of a person's genes
Inherited only from the mother, through the egg cell
Discontinuous variation (such as blood group) is usually controlled by one or a few genes.
the-human-genome-project: hgp-1
The Human Genome Project aimed to:
Clone humans
Map the sequence of bases in human DNA
Cure all diseases
Count human cells
It sequenced the entire human genome.
hgp-2
A benefit of the HGP is:
Identifying genes linked to diseases
Making everyone identical
Removing all mutations
Eliminating bacteria
It helps find disease-linked genes and develop personalised medicine.
hgp-3
Give one concern about using genome information.
Discrimination by insurers or employers; stress from knowing about disease risk; privacy of genetic data.
g07-hgp-1
What is meant by the human genome?
The number of chromosomes in a gamete
All the proteins made in a human body
The entire set of genetic material (DNA) in a human cell
Only the genes that cause disease
The genome is the complete set of genetic material of an organism, including all its genes and the base sequence of its DNA.
g07-hgp-2
How has the Human Genome Project helped scientists trace human migration?
By showing all humans have identical DNA
By comparing genomes of populations to track how groups moved around the world
By finding the gene for travelling
By dating fossils
Comparing genome differences between populations allows scientists to trace how early humans migrated across the world.
g07-hgp-3
A person has their genome tested and is found to carry an allele that increases risk of a heart condition. How could this help them?
They can change lifestyle and be monitored to reduce the risk
It cures the condition
It changes their alleles
It guarantees they will get the disease
Knowing about a higher risk allows preventative lifestyle changes and early screening. It does not guarantee disease.
g07-hgp-4
Which is an advantage of knowing a patient's genome when choosing a drug?
Side effects are impossible
The patient does not need a doctor
The drug can be chosen to suit their genes, giving personalised medicine
All drugs become free
Genetic information lets doctors predict how a patient will respond to a drug and choose the most effective one.
g07-hgp-5
The Human Genome Project was completed in 2003. Which statement about the sequence it produced is correct?
It sequenced only the Y chromosome
It identified the position of every gene in one individual only
It determined the order of the roughly 3 billion base pairs and located many genes
It created a new human chromosome
The project sequenced about 3 billion base pairs of human DNA and identified the location of many genes.
g07-hgp-6
Explain how the Human Genome Project has helped in the diagnosis and treatment of inherited disorders. (3 marks)

Genes linked to inherited disorders can be identified/located; people can be tested to see if they carry the faulty allele (diagnosis, screening, risk); this allows earlier treatment or prevention and the development of targeted drugs/gene therapies.
g07-hgp-7
Give two possible disadvantages of a person's genome being sequenced and stored. (2 marks)
Insurers or employers could discriminate against people with risky alleles; stress or anxiety from learning about future disease risk; loss of privacy if the data is leaked/misused.
g07-hgp-8
Explain why the Human Genome Project involved many scientists in different countries sharing data. (2 marks)
The genome is very large (about 3 billion base pairs) so the work was shared out to finish faster; results were shared so work was not repeated and findings could be checked/validated by others.
gcse-bio-the-human-genome-project-c1
Which is a possible drawback of genome sequencing for individuals?
It will make every genetic disease curable, so medical research is no longer needed
Sequencing a person's genome permanently changes some of the genes in their cells
People could be discriminated against by insurers or employers because of genetic risks
It cannot identify any alleles that are linked to an increased risk of disease
Benefits include identifying disease-linked alleles and personalising medicines.
darwin-and-natural-selection: nat-1
In natural selection, which individuals are most likely to survive and reproduce?
The largest
Those best adapted to the environment
The oldest
Those with the most mutations
Better adapted individuals survive, reproduce and pass on their alleles.
nat-2
What is the original source of new variation in a population?
Mutation
Selective breeding
Competition
Extinction
Mutations create new alleles.
nat-3
Antibiotic resistance in bacteria is evidence for:
Selective breeding
Evolution by natural selection
Genetic engineering
Asexual reproduction only
Resistant bacteria survive treatment and reproduce, so the resistant allele becomes more common.
nat-4
Explain how a population of bacteria becomes resistant to an antibiotic.

A random mutation gives some bacteria resistance. When the antibiotic is used, non-resistant bacteria die but resistant ones survive and reproduce, passing on the resistance allele. Over generations most of the population becomes resistant.
g07-nat-1
Which of these is a key idea in Darwin's theory of natural selection?
Only large organisms survive
Organisms change during their lifetime and pass on the changes
Individuals in a population show variation, and those best suited survive and reproduce
All offspring are identical to the parent
Variation exists, some individuals are better adapted, they survive and breed, and pass on their alleles.
g07-nat-2
Why was Darwin's theory not immediately accepted by all scientists?
He had no evidence at all
It conflicted with religious beliefs and the mechanism of inheritance was not yet known
Fossils had not been discovered
He published it as a joke
Many people held religious views about creation, there was limited evidence, and the mechanism of inheritance (genes) was not understood until later.
g07-nat-3
Lamarck suggested that giraffes grew longer necks because they stretched to reach leaves and passed this on. What is wrong with this idea?
Characteristics acquired during life are not inherited; only alleles are passed on
Necks cannot get longer
Giraffes do not reproduce
Giraffes do not eat leaves
Acquired characteristics are not passed on through gametes. Natural selection acts on inherited variation.
g07-nat-4
Alfred Russel Wallace is important in the history of evolution because he:
Invented the microscope
Proposed that acquired characteristics are inherited
Discovered DNA
Independently proposed natural selection and gathered evidence on species distribution
Wallace worked out natural selection independently and collected evidence on variation and geographical distribution.
g07-nat-5
A species of moth has pale and dark forms. After industrial pollution darkens tree bark, dark moths become more common. What is the best explanation?
Dark moths ate more
Pale moths changed colour to dark
Dark moths were better camouflaged, survived predation and reproduced more
Pollution caused the dark allele to form in every moth
Selection pressure from predators favoured the dark form, so the dark allele became more frequent.
g07-nat-6
Explain how natural selection could lead to a population of rabbits having thicker fur after a series of very cold winters. (4 marks)

There is variation in fur thickness in the population (due to alleles/mutation); rabbits with thicker fur are better able to survive the cold; they survive and reproduce more; they pass on the alleles for thick fur, so over many generations the frequency of the allele increases.
g07-nat-7
Describe how a new species may form according to the theory of evolution. (3 marks)

Populations become isolated (e.g. by geography); different environments give different selection pressures; over many generations the populations change so much that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, forming new species.
g07-nat-8
Give two reasons why scientists need evidence before a new theory such as natural selection is accepted. (2 marks)
Theories must be supported by many observations/experiments; results should be repeated and checked by other scientists (peer review); evidence allows alternative ideas to be tested and rejected.
gcse-bio-darwin-and-natural-selection-c1
Which sequence correctly describes how antibiotic resistance becomes common in bacteria?
Mutation gives variation → antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria → resistant ones survive and reproduce → resistance allele becomes more common
Antibiotic causes resistance mutations → mutated bacteria survive → they reproduce → resistance allele becomes more common
Bacteria are exposed to antibiotic → they adapt during their lifetime → they pass on the acquired resistance → all become resistant
Antibiotic is used → bacteria choose to change their genes → resistant bacteria divide → the whole population becomes resistant
The antibiotic is a selection pressure; it does not cause the mutation.
evidence-for-human-evolution: Which hominid fossil, about 3.2 million years old, is known as 'Lucy'?
Lucy is an Australopithecus afarensis fossil. She walked upright.
Over time, hominid brain size has generally:
Brain volume increased from Ardi to Homo sapiens.
Stone tools can be dated by:
The rock layer (stratum) they are found in
Deeper layers are usually older. Tools also become more complex over time.
Describe how stone tools changed over time.
They became more complex and refined: from simple pebble tools to shaped hand axes to smaller, sharper tools like blades and arrowheads, suggesting increasing intelligence.
Why is the fossil record for early hominids incomplete?
Scientists only look in one country
Soft body parts decay and fossils are rarely formed and found
Fossils are always destroyed by volcanoes
Fossils form only in particular conditions and many remains decayed or have not been found, leaving gaps.
Ardipithecus ramidus ('Ardi') lived about 4.4 million years ago. What does the evidence suggest about it?
It had a brain larger than modern humans
It could walk upright and also climb trees
It was identical to Homo sapiens
Ardi's skeleton shows adaptations for both walking upright and climbing, an early stage in the evolution towards humans.
Which method is used to estimate the age of very old rocks and fossils?
Radioactive dating using decay of isotopes
Radioactive isotopes decay at a known rate, so the proportion remaining gives the age.
Which feature is a sign that a hominid fossil walked upright (bipedalism)?
The foramen magnum positioned beneath the skull
A skull whose spinal opening lies underneath indicates the head was balanced on an upright spine.
Which pairing correctly links the evidence with its use?
Stone tools: show hominid intelligence and behaviour
Stone tools show what hominids could make and do. More complex tools suggest greater intelligence.
Describe two ways in which hominid fossils show evolutionary change towards modern humans. (2 marks)
Brain size increased (larger cranial volume); skeleton adapted for walking upright; jaws and teeth became smaller; limbs/proportions changed (any two).
Explain why scientists sometimes disagree about how fossil hominids are related to each other. (3 marks)
The fossil record is incomplete and fossils are fragmentary; few specimens exist for some species; scientists interpret the same evidence differently; new discoveries can change existing ideas.
A fossil is found in a rock layer. Explain how the age of the fossil can be estimated. (2 marks)
Deeper rock layers are older, so position in strata indicates relative age; radioactive dating of isotopes in the rock gives an actual age.
Which order places these hominid fossils from oldest to youngest?

Ardi (Ardipithecus ramidus) is about 4.4 million years old, Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis) about 3.2 million and Turkana Boy (Homo erectus) about 1.6 million. Brain size and upright walking increase across these fossils.
classification: cla-1
In the five kingdom system, which kingdom contains bacteria?
Protoctista
Fungi
Prokaryotes
Plants
The five kingdoms: animals, plants, fungi, protoctists, prokaryotes.
cla-2
The three-domain system was proposed after studying:
Fossil shapes
Chemical analysis such as RNA sequences
Bird songs
Skin colour
Carl Woese's work on RNA led to the domains Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
cla-3
Which group is the most specific level of classification?
Kingdom
Family
Genus
Species
Kingdom → phylum → class → order → family → genus → species.
cla-4
Why has classification changed over time?
New technology (better microscopes, genetic analysis) revealed new evidence about how organisms are related, e.g. DNA/RNA sequences showing archaea differ from bacteria.
g07-cla-1
What is the binomial name of an organism made up of?
Its kingdom and phylum
Its common name in two languages
Its family and class
Its genus followed by its species
Binomial names use the genus (capital letter) then the species (lower case), e.g. Homo sapiens.
g07-cla-2
Which is the correct way to write the binomial name of the domestic dog?
Canis, Familiaris
canis Familiaris
Canis familiaris
CANIS FAMILIARIS
Genus starts with a capital letter, species is lower case, and the whole name is italicised or underlined.
g07-cla-3
Which is the correct order of taxonomic groups from largest to smallest?
Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
Kingdom, class, phylum, order, genus, family, species
Species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom
Phylum, kingdom, class, family, order, species, genus
The hierarchy runs kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
g07-cla-4
Which domain contains extremophile organisms that were once classed as bacteria?
Archaea
Fungi
Protoctista
Eukaryota
Archaea are single-celled prokaryotes, often found in extreme environments, now in their own domain.
g07-cla-5
Two organisms have very similar DNA sequences. What does this suggest?
They live in the same habitat
They have the same diet
They are unrelated
They share a recent common ancestor
The more similar the DNA, the more recently the organisms shared a common ancestor.
g07-cla-6
Explain why scientists use a binomial system to name organisms rather than common names. (2 marks)
Common names vary between languages and places and can refer to different species; binomial names are universal, so scientists worldwide know exactly which organism is meant.
g07-cla-7
Describe how an evolutionary tree is used to show how species are related. (3 marks)

Branches show how species split from a common ancestor; species on nearby branches are more closely related; the branching points show where the common ancestor lived; trees are made using DNA/fossil/anatomical evidence.
g07-cla-8
Name the three domains in the three-domain system and give one way in which one of them differs from the other two. (3 marks)

Archaea, Bacteria and Eukaryota (Eukarya); Eukaryota have cells with a nucleus (the others do not); Archaea and Bacteria are prokaryotes; Archaea have different RNA/membrane chemistry from bacteria (any one difference).
gcse-bio-classification-c1
The three-domain system was proposed because:
Genetic analysis (RNA sequencing) showed that archaea are very different from bacteria
Electron microscopes showed that all prokaryotic cells have the same internal structure
Genetic analysis showed that plants and animals really belong to the same kingdom
Fungi were found to be bacteria, so two of the five kingdoms had to be merged
Carl Woese split organisms into Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
selective-breeding: sbr-1
Selective breeding is:
Humans choosing parents with desired characteristics to breed
Natural selection in the wild
Inserting genes from another species
Cloning only
Humans select organisms with useful traits and breed them over many generations.
sbr-2
A disadvantage of selective breeding is:
It increases variation
It reduces the gene pool, increasing inherited disease risk
It is very fast
It always creates new species
Inbreeding reduces variation, so harmful recessive alleles and vulnerability to disease increase.
sbr-3
Which is an example of selective breeding?
Disease-resistant wheat varieties
Bacteria producing insulin
Antibiotic resistance
Plant tissue culture
Crops have been bred for yield and disease resistance.
sbr-4
Describe the steps a farmer would take to breed cows with high milk yield.
Select cows with high milk yield and a bull from high-yield parents; breed them; select the highest-yielding offspring and breed them; repeat over many generations.
g07-sbr-1
Which is an example of selective breeding in animals?
Injecting growth hormone into a calf
Cloning a cell
Adding a jellyfish gene to a pig
Breeding sheep that produce more wool
Selective breeding is choosing parents with desired characteristics, such as high wool yield.
g07-sbr-2
Why does selective breeding take many generations to produce a desired result?
Each animal must be cloned
Mutations must be switched off
Alleles must be gradually increased in frequency by repeated selection
It requires special equipment
Only a small improvement may be passed on each generation, so repeated selection is needed.
g07-sbr-3
A dog breed has a high rate of a genetic disease. What is the most likely cause?
The dogs are too well fed
Too much variation in the gene pool
Inbreeding has increased the frequency of harmful recessive alleles
Natural selection
Breeding closely related individuals reduces variation and raises the chance of two copies of a harmful recessive allele.
g07-sbr-4
Wheat farmers want a crop that is both high-yielding and resistant to a fungal disease. What should they do?
Cross plants with each trait and select offspring showing both
Use only the tallest plants
Spray fungicide every day
Plant seeds of one plant only
Breed plants with each desired trait, then select offspring with both and repeat the process.
g07-sbr-5
Which of these is a likely benefit of selective breeding in crops?
Higher yield or improved disease resistance
Immediate results
It creates entirely new genes
Greater genetic variation
Crops are bred to improve yield, disease resistance or other useful traits.
g07-sbr-6
Explain why a population produced by selective breeding may be at risk from a new disease. (3 marks)
Selective breeding reduces the gene pool/variation; individuals are genetically similar; if a new disease appears, few or no individuals may carry resistance alleles, so many could die.
g07-sbr-7
Describe how selective breeding differs from natural selection. (2 marks)

In selective breeding humans choose which individuals breed for characteristics useful to humans; in natural selection the environment determines which individuals survive and reproduce, favouring survival.
g07-sbr-8
Give two characteristics that might be selected for in a domestic animal or crop, and one reason each is useful. (3 marks)
Any two with reasons, e.g. high milk yield (more milk to sell); disease resistance (less loss/medication); large fruit (more food per plant); docile nature (safer to handle).
gcse-bio-selective-breeding-c1
A risk of intensive selective breeding in dogs is that:
Genes from other species are added, which can cause unexpected new diseases in the breed
Offspring of closely related parents are always sterile, so the breed soon dies out
It increases genetic variation, so the breed's appearance becomes unpredictable
Inbreeding reduces the gene pool, so harmful recessive alleles are more likely to be expressed
Breeding closely related individuals raises the chance of inheriting two copies of a harmful allele.
genetic-engineering: Changing an organism's genome, often by adding a gene from another organism
A gene is transferred into an organism's DNA to give it a new characteristic.
Which enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences?
Which enzyme joins a gene into a plasmid?
DNA ligase joins sticky ends together.
What is a vector in genetic engineering?
Something that carries the gene into the host cell, e.g. a plasmid
Plasmids or viruses are used as vectors.
Describe how bacteria can be engineered to produce human insulin.

Cut the insulin gene out of human DNA with a restriction enzyme; cut a plasmid with the same enzyme to leave matching sticky ends; join them with ligase; insert the recombinant plasmid into bacteria; grow the bacteria in fermenters and extract the insulin.
Golden rice has been genetically engineered to help prevent which problem?
Genes were added so the rice grain produces beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A, reducing blindness in areas where rice is the staple food.
An organism that contains a gene transferred from a different species is described as:
Transgenic organisms contain genes from another species, inserted using genetic engineering.
What are 'sticky ends' in genetic engineering?
Regions where ligase has joined two fragments
The ends of a plasmid that attach to the cell membrane
Short single-stranded overhangs left when a restriction enzyme cuts DNA
Restriction enzymes cut DNA leaving short unpaired bases. Complementary sticky ends on the gene and plasmid can pair up, then ligase seals them.
Why is the same restriction enzyme used to cut both the human gene and the plasmid?
It stops the bacteria rejecting the gene
It makes the plasmid replicate faster
It produces complementary sticky ends that can join together
The same enzyme cuts at the same base sequence, giving matching complementary sticky ends so the gene fits into the plasmid.
Which is a benefit of using bacteria to make human insulin rather than extracting it from pigs?
The insulin is a different shape so works better
Large quantities can be made cheaply and it is identical to human insulin
Bacteria divide rapidly and the insulin produced is the human protein, so fewer side effects and no animals needed.
Describe what is meant by genetic engineering. (2 marks)
Changing the genome of an organism; by transferring a gene (from another species) into its DNA to give it a desired characteristic.
Give two reasons some people are concerned about genetically engineering crops or animals. (2 marks)

Transferred genes might spread to wild plants/species; may harm other organisms or biodiversity; unknown long-term effects on human health; ethical concerns about interfering with nature; seeds/patents controlled by companies (any two).
A gene for herbicide resistance is inserted into a crop plant. Explain how this could benefit a farmer. (3 marks)
Farmer can spray herbicide to kill weeds; the crop plants survive because they are resistant; less competition from weeds for light, water and minerals so higher yield.
In making bacteria that produce human insulin, which enzymes are used?
Ligase to cut DNA leaving sticky ends, and restriction enzymes to join the gene into the plasmid
Amylase to cut the plasmid open, and lipase to join the insulin gene into the plasmid
Proteases to cut out the insulin gene, and ligase to make the insulin protein from it
Restriction enzymes to cut DNA leaving sticky ends, and ligase to join the gene into the plasmid
The plasmid acts as a vector carrying the gene into the bacterium.
plant-tissue-culture: ptc-1
Tissue culture produces plants that are:
Genetically different
Clones of the parent
Always sterile
Hybrids
Small pieces of tissue grow into genetically identical plants.
ptc-2
Why must tissue culture be done in aseptic conditions?
To speed up photosynthesis
To prevent contamination by microorganisms
To increase variation
To make the plants smaller
Microbes would grow on the nutrient medium and kill the explants.
ptc-3
Give two advantages of plant tissue culture.
Large numbers of identical plants quickly; desirable traits preserved; can grow plants all year; preserves rare/endangered species; disease-free plants.
g08-ptc-1
In tissue culture, the small piece of plant tissue used to start the culture is called the:
Vector
Scion
Explant
Plasmid
An explant is a small piece of tissue (often from the shoot tip) placed on nutrient medium.
g08-ptc-2
Which hormones are added to the growth medium to encourage cells to divide and form roots and shoots?
Gibberellin only
Insulin
Auxins and cytokinins
Adrenaline
Plant growth substances such as auxins and cytokinins control cell division and differentiation in the culture.
g08-ptc-3
Why do growers often use tissue culture to propagate a rare orchid?
It creates new varieties
It makes plants resistant to disease by mutation
It produces many identical plants quickly from very little tissue
It increases genetic variation
Many clones can be made from a small amount of tissue, helping conservation of rare species.
g08-ptc-4
A disadvantage of producing crops by tissue culture is that:
A single new disease could wipe out all the genetically identical plants
The plants grow too slowly
The plants are always infertile
The plants cannot photosynthesise
Clones have no genetic variation, so they are all equally susceptible to the same pathogen.
g08-ptc-5
Which step is needed to make sure the explant and medium stay sterile?
Exposing it to UV light for days
Keeping the culture in the dark
Adding extra fertiliser
Sterilising equipment and working with aseptic technique
Microbes grow quickly on nutrient agar and would outcompete or kill the explants, so sterile technique is essential.
g08-ptc-6
Describe the main steps in producing new plants by tissue culture. (4 marks)

Take a small piece of tissue (explant) from the parent plant; sterilise it; place it on sterile nutrient medium (agar) containing growth hormones; incubate in suitable conditions; cells divide to form a mass then shoots and roots; transfer the plantlets to compost.
g08-ptc-7
Explain why tissue culture plants are genetically identical to the parent plant. (2 marks)
Cells divide by mitosis; so each new cell has the same genes as the parent cell, no gametes or fertilisation involved.
g08-ptc-8
Suggest two advantages of tissue culture over growing plants from seed for a commercial grower. (2 marks)
Many identical plants of a desired trait quickly; can be done all year round; takes up little space; plants are disease-free if the tissue is clean; seedless varieties can be propagated (any two).
gcse-bio-plant-tissue-culture-c1
Why must aseptic technique be used in plant tissue culture?
Microorganisms would grow on the nutrient medium and kill or outcompete the plant tissue
Plant tissue needs completely sterile soil before it can grow any roots
Contamination makes the clones genetically different from the parent plant
Microorganisms on the tissue would stop it photosynthesising in the light
The medium contains sugars and nutrients that microbes also use.
biological-control-and-gm-crops: bio-1
Biological control means:
Using chemical pesticides
Using a natural predator or parasite to control a pest
Genetically modifying crops
Burning crops
E.g. ladybirds eating aphids.
bio-2
Bt crops have been modified to:
Grow faster
Produce a toxin that kills insect pests
Resist drought
Make vitamin A
A gene from Bacillus thuringiensis makes a toxin harmful to insect larvae.
bio-3
A risk of biological control is:
The control organism may become a pest itself
It pollutes water
It builds up in food chains
It is a chemical
E.g. cane toads in Australia spread and harmed native species.
bio-4
Give one advantage and one concern about GM crops.

Advantages: higher yields, pest/herbicide resistance, extra nutrients, less pesticide use. Concerns: genes could spread to wild plants; reduced biodiversity; unknown long-term health effects; seed cost for farmers.
g08-bgm-1
Which is an example of biological control?
Adding nitrate fertiliser
Spraying crops with insecticide
Releasing parasitic wasps to kill whitefly in a greenhouse
Ploughing weeds into the soil
Biological control uses living organisms, such as parasites or predators, to reduce pest numbers.
g08-bgm-2
A benefit of biological control compared with chemical pesticides is that it:
Works instantly
Does not leave toxic chemical residues in the environment
Completely removes the pest
Is always cheaper
No chemicals build up in food chains, although control is usually slower and rarely wipes out the pest entirely.
g08-bgm-3
Herbicide-resistant GM crops allow farmers to:
Avoid planting seeds
Stop crops needing water
Prevent insect attack
Spray weeds without killing the crop
The inserted gene makes the crop tolerant to the herbicide, which kills only the weeds.
g08-bgm-4
Why might biological control be less effective than pesticides at first?
Pests become immune to predators in one day
Predators cannot eat insects
Predators need time to build up their numbers
Predators are poisonous to crops
The predator or parasite population takes time to grow, and a small pest population will always remain to feed it.
g08-bgm-5
A concern with GM crops is that:
They need more fertiliser than ever
Their DNA cannot be digested
Inserted genes could spread to wild relatives by cross-pollination
They never produce seeds
Gene transfer to wild plants could create herbicide-resistant weeds or affect biodiversity.
g08-bgm-6
Explain how Bt maize can increase crop yield. (3 marks)
Contains a gene from Bacillus thuringiensis; produces a toxin that kills insect pests that eat the plant; less damage to the crop so higher yield (and less insecticide needed).
g08-bgm-7
Give two disadvantages of using biological control. (2 marks)
Slow to work; pest is not completely eliminated; introduced organism may become a pest itself or harm native species; may not suit all conditions; hard to predict effects on the ecosystem (any two).
g08-bgm-8
Evaluate the use of GM crops to feed a growing population. (4 marks)

Advantages: higher yields, resistance to pests/disease/drought, added nutrients, less pesticide used; Concerns: gene flow to wild plants, effects on biodiversity, unknown long-term health effects, cost/patents for farmers; conclusion weighing the evidence.
gcse-bio-biological-control-and-gm-crops-c1
A risk of growing Bt maize (which produces an insect toxin) over large areas is that:
The maize will stop photosynthesising
Humans will become resistant to insects
Insect pests may evolve resistance to the Bt toxin
The toxin will make the maize grow too fast
Strong selection pressure favours rare resistant insects.
health-and-types-of-disease: A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being
Health is more than just not being ill.
A communicable disease is one that:
Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and can be transmitted.
CHD is not caused by a pathogen and cannot be passed on.
Explain why HIV can make a person more likely to catch other diseases.
HIV attacks white blood cells (T cells), weakening the immune system, so other pathogens are not destroyed as effectively.
Which of the following is a non-communicable disease?
Type 2 diabetes is not caused by a pathogen and cannot be passed between people.
How can poor mental health affect physical health?
It only affects the nervous system
Stress can weaken the immune system and make infections more likely
Physical, mental and social health interact, so a problem in one can lead to problems in another.
Which factor does NOT directly increase the risk of a non-communicable disease?
Vaccination protects against communicable disease; the others are lifestyle risk factors for diseases such as cancer, CHD and liver disease.
A person with a poor diet becomes malnourished and then catches infections more often. This is an example of:
A communicable disease causing a non-communicable one
A non-communicable condition making a person more vulnerable to a communicable disease
Malnutrition weakens the immune system, so infections are more likely.
Which statement about the causes of disease is correct?
Many diseases have multiple causes, including genes, lifestyle and environment
Cancer is always caused by a virus
All diseases are caused by pathogens
Diseases such as cancer and CHD result from combinations of risk factors.
Explain why people living in poorer countries may be more at risk of both communicable and non-communicable diseases. (3 marks)

Poor sanitation/clean water and crowding spread pathogens; less access to vaccines and healthcare; malnutrition weakens immunity and causes deficiency diseases; poor diet or limited health education can raise risk of non-communicable disease.
Describe what is meant by a communicable disease and give one example. (2 marks)
A disease caused by a pathogen that can be passed from one organism to another; e.g. measles, cholera, TB, malaria (any valid example).
Explain how smoking can lead to a person developing a communicable disease more easily. (2 marks)
Damages cilia and lung lining so mucus and pathogens are not removed; increases risk of lung infection such as pneumonia or TB.
People with HIV are more likely to develop tuberculosis because:
HIV destroys white blood cells, weakening the immune system
HIV and TB are the same pathogen at different stages of infection
TB is a non-communicable disease that HIV triggers in the lungs
HIV damages lung tissue directly, letting TB bacteria grow there
Having one disease can increase the risk of another.
pathogens-and-communicable-diseases: Which disease is caused by a protist?
Malaria is caused by the protist Plasmodium, spread by mosquitoes.
TB is a bacterial disease affecting the lungs.
Chalara ash dieback is caused by a:
A fungus that kills ash trees, causing leaf loss and bark lesions.
Ebola is a virus causing internal bleeding (haemorrhagic fever).
Name the pathogen that causes stomach ulcers and how it spreads.
Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium spread by oral transmission, e.g. contaminated food or water.
Which disease is caused by a virus and produces a red skin rash and fever?
Measles virus spreads by droplets; symptoms include fever and a red rash, and complications can include pneumonia or brain damage.
Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) affects plants by:
Forming a mosaic pattern of discolouration that reduces photosynthesis
Discoloured patches have less chlorophyll, so less photosynthesis and poorer growth.
Which of these is a bacterial disease passed on by sexual contact?
Gonorrhoea is bacterial, with symptoms including a thick yellow or green discharge and pain on urinating; it is treated with antibiotics, though resistant strains have appeared.
Rose black spot is caused by a:
The fungus produces black spots on leaves, which turn yellow and drop early, reducing photosynthesis.
Which is the correct pairing of a disease and its type of pathogen?
Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a protist. Salmonella and cholera are bacterial; HIV is a virus.
Describe how the malaria protist is spread and how the spread can be reduced. (4 marks)

Mosquito is a vector; it picks up Plasmodium when feeding on infected blood and passes it on when biting another person; reduce by mosquito nets; insect repellent/insecticide; draining standing water where mosquitoes breed; antimalarial drugs.
Explain how HIV leads to AIDS. (3 marks)
HIV infects and destroys white blood cells (T helper cells); immune system becomes severely weakened over time; the body cannot fight other infections or cancers, which is AIDS.
Salmonella food poisoning is a bacterial disease. State two symptoms and two ways of reducing its spread. (4 marks)
Symptoms: fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting, diarrhoea (any two); prevention: cook meat and eggs thoroughly; wash hands and utensils; store food correctly/refrigerate; vaccinate poultry (any two).
Which correctly matches the disease with its pathogen type and how it spreads?
Chalara ash dieback: bacterium, spread by water
Cholera is a bacterium in water; ash dieback is a fungus spread by wind; TB is a bacterium spread in the air.
how-pathogens-spread: Cholera bacteria spread through water contaminated with faeces.
Which is the best way to reduce the spread of TB?
Avoid crowded spaces and isolate infected people
Chlamydia is a sexually transmitted bacterium.
Explain why washing hands reduces the spread of disease.
It removes pathogens from the hands so they are not transferred to food, surfaces, or into the body via the mouth, nose or eyes.
Malaria is spread from person to person by:
A vector, the female Anopheles mosquito
The malaria pathogen (a protist) is carried between people by mosquitoes, which are vectors.
Which pair correctly matches a disease with how it is spread?
Salmonella food poisoning, undercooked or contaminated food
Salmonella bacteria are spread in undercooked poultry, eggs and other contaminated food. Measles is airborne, HIV passes through body fluids and cholera through contaminated water.
Which action is most effective at reducing the spread of an airborne virus in a school?
Covering the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing
Airborne viruses spread in droplets, so covering the mouth and nose reduces the number of pathogens released.
Exchange of body fluids such as blood during unprotected sex or by sharing needles
HIV is transmitted by direct exchange of body fluids. It is not spread through the air or by casual contact.
A sudden outbreak of cholera follows a flood that damages sewage pipes. Why does the disease spread quickly?
Faeces containing cholera bacteria contaminate drinking water
The bacteria become airborne in wet weather
Cholera is a waterborne disease, so sewage mixing with drinking water spreads the bacteria rapidly.
Explain how the rate of spread of a communicable disease could be reduced in a crowded city. (3 marks)

Isolate infected people so they cannot pass on the pathogen; vaccinate people so fewer are susceptible; improve hygiene, e.g. hand washing and clean water/sewage treatment; control vectors or use barriers such as condoms; (any three with a link to reducing transmission).
What is meant by a vector? Give one example of a disease it spreads. (2 marks)
An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another without usually being harmed/without causing the disease itself; example: mosquito spreading malaria.
Describe how the number of cases of a disease spread by mosquitoes could be reduced. (3 marks)
Drain standing water/destroy breeding sites; use insecticides; use mosquito nets over beds; use repellents or screens; introduce predators of mosquito larvae; (any three).
Which measure best reduces the spread of malaria?
Washing hands with soap before meals and after using the toilet
Boiling all drinking water and cooking food thoroughly before eating it
Using insecticide-treated nets and draining standing water where mosquitoes breed
Wearing face masks in crowded places and covering coughs and sneezes
Controlling the vector breaks the transmission chain.
plant-diseases-and-defences: pdd-1
Which is a physical plant defence?
Antibacterial chemicals
Waxy cuticle
Poisons
Hormones
The waxy cuticle and cellulose cell walls are physical barriers.
pdd-2
Plants can be identified as diseased by:
Stunted growth, spots or discoloured leaves
Faster growth
More flowers
Larger roots
Visible symptoms help diagnosis, alongside lab tests.
pdd-3
A plant lacking magnesium ions would show:
Chlorosis (yellow leaves)
Stunted growth only
Extra flowers
Thick roots
Magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll.
pdd-4
Describe two ways scientists can identify a plant disease.
Observe symptoms; compare with a reference/gardening manual; send samples to a lab; use monoclonal antibody testing kits; analyse DNA of the pathogen; check distribution of affected plants.
g09-plant-1
Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) affects plants by:
Making leaves curl due to insects
Causing purple or black spots on leaves
Producing a mosaic pattern of discolouration so photosynthesis is reduced
Causing roots to rot
TMV leaves a mosaic of light and dark patches. Reduced chlorophyll means less photosynthesis and stunted growth.
g09-plant-2
Rose black spot is caused by a:
Virus
Bacterium
Fungus
Protist
Black spot is a fungal disease. Spores spread by wind and water, and treatment includes fungicides and removing infected leaves.
g09-plant-3
A gardener finds yellow leaves and stunted growth on a plant. A lab test shows low nitrate ions in the soil. Why does nitrate deficiency stunt growth?
Nitrates are needed to make amino acids and proteins
Nitrates are used in respiration to release energy
Nitrates make cell walls from cellulose
Nitrates are needed to make starch for storage
Plants use nitrate ions to make amino acids and so proteins for growth. Magnesium is the ion needed for chlorophyll.
g09-plant-4
Which of these is a chemical plant defence?
Antibacterial compounds in the leaves
Layers of dead cells in bark
Thorns
Leaves that fold when touched

A deficiency symptom
A chemical defence
Mimicry to deter herbivores or egg-laying insects
A cuticle

Symptoms such as a mosaic pattern differ from deficiency symptoms; send samples to a laboratory/use testing kits (monoclonal antibodies) to detect the pathogen; compare with a gardening manual; test the soil for mineral ions and add fertiliser to see if symptoms improve.

Explain how the waxy cuticle and cell walls protect a plant from disease. (2 marks)
They are physical barriers; pathogens cannot easily get through them into the plant cells / the cuticle also stops water collecting where pathogens could grow.

Explain why aphids can cause serious damage to crop plants. (3 marks)
Aphids pierce phloem and feed on sugars; this removes sugars/nutrients needed for growth; they can transmit viruses/pathogens; wounds allow pathogens to enter; so yield falls.

A thick waxy cuticle on the surface of the leaves
Strong cellulose cell walls around every cell
Producing antiseptic or antibacterial substances
Layers of dead cells forming bark on the stems

Mucus traps pathogens. Cilia waft it to the throat to be swallowed.

It is a physical barrier; damaged skin forms scabs; it secretes antimicrobial substances; and it hosts harmless microbes that compete with pathogens.

Ciliated cells move mucus and trapped microbes up to the throat where they are swallowed.

Forming a clot that dries to a scab
Platelets trigger clotting, forming a scab that seals the wound.

Hydrochloric acid in the stomach provides a pH low enough to destroy most microorganisms in food and drink.

Hairs trap particles/pathogens; mucus traps pathogens (and contains enzymes); cilia move the mucus away from the lungs.
Tears and saliva contain lysozyme. Explain how this helps protect the body. (2 marks)
Lysozyme is an enzyme that breaks down the cell walls of bacteria; this kills the bacteria so they cannot infect the eyes or mouth.

Blood vessels leak; platelets clump and trigger clotting; a clot forms and dries to a scab; the scab acts as a barrier so pathogens cannot enter; it also stops blood loss.
Lysozyme in tears protects against infection by:
Lysozyme is an enzyme; stomach acid and mucus are other barriers.

A protein on the surface of a pathogen that the immune system recognises
A type of white blood cell
Antigens are unique molecules that trigger an immune response.

Memory cells quickly produce large numbers of antibodies.

A specific lymphocyte recognises the antigen, divides rapidly (clones), and produces antibodies that bind to the antigen; memory lymphocytes are also produced.
A phagocyte destroys a pathogen by:
Phagocytosis means the white blood cell engulfs the pathogen and digests it with enzymes.
Antitoxins are produced by white blood cells and bind to toxins to neutralise them.
Why can an antibody for one pathogen not be used against another?
Antibodies are only made after vaccination
The antibody shape is complementary to one specific antigen
Other pathogens do not have antigens
Each antibody has a shape that fits only one antigen, so a different pathogen with different antigens needs different antibodies.

They remain in the body and produce antibodies quickly if the same antigen is met again
Memory cells give a faster, larger secondary response to the same antigen.
A person is infected by a pathogen for the first time. What happens to the antibody concentration in their blood compared to a second infection with the same pathogen?
It rises slowly and to a lower level the first time
It is the same each time
It does not rise the first time
It rises faster and higher the first time
The primary response is slower and smaller because memory cells are not yet present.

Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies specific to the antigen; antibodies bind to the pathogen and help destroy it/cause clumping; antitoxins neutralise toxins; memory cells provide future immunity.
Explain why a person who has recovered from chickenpox is unlikely to get it again. (3 marks)
Memory lymphocytes remain after infection; they recognise the same antigen if the virus re-enters; they quickly produce large numbers of antibodies so the virus is destroyed before symptoms develop.
A person catches a new strain of flu even though they had flu last year. Explain why. (2 marks)
The new strain has different antigens; memory cells for last year's strain do not recognise them / antibodies are not complementary, so a new primary response is needed.
People rarely get chickenpox twice but can catch flu many times. The main reason is that:
Flu viruses change their antigens often, so memory lymphocytes no longer recognise them
Chickenpox is caused by bacteria, which the body can remember, but flu is caused by a virus
Flu viruses have no antigens, so lymphocytes cannot make antibodies against them
Memory lymphocytes form only after chickenpox, never after an infection with flu
Memory lymphocytes recognise a specific antigen; new strains need new responses.

Antibiotics
Antibodies only

If enough people are vaccinated, the disease spreads less, protecting the unvaccinated
Everyone gets ill together
Vaccines work instantly

Killing pathogens directly
Causing production of memory lymphocytes
Replacing red blood cells
Blocking all antigens
Memory cells give a fast secondary response on future infection.

Advantages: prevents disease, can control epidemics, herd immunity. Disadvantages: side effects (usually mild), doesn't always give immunity, some people can't be vaccinated.
g09-vacc-1
Why are booster vaccinations sometimes given?
To replace white blood cells
To kill any remaining pathogens
To increase memory cell numbers and antibody levels for longer protection
To provide antibiotics
A second dose stimulates a secondary response, creating more memory cells and longer-lasting immunity.
g09-vacc-2
The flu vaccine has to be updated every year because:
The vaccine loses its effect in storage
Flu viruses mutate so antigens change
Flu is caused by bacteria
Antibodies last only a week
Mutations change the surface antigens of the virus, so memory cells from the previous vaccine may not recognise the new strain.

Which is a reason some people cannot be vaccinated and rely on herd immunity?
Vaccines only work on children
They are immune to all diseases
Herd immunity makes vaccines unnecessary for everyone
They have a weakened immune system or an allergy to a vaccine ingredient
Some individuals cannot safely have vaccines. If most others are vaccinated, the pathogen is less likely to reach them.

Why do vaccines contain dead or weakened pathogens rather than live, harmful ones?
They work as antibiotics
They make antibodies directly
They are cheaper to make
They still carry antigens but cannot cause the disease
The antigens stimulate lymphocytes to produce antibodies and memory cells without causing the illness.

Nothing can be concluded
Herd immunity is reached because the number is over 95%

Herd immunity is reached because the number is over 80%
17 800 ÷ 20 000 × 100 = 89%, which is below the 95% needed, so the disease could still spread.
g09-vacc-6
Explain how a vaccine gives protection against a disease. (4 marks)

The vaccine contains dead/weakened pathogens or antigens; lymphocytes recognise the antigen; they produce antibodies and memory cells; if the live pathogen is met later, memory cells rapidly produce large amounts of antibodies, so the pathogen is destroyed before it makes the person ill.
g09-vacc-7
Explain why a high vaccination rate protects people who are not vaccinated. (3 marks)
Fewer people are susceptible; the pathogen is less likely to be passed on/chains of transmission are broken; this is herd immunity, so unvaccinated people are less likely to be exposed.
g09-vacc-8
Suggest why some parents choose not to vaccinate their children, and explain a possible consequence for the population. (3 marks)

Fear of side effects or belief in unproven risks; vaccination rate falls below the level needed for herd immunity; disease spreads more easily so outbreaks and epidemics occur, harming those who cannot be vaccinated.

The pathogen dies out immediately once a few people are vaccinated
When most people are immune, the pathogen has few hosts to spread through
The vaccine spreads from vaccinated people to others by touch

antibiotics: Antibiotics kill or inhibit bacteria. They do not affect viruses.
Why can't antibiotics treat viral infections?
Viruses live inside host cells and lack the structures antibiotics target
Viruses reproduce inside cells, so antibiotics cannot target them without harming body cells.
Which reduces the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria?
Only prescribing antibiotics when needed and finishing the course
Adding antibiotics to all animal feed
Overuse and incomplete courses let resistant bacteria survive and spread.
Explain why it is important to finish a course of antibiotics.
To kill all the bacteria; stopping early may leave the most resistant bacteria alive to reproduce, increasing resistance.
Who first noticed that a mould (Penicillium) killed bacteria growing on an agar plate?
Alexander Fleming observed that bacteria did not grow near the Penicillium mould, leading to the discovery of penicillin.
How do antibiotic-resistant strains of bacteria arise?
Antibiotics cause the bacteria to digest themselves
Resistant bacteria are made by the patient's white blood cells
The bacteria choose to become resistant
A random mutation gives resistance and the resistant bacteria survive and reproduce when antibiotics are used
Mutation produces a resistant allele; antibiotic use is a selection pressure so resistant bacteria survive, reproduce and pass on resistance.
Why is MRSA difficult to treat?
It is resistant to many antibiotics
MRSA is a strain of bacteria resistant to methicillin and many other antibiotics.
Which of these is the best treatment for a person with a headache caused by a cold virus?
A painkiller to relieve the symptoms
Painkillers relieve symptoms but do not kill pathogens; antibiotics do not work against viruses.
A culture of bacteria doubles in number every 20 minutes. Starting with 200 bacteria, how many are there after 2 hours (assuming no resistance and no deaths)?
Explain how the overuse of antibiotics has led to an increase in antibiotic-resistant bacteria. (4 marks)

Random mutations in bacteria produce some resistant individuals; antibiotics kill non-resistant bacteria; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce; they pass on the resistance allele so the proportion of resistant bacteria in the population increases (natural selection).
Describe an experiment using agar plates to test which of two antibiotics is more effective against a bacterium. (4 marks)

Spread a culture of the bacterium evenly over sterile agar; place paper discs soaked in each antibiotic (and a control disc with no antibiotic) on the plate; seal loosely, incubate at about 25 °C (not body temperature, to avoid harmful pathogens); the larger clear zone (zone of inhibition) shows the more effective antibiotic.
Suggest two ways that doctors and the public can help slow the spread of antibiotic resistance. (2 marks)

Doctors should not prescribe antibiotics for viral infections or minor infections; patients should complete the full course; use of antibiotics in farming should be restricted; develop new antibiotics; good hygiene to reduce spread of resistant strains. (any two)
Why are antibiotics not prescribed for colds?
Colds are caused by bacteria that are too small
Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics only act on bacteria
Unnecessary antibiotic use also increases selection for resistant bacteria.

What is the first stage of testing a new drug?
Testing on patients
Preclinical testing on cells, tissues and animals
Selling it
Testing on volunteers with high doses
Drugs are tested in the lab for toxicity and efficacy before human trials.
dnm-2
In a double-blind trial:
Only patients don't know who gets the drug
Neither patients nor doctors know who gets the drug or placebo
Everyone knows
Only animals are used

dnm-3
A placebo is:
A stronger dose
A substance that looks like the drug but has no active effect
A vaccine
An antibiotic
Placebos allow comparison to show the drug's real effect.
dnm-4
Why is a new drug tested on healthy volunteers first, at low doses?
To check it is safe and find any side effects before testing efficacy on patients.

Which medicine was originally discovered in the bark of the willow tree?
Digitalis

Penicillin
Aspirin was developed from salicylic acid found in willow bark.

Which drug, used to treat heart conditions, comes from the foxglove plant?

Statin
Digitalis
Aspirin
Digitalis comes from foxgloves and is used for heart problems.

Why do scientists publish their drug trial results in peer-reviewed journals?

To make the drug cheaper
So other experts can check the methods and conclusions before they are accepted
So the drug can be sold immediately
Peer review is checking by independent experts to ensure the work is valid and reliable.

Why must a clinical trial use a large number of patients?

To reduce the effect of chance and individual differences so results are reliable
To make sure everyone gets the drug
To avoid using a placebo
Larger samples make results more representative and more reliable.

Drugs must be thoroughly tested, including effects on pregnancy, before being licensed
Placebos are unnecessary
Only healthy volunteers should be used
Drugs should never be tested on animals
The tragedy led to much stricter testing, including effects on unborn babies, before drugs are approved.

g10-dnm-7

Preclinical tests on cells, tissues and live animals to check toxicity, efficacy and dose; clinical trials on healthy volunteers at low doses to check safety; trials on patients to find the optimum dose and efficacy; use of double-blind trials with a placebo; results peer reviewed before the drug is licensed.
g10-dnm-8

For: avoids harming humans and gives information on whole-body effects that cell cultures cannot show; against: causes suffering to animals, and animals may react differently from humans.

Why are clinical trials often double-blind?
So the drug can be tested on animals and on human cells at the same time
So the drug is given only to healthy volunteers before any patients
So neither patients nor doctors know who receives the drug, removing bias
So the trial costs less, because fewer patients are needed for results
A placebo group allows the drug's real effect to be measured.

Inject a mouse with the antigen; lymphocytes that produce the specific antibody are collected; fused with tumour cells to form hybridoma cells; hybridoma cells are cultured, divide rapidly and secrete large amounts of the identical antibody, which is collected and purified.

Cancer cells have specific antigens (tumour markers) on their surface; the antibody is made specific to that antigen so it binds only to cancer cells; the drug attached to the antibody is delivered only to those cells, so healthy cells are not harmed.
g10-mab-8

Smoking, high fat diet, obesity and lack of exercise increase risk.

Alcohol damages liver cells, causing scarring.

A cancer that has spread to other organs

A growth of abnormal cells that stays in one place and does not invade other tissues

Ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays), UV light, tar in tobacco smoke and some viruses can cause mutations leading to cancer.

Costs to health services of treating long-term illnesses; people unable to work causing lost income and reduced productivity; families lose earnings and may need to provide care, causing stress.

Lifestyle: smoking, obesity, alcohol, UV exposure from sunbeds or sunbathing, poor diet; genetic: inherited faulty alleles such as BRCA1 and BRCA2 for breast cancer.

Anticoagulants such as warfarin make blood clot less easily, reducing the risk of heart attack and stroke.

Statins lower blood cholesterol but can have side effects, and they must be taken for a long time.

An animal such as a pig or cow

The valve makes blood too thin
To stop the immune system attacking the valve

Which is a disadvantage of statins compared with stents?

They are often rejected by the immune system soon after they are given
They only work in children, so most adult patients cannot use them
Statins lower blood cholesterol; stents open a blocked artery but involve a procedure with risks.

What is the word equation for photosynthesis?
Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water, with light energy, to make glucose and oxygen.

Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.

Xylem carries water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves.
What substance strengthens the walls of xylem vessels?
Lignin makes the walls rigid and waterproof, and supports the plant.
Which is a function of companion cells in the phloem?
Companion cells have many mitochondria that supply energy (ATP) for active loading of sucrose into sieve tubes.
Water enters a root hair cell by osmosis because the cell sap has:
A lower water potential than the soil
The same water potential as the soil
A higher water potential than the soil
The cell sap is more concentrated, so water moves from the soil (higher water potential) into the cell.
Phloem sieve tube cells have few organelles and holes in their end walls. What is the benefit of this?
Increases the size of the nucleus
Lets sucrose solution flow easily between cells
Sieve plates and reduced contents allow easy flow of dissolved sugars.
Describe the path taken by water from the soil to the air through a plant. (4 marks)
Absorbed by osmosis into root hair cells; moves across the root to the xylem; travels up the xylem to the leaf; evaporates from mesophyll cells and diffuses out through the stomata (transpiration).
Explain why root hair cells have many mitochondria. (2 marks)
Mineral ions are absorbed by active transport against the concentration gradient; which needs energy from respiration released in mitochondria.
Explain two ways in which xylem vessels are adapted for their function. (4 marks)

No end walls between cells so form a continuous hollow tube; allows continuous flow of water; walls thickened with lignin; provide strength and stop vessels collapsing under tension / support the plant; dead cells with no cytoplasm so no obstruction.
Which statement correctly compares xylem and phloem?
Xylem vessels are living, with companion cells; phloem sieve tubes are dead and strengthened with lignin
Both are made of living cells, but only xylem has companion cells to supply it with energy
Xylem carries sucrose in both directions; phloem carries water upwards from the roots
Xylem vessels are dead and strengthened with lignin; phloem sieve tubes are living, with companion cells
Xylem carries water and minerals upwards; phloem carries sucrose in both directions.
transpiration: trn-1
Transpiration is:
The loss of water vapour from leaves
The movement of sugars
Absorption of light
Root growth
Water evaporates and diffuses out through stomata.
trn-2
Which conditions increase the rate of transpiration?
Cold and humid
Warm, windy and dry
Dark and still
Cold and still
Higher temperature, wind, low humidity and bright light all increase transpiration.
trn-3
What controls the opening and closing of stomata?
Root hair cells
Guard cells
Phloem
Xylem
Guard cells become turgid to open the stoma, flaccid to close it.
trn-4
Which apparatus measures water uptake by a shoot?
Calorimeter
Potometer
Quadrat
Respirometer
A potometer measures how fast an air bubble moves as the shoot takes up water.
trn-5
An air bubble in a potometer moves 30 mm in 5 minutes. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm/min.
30 ÷ 5 = 6 mm/min
g12-trn-1
Which statement best describes the transpiration stream?
Sugars moving from leaves to roots in phloem
Water moving up xylem from roots to leaves, pulled by evaporation from the leaves
Oxygen diffusing into the leaf through stomata
Mineral ions being actively transported into root hairs
Evaporation from the leaves lowers water potential in the leaf, so water is pulled up the xylem in a continuous stream.
g12-trn-2
Which adaptation of a leaf reduces water loss while still allowing gas exchange?
Stomata that can close when water is scarce
Xylem vessels with no lignin
A very large number of stomata open at all times
A thin cuticle on the upper surface
Guard cells close the stomata when water is short, which cuts transpiration.
g12-trn-3
Why do most stomata in a typical leaf lie on the lower surface?
Water enters the leaf there
Sugars leave the leaf there
To absorb more light
It is cooler and less exposed to sun and wind, so less water is lost
The lower surface is shaded and cooler, so less water evaporates.
g12-trn-4
On a hot, dry, windy day the rate of transpiration is high. Which explains the effect of wind?
Wind lowers the temperature so evaporation stops
Wind closes the stomata
Wind blows away water vapour near the leaf, keeping the concentration gradient steep
Wind increases humidity around the leaf
Removing water vapour from around the leaf maintains a steep diffusion gradient, so water vapour leaves faster.
g12-trn-5
A potometer is used to compare transpiration in still air and with a fan. Which variable must be kept the same?
The speed of the fan
The species and size of the shoot, and the light and temperature
The distance the bubble moves
The time taken for the bubble to move
Only one variable (air movement) should change; the shoot, light and temperature are control variables.
g12-trn-6
Explain how guard cells open and close a stoma. (3 marks)
Guard cells take in water by osmosis and become turgid; their uneven (thickened inner) walls make them bend apart so the stoma opens; when they lose water they become flaccid and the stoma closes.
g12-trn-7

In a potometer experiment the bubble moved 42 mm in 6 minutes in the light, and 18 mm in 6 minutes in the dark. Calculate the rate of water uptake in each condition and suggest why they differ. (3 marks)
Light: 42 ÷ 6 = 7 mm/min; dark: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 mm/min; in the light the stomata are more open (guard cells turgid) so more water vapour is lost by transpiration and more water is taken up.
g12-trn-8
Give two reasons why transpiration is useful to a plant despite the water lost.
It brings water up to the leaves for photosynthesis; it carries mineral ions up from the roots; it cools the leaf by evaporation; it keeps cells turgid to support the plant.
gcse-bio-transpiration-c1
In a potometer, a bubble moves 15 mm in 5 minutes along a capillary tube of radius 0.5 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ per minute.
About 2.4 mm³/min
Volume = πr²l = π × 0.5² × 15 ≈ 11.8 mm³ in 5 min, so 2.4 mm³/min.
translocation: tra-1
Translocation is the movement of:
Water in xylem
Sucrose in phloem
Oxygen through stomata
Minerals into roots
Phloem transports dissolved sugars around the plant.
tra-2
Phloem cells have:
Lignin walls
Sieve plates and companion cells
No cytoplasm
Root hairs
Sieve tubes have sieve plates; companion cells provide energy via mitochondria.
tra-3
Translocation requires energy because:
Sucrose is actively loaded into the phloem
Water evaporates
Light is absorbed
It is passive
Companion cells use ATP from respiration for active transport.
tra-4
State two differences between xylem and phloem.
Xylem carries water and minerals; phloem carries sugars. Xylem moves one way (up); phloem moves both ways. Xylem cells are dead; phloem cells are living.
g12-tra-1
Where are sugars made and where are they delivered during translocation?
Made in stomata, delivered to the air
Made in roots, delivered to leaves
Made in leaves (sources), delivered to growing and storage regions (sinks)
Made in xylem, delivered to phloem
Sucrose made by photosynthesis in leaves is moved to roots, shoots, fruits and storage organs.
g12-tra-2
A metabolic poison that stops respiration reduces translocation. This is because:
Water cannot enter the xylem
Active loading of sucrose into phloem needs energy from respiration
Stomata will not open
Sieve plates dissolve
Loading sucrose into the phloem is active transport, which needs ATP from respiration.
g12-tra-3
Which statement about phloem tissue is correct?
It is made of living sieve tube cells with companion cells alongside
It only carries water upwards
It has no cytoplasm in any of its cells
It is made of dead cells strengthened with lignin
Sieve tubes are living but have few organelles; companion cells have the mitochondria that supply energy.
g12-tra-4
A plant stores energy in a potato tuber as starch rather than sucrose. Why is starch better for storage?
It is easier to transport
It contains more nitrogen
It is soluble and affects osmosis in cells
It is insoluble and does not change the water potential of the cells
Insoluble starch does not draw water into cells by osmosis, unlike soluble sugars.
g12-tra-5
Which is a correct difference between translocation and transpiration?
Transpiration needs energy from respiration in companion cells
Translocation moves water; transpiration moves sugars
Translocation can move substances in both directions; transpiration moves water upwards only
Translocation needs no living cells
Phloem transport can go up or down depending on source and sink; the transpiration stream in xylem is one way, upwards.
g12-tra-6
Describe how phloem is adapted for transporting sugars. (3 marks)

Sieve tubes are living cells with perforated sieve plates between them so sap can flow; few organelles and little cytoplasm leaves space for flow; companion cells with many mitochondria provide energy for active loading.
g12-tra-7
Explain why sugars made in the leaves of a plant in summer are moved to the roots by autumn.
Sucrose is translocated from the leaves (source) in phloem to the roots (sink); converted to insoluble starch for storage; provides energy for growth next spring.
g12-tra-8
A scientist ring-barks a tree by removing a ring of bark including the phloem. Explain why sugars build up above the ring, but the tree does not immediately lose water uptake. (3 marks)
Phloem is removed so sugars cannot be translocated past the ring and accumulate above it; xylem lies deeper inside the stem and is intact; so water and minerals still move up.
gcse-bio-translocation-c1
Which statement about translocation is correct?
Water is moved upwards in the phloem by transpiration, and the process needs no energy
Sucrose moves only upwards, in the xylem, pulled by water evaporating from the leaves
Sucrose is moved in the phloem from the roots to the leaves only, and needs no energy
Sucrose is moved in the phloem, both up and down the plant, and the process needs energy
Sucrose moves from sources (leaves) to sinks (roots, fruits, growing tips).
plant-hormones: Auxins cause shoots to bend towards light because:
Auxin collects on the shaded side and causes cells there to elongate
Unequal auxin distribution causes unequal growth: phototropism.
Auxin accumulates on the lower side and slows growth, so roots bend downwards (gravitropism).
Which hormone causes fruit to ripen?
Auxin collects on the lower side of the root. In roots auxin inhibits elongation, so the upper side grows faster and the root bends downwards.
Gibberellins break dormancy and stimulate seeds to germinate; they also promote stem growth and flowering.
A shoot tip is covered with an opaque cap. The shoot is lit from one side. What happens?
It grows straight with no bending
It bends away from the light
Auxin is made in the tip; the light-sensing tip is covered so auxin is not redistributed and growth is even.
Why is a rooting powder containing auxin used on plant cuttings?
It stimulates root growth so new plants can be produced quickly
It causes leaves to fall off
Auxin promotes root development, so cuttings can be cloned rapidly.
Selective weedkillers contain synthetic auxins. How do they kill broad-leaved weeds in lawns?
They cause abnormally fast, uncontrolled growth in broad-leaved weeds so they die
They block water uptake in grass
Broad-leaved plants respond to the excess auxin with uncontrolled growth; narrow-leaved grass is not affected as much.
