Fruit growers store bananas in a sealed room with a controlled gas. Which hormone could be removed to delay ripening, or added to speed it up?
Ethene stimulates ripening, so controlling it controls timing.
Explain how unequal distribution of auxin causes a shoot to grow towards light. (3 marks)
Auxin moves to the shaded side; it stimulates cell elongation there; shaded side grows faster so the shoot bends towards the light (positive phototropism).
Give three uses of plant hormones in agriculture or horticulture.

Auxins as rooting powder for cuttings; auxins as selective weedkillers; ethene to ripen fruit; gibberellins to end seed dormancy; gibberellins to make seedless fruit grow larger; gibberellins to promote flowering.
A seedling is placed on its side in the dark. Describe and explain the response of the shoot. (3 marks)
The shoot grows upwards (negative gravitropism); auxin collects on the lower side; in shoots auxin stimulates elongation so the lower side grows faster and the shoot bends up.
A shoot is lit from one side. Auxin:
Accumulates on the lit side, causing more cell elongation there, so the shoot bends away from the light
Accumulates on the shaded side, causing more cell elongation there, so the shoot bends towards the light
Is destroyed by light on both sides, so the shoot stops growing until it is lit evenly
Accumulates on the shaded side, slowing cell elongation there, so the shoot bends away from the light
This is positive phototropism. In roots, auxin inhibits elongation instead.
plant-adaptations: Which adaptation helps cacti reduce water loss?
Spines reduce surface area for transpiration.
Why do leaves have a large surface area?
More light can be absorbed for photosynthesis.
Plants in dry climates often have:
Give two adaptations of plants living in extreme cold.
Small leaves or needles; waxy coating; grow low to the ground; dark colours to absorb heat; antifreeze proteins.
Which feature helps a plant in a very dry desert to survive?
Thin cuticle and many open stomata
Succulent stems store water, and other features reduce water loss.
Marram grass, which grows on windy sand dunes, rolls its leaves with stomata inside. This reduces water loss because:
It traps a humid layer of air around the stomata, reducing the diffusion gradient
Trapped humid air lowers the concentration gradient so less water vapour diffuses out.
Why do cacti have extensive shallow root systems?
To absorb water quickly from brief rainfall near the surface
Wide shallow roots rapidly absorb rain before it evaporates or drains away.
A water lily has stomata mainly on the upper surface of floating leaves. Why?
The lower surface is in water so gas exchange with air is only possible on the upper surface
The underside rests on water, so stomata are on the upper surface in contact with air.
Which adaptation would NOT help a plant to reduce water loss?
A large number of stomata on both surfaces
More open stomata allow more water vapour to escape.
Explain how a thick waxy cuticle and a reduced leaf surface area help a plant live in a hot, dry habitat. (3 marks)

Wax is waterproof so less water evaporates from the leaf surface; smaller surface area means less area for evaporation/transpiration; therefore less water lost and the plant is more likely to survive.
Describe two adaptations of a plant living in a water-logged habitat such as a pond.

Air spaces in stems and leaves to help buoyancy and carry oxygen to roots; stomata on the upper surface of floating leaves; thin or little cuticle; flexible stems; reduced or no root system needed for water uptake.
Some plants have thorns or poisons. Explain how these adaptations help the plant survive.
Thorns/spines deter herbivores from eating the plant; poisons or bad taste make grazers avoid it; so less tissue is eaten and the plant can carry on photosynthesising and reproduce.
Marram grass has rolled leaves, sunken stomata and hairs. These reduce water loss because they:
Increase the surface area of the leaf, so water vapour diffuses out more slowly
Help the leaves absorb water vapour from the air to replace the water that is lost
Trap humid air near the stomata, reducing the concentration gradient for water vapour
Increase the rate of photosynthesis, so the plant needs less water overall
Less diffusion of water vapour out of the leaf means less transpiration.
hormones-and-endocrine-glands: Hormones are carried around the body in:
Hormones are secreted by glands into the blood.
Which gland is called the 'master gland'?
The pituitary secretes hormones that control other glands.
Act more slowly and for longer
Hormonal responses are slower but longer-lasting.
Name the gland that produces insulin and the target organ.
Pancreas; target organ is the liver (also muscles).
Which pair correctly matches an endocrine gland with a hormone it secretes?
The ovaries secrete oestrogen. Thyroid makes thyroxine, pancreas makes insulin, testes make testosterone.
Hormones only affect certain cells in the body. This is because:
Only those cells have receptors for that hormone
Hormones are destroyed before reaching other cells
Only those cells are near the gland
Only those cells are supplied by blood
Target cells have specific receptor proteins that the hormone fits; other cells lack them.
Which gland is the main source of testosterone?
The testes secrete testosterone in males.
Which of these is a feature of hormonal control but NOT of nervous control?
Acts on a precise area only
Chemical messenger travels in the blood
Hormones are chemical messengers carried by the blood; nerves use electrical impulses.
Which gland releases hormones that act on other endocrine glands?
The pituitary secretes hormones such as FSH, LH and TSH which control other glands, hence 'master gland'.
Explain why the response to a hormone is usually slower than the response to a nerve impulse. (2 marks)
Hormones are secreted into the blood and must be carried in the circulation to the target organ; this takes longer than an electrical impulse travelling along a neurone.
State two differences between the endocrine system and the nervous system. (2 marks)
Endocrine uses hormones (chemicals) in blood, nervous uses electrical impulses; endocrine response slower; endocrine effects last longer; endocrine effects more widespread / nervous more precise.
Name the gland that secretes each of: (a) ADH, FSH, LH (b) testosterone (c) adrenaline. (3 marks)
The pituitary gland is often called the 'master gland' because it:
Releases hormones that control other endocrine glands, such as TSH and FSH
Produces insulin and glucagon, which control all the other glands
Controls all reflex actions by sending nerve impulses to the glands
Makes adrenaline, which switches every other gland on and off
TSH acts on the thyroid; FSH and LH act on the ovaries.
adrenaline-and-thyroxine: Adrenal glands above the kidneys release adrenaline in stressful situations.
Which is an effect of adrenaline?
Increased heart rate and blood glucose
It prepares the body for 'fight or flight'.
Describe the negative feedback control of thyroxine.

When thyroxine levels fall, the hypothalamus releases TRH which causes the pituitary to release TSH, which stimulates the thyroid to release more thyroxine. High thyroxine inhibits TRH and TSH release.
During a fright, adrenaline causes blood vessels to the muscles to:
Adrenaline diverts blood to muscles by dilating their vessels, delivering more oxygen and glucose.
Why does adrenaline increase blood glucose concentration?
To supply more glucose for respiration in muscles
To make the pancreas release more insulin
More glucose for respiration releases more energy for 'fight or flight'.
An underactive thyroid gland would most likely cause:
Low thyroxine means low metabolic rate: tiredness, weight gain and feeling cold.
Thyroxine contains which element, essential in the diet for its production?
Thyroxine is made using iodine; lack of iodine can cause an enlarged thyroid (goitre).
When blood thyroxine level rises above normal, what happens?
TRH and TSH release is inhibited
Negative feedback: high thyroxine inhibits the hypothalamus and pituitary, so less TRH and TSH, and thyroxine falls.
Describe the effects of adrenaline on the body during a stressful situation. (3 marks)
Increases heart rate; increases blood flow to muscles; increases breathing rate; raises blood glucose; so more oxygen and glucose reach muscles for respiration.
Explain why a person with too little thyroxine may gain weight. (2 marks)
Thyroxine controls metabolic rate; low thyroxine means lower metabolic rate so less energy used and more food stored as fat.
Explain how negative feedback keeps thyroxine level constant. (3 marks)

If thyroxine falls, hypothalamus releases TRH which causes pituitary to release TSH; TSH stimulates thyroid to release thyroxine; when level rises, TRH and TSH release is inhibited so thyroxine falls back.
When the level of thyroxine in the blood is high:
More TSH is released by the pituitary, so thyroxine levels rise further
Adrenaline release is inhibited, so the metabolic rate falls
TSH release from the pituitary is inhibited, so thyroxine levels fall
The thyroid makes more thyroxine, so the metabolic rate rises further
Negative feedback keeps the metabolic rate steady.
the-menstrual-cycle: A surge in LH triggers release of an egg around day 14.
Which hormone causes an egg to mature in the ovary?
FSH stimulates follicle and egg maturation.
Progesterone keeps the lining thick for a possible pregnancy.
Explain how oestrogen and progesterone affect FSH and LH.
Oestrogen inhibits FSH and (at high levels) stimulates an LH surge; progesterone inhibits both FSH and LH.
On which day of a typical 28-day cycle does ovulation usually occur?
Ovulation, release of a mature egg, usually occurs around day 14.
Which structure releases progesterone after ovulation?
The follicle left behind forms the corpus luteum which secretes progesterone.
Menstruation is the breakdown and loss of the uterus lining, days 1 to about 5.
Which hormone is secreted by the ovaries and repairs and thickens the uterus lining?
Oestrogen from the ovaries causes the lining to thicken and repair after menstruation.
A surge in which hormone causes ovulation?
A peak in LH from the pituitary triggers release of the egg.
Describe the roles of FSH in the menstrual cycle. (2 marks)
Secreted by the pituitary gland; causes an egg to mature in a follicle in the ovary; stimulates the ovary to release oestrogen.
Explain why progesterone level falls if the woman does not become pregnant. (2 marks)
The corpus luteum breaks down if no embryo implants, so progesterone is no longer secreted; the uterus lining then breaks down.
Explain how oestrogen and progesterone affect FSH and LH. (4 marks)
Rising oestrogen inhibits FSH (stops more eggs maturing); high oestrogen stimulates LH surge which causes ovulation; progesterone maintains the uterus lining; progesterone inhibits FSH and LH.
A surge in LH from the pituitary
Rising oestrogen stimulates the LH surge around day 14.
contraception: Which contraceptive also protects against STIs?
Barrier methods like condoms stop body fluids passing between partners.
These hormones inhibit FSH and LH, so no eggs mature or are released.
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of hormonal contraception compared with barrier methods.
Advantage: more effective; doesn't interrupt sex. Disadvantage: no STI protection; possible side effects; must remember to take pill daily.
How does the combined contraceptive pill prevent pregnancy?
It kills sperm in the vagina
It stops FSH release so no eggs mature
Oestrogen in the pill inhibits FSH so eggs do not mature, preventing ovulation.
Which method is a barrier method of contraception?
A diaphragm is placed over the cervix to stop sperm reaching the egg.
A contraceptive implant releases progesterone for several years. A disadvantage compared with condoms is that it:
Hormonal methods do not stop transmission of STIs; condoms do.
Surgical sterilisation in a man involves:
Blocking the urethra with a plug
Cutting and tying the sperm ducts
Vasectomy cuts and ties the sperm ducts so semen contains no sperm.
A copper IUD prevents pregnancy mainly by:
Preventing sperm surviving and egg implanting
The IUD stops sperm surviving and prevents implantation of a fertilised egg in the uterus.
Give two advantages of using a condom rather than the contraceptive pill. (2 marks)
Protects against sexually transmitted infections; no hormonal side effects; only needed when having sex (no daily dose).
Explain why the progesterone-only pill can prevent pregnancy even if it does not stop ovulation. (2 marks)
Progesterone thickens cervical mucus so sperm cannot reach the egg; it may also stop the uterus lining developing so implantation fails.
Evaluate the use of hormonal contraceptives for family planning. (3 marks)

Very effective if used correctly; allows planning of family size / career; but may cause side effects (e.g. headaches, mood changes, weight gain); do not protect against STIs; must be taken regularly.
Which contraceptive method also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections?
Barrier methods stop body fluids being exchanged; hormonal methods do not.
assisted-reproductive-technology: art-1
In IVF, fertilisation takes place:
In the uterus
In a dish in a laboratory
In the oviduct
In the ovary
Eggs are fertilised outside the body, then embryos are implanted.
art-2
Clomifene therapy treats infertility by:
Blocking sperm
Increasing FSH and LH release
Lowering oestrogen
Destroying eggs
It stimulates FSH and LH, causing eggs to mature and be released.
art-3
Give two disadvantages of IVF.
Low success rate; expensive; emotionally and physically stressful; risk of multiple births; ethical issues about unused embryos.
g14-art-1
In IVF, what is done to the woman before her eggs are collected?
She is given testosterone to stop ovulation permanently
Her uterus lining is removed
She is given insulin to prepare the ovaries
She is given FSH and LH to stimulate several eggs to mature
FSH and LH are given so that several eggs mature at once, increasing the chance of fertilisation.
g14-art-2
Which statement about clomifene therapy is correct?
It stops the embryo being rejected
It fertilises eggs outside the body
It is given to men to increase sperm count
It is a hormone treatment that helps women who do not ovulate
Clomifene stimulates the release of FSH and LH so eggs mature and are released.
g14-art-3
After fertilisation in an IVF dish, embryos are allowed to develop until they are:
Mixed with a second woman's eggs
Tiny balls of cells, then one or two are placed in the uterus
Fully formed foetuses
Frozen permanently
Embryos are grown to a small ball of cells before being transferred into the uterus.
g14-art-4
Why are only one or two embryos usually transferred to the uterus in IVF?
Embryos are too large for more
To reduce the risk of multiple births
More embryos make fertilisation less likely
The uterus cannot hold any more cells
Transferring many embryos increases the risk of multiple pregnancies, which carry health risks for mother and babies.
g14-art-5
Which is a reason some people object to IVF?
It never works
Spare embryos are often destroyed or frozen
It uses no hormones
It uses antibiotics
Unused embryos may be discarded, which raises ethical objections for some people.
g14-art-6
Describe the main stages of IVF. (4 marks)

Mother given FSH and LH to stimulate eggs to mature; eggs collected from the ovaries; eggs fertilised with sperm in a lab dish; fertilised eggs develop into embryos; one or two embryos inserted into the uterus.
g14-art-7
Explain how clomifene therapy can help a woman become pregnant. (3 marks)
Clomifene causes more FSH and LH to be released; so eggs mature in the ovary; and ovulation occurs, so the egg can be fertilised.
g14-art-8
Evaluate the use of IVF for a couple who cannot conceive naturally. (3 marks)
Advantage: gives infertile couples a chance of having a baby; Disadvantage: low success rate, expensive and stressful, risk of multiple births; ethical concerns about spare embryos.
gcse-bio-assisted-reproductive-technology-c1
Clomifene therapy helps some women become pregnant by:
Causing more FSH and LH to be released, so eggs mature and are released
Fertilising eggs outside the body before they are placed in the uterus
Blocking oestrogen permanently so that the uterus lining stays thick
Preventing the uterus lining from thickening so an embryo can implant
IVF, by contrast, fertilises eggs in a laboratory.
homeostasis: E.g. temperature, blood glucose and water levels are kept within limits.
A change triggers a response that reverses the change
Negative feedback returns a factor to its set point.
Why must body temperature be kept around 37 °C?
So enzymes work at their optimum
Too hot or cold reduces enzyme activity.
Name three conditions controlled by homeostasis in humans.
Body temperature; blood glucose concentration; water content/osmoregulation.
A thermometer in a fridge switches the cooling on when the temperature rises. This is similar to a body's:
A sensor detects the change (receptor) and the cooling unit responds (effector), like a body control system.
In a homeostatic control system, what is the job of the coordination centre?
To process information and send instructions to effectors
The coordination centre (e.g. brain, pancreas) receives information from receptors and sends instructions to effectors.
Which of these is an effector?
A temperature receptor in the skin
Effectors (muscles and glands) carry out the response; sweat glands release sweat.
Both nervous and hormonal systems are used in homeostasis. Which is a difference?
Nervous responses are usually shorter lasting
Nerves use chemicals carried in blood
Nervous responses are fast and short-lived; hormones travel in blood and have slower, longer lasting effects.
If the control of internal conditions fails and blood glucose stays too high, this is most likely to:
Internal conditions outside normal limits disrupt cell function and can cause illness.
Explain why it is important that the water content of the body is kept constant. (3 marks)
Too much water enters cells by osmosis and they may burst; too little water leaves cells by osmosis and they shrivel; this stops cells working properly.
Describe the roles of a receptor, a coordination centre and an effector in a control system. (3 marks)
Receptor detects a change/stimulus; coordination centre processes the information and sends a signal; effector (muscle or gland) carries out a response to restore the condition.
Explain why a drop in body temperature below the optimum slows down metabolism. (2 marks)
Enzymes have less kinetic energy; fewer collisions between enzymes and substrates so reactions are slower.
Maintaining a constant internal environment despite changes, mostly by negative feedback
Keeping all body processes running as fast as possible, mostly by positive feedback
Changing the internal environment to match the external surroundings at all times
Producing as many hormones as possible so the body can react to any change
Examples include temperature, blood glucose and water balance.
thermoregulation: Which part of the brain monitors body temperature?
The thermoregulatory centre is in the hypothalamus.
When too hot, blood vessels near the skin:
Vasodilation brings more blood to the surface so heat is lost by radiation.
Shivering helps warm the body because:
Muscles contract and respiration releases heat
Muscle contraction needs respiration, which transfers heat.
Explain how sweating cools the body.
Sweat is released onto the skin; water evaporates, transferring heat energy from the skin to the environment.
In hot conditions, the thermoregulatory centre sends signals that cause:
Sweating and vasodilation increase heat loss when the body is too hot.
In cold conditions, what happens to skin hairs?
They are pulled upright to trap an insulating layer of air
Hair erector muscles raise the hairs, trapping air which insulates the skin.
Vasoconstriction in the cold means that:
Blood vessels move deeper into the body
Blood vessels near the skin surface narrow, reducing heat loss
Blood vessels widen to bring more blood to the skin
Less blood flows near the skin surface so less heat is lost by radiation. Vessels do not physically move.
Which receptors detect the temperature of the blood passing through the brain?
The hypothalamus monitors blood temperature and also receives information from skin receptors.
On a very hot day a person sweats heavily. Why does the person's temperature fall as the sweat evaporates?
Evaporation transfers heat energy from the skin to the surroundings
Evaporation needs energy, which is taken from the skin, cooling the body.
Describe how the body responds when the core temperature rises above 37 °C. (3 marks)
Receptors detect the rise; thermoregulatory centre in the hypothalamus signals effectors; sweat glands release more sweat which evaporates; vasodilation increases heat loss from the skin.
Explain how shivering helps to raise body temperature. (3 marks)
Muscles contract rapidly; this requires respiration; respiration transfers energy as heat which warms the body.
Explain why a person who is too cold may feel less coordinated and have slower reactions. (2 marks)
Enzyme activity is reduced at low temperature; so metabolic reactions in nerve and muscle cells are slower.
Blood vessels move deeper into the skin
The heart stops pumping to the skin
Less blood flows through capillaries near the skin surface
Arterioles narrow; vessels do not move.
controlling-blood-glucose: When blood glucose is too high, the pancreas releases:
Insulin causes cells to take in glucose and the liver to store it as glycogen.
Glycogen to be converted into glucose
Glucagon raises blood glucose when it is too low.
Excess glucose is stored as glycogen in liver and muscle cells.
Describe what happens when blood glucose falls after exercise.
The pancreas detects the low level and releases glucagon, which makes the liver convert glycogen into glucose, raising blood glucose.
Which organ detects changes in blood glucose and releases insulin and glucagon?
The pancreas monitors blood glucose and secretes both hormones.
After a meal rich in carbohydrate, what happens to blood glucose concentration and the insulin level?
The rise in glucose stimulates insulin release to bring it back down.
Making cells take in glucose and the liver convert it to glycogen
Insulin enables glucose uptake by cells and conversion to glycogen in liver and muscle.
Why do glucagon and insulin form a negative feedback system?
They are made in the liver
They work only when glucose is normal
They have opposite effects that return glucose to the normal level
Insulin lowers glucose, glucagon raises it, keeping the concentration within narrow limits.
A person's blood glucose falls during a long fast. Which response is correct?
Insulin is released and glucose is stored
Glucagon is released and the liver converts glycogen to glucose
Glucagon acts on the liver cells to break down glycogen into glucose which enters the blood.
Explain how blood glucose concentration is lowered after a meal. (4 marks)

Rise in glucose is detected by the pancreas; pancreas releases insulin into the blood; insulin makes liver and muscle cells take up glucose; glucose is converted to glycogen for storage; blood glucose falls (negative feedback).
Describe the roles of glucagon in controlling blood glucose. (3 marks)
Released by the pancreas when blood glucose is too low; acts on liver cells; causes glycogen to be converted to glucose released into the blood.
A person's blood glucose is measured at 5 mmol/dm³ before a meal and 9 mmol/dm³ after. Suggest what happens next and why. (2 marks)
Insulin is released from the pancreas; glucose concentration falls back toward the normal level as cells take up glucose and it is stored as glycogen.
After a meal, insulin lowers blood glucose mainly by:
Causing the liver and muscles to convert stored glycogen back into glucose
Causing cells to take up glucose and the liver and muscles to convert it to glycogen
Increasing the release of glucagon, which converts glucose into glycogen
Making the kidneys excrete the extra glucose in the urine after a meal
Glucagon does the opposite, converting glycogen back to glucose.
diabetes: The pancreas not producing enough insulin
It's usually an autoimmune condition destroying insulin-producing cells.
In type 2 body cells become resistant to insulin.
Give two ways type 2 diabetes can be controlled.
Low sugar/carbohydrate diet; regular exercise; weight loss; medication (e.g. metformin) or insulin.
Which organ detects a rise in blood glucose concentration and releases insulin?
The pancreas detects high blood glucose and secretes insulin into the blood.
After a meal, insulin causes the liver to:
Convert glucose into glycogen for storage
Insulin stimulates liver and muscle cells to take up glucose and convert it to glycogen, lowering blood glucose.
Glucagon is released when blood glucose concentration is too low. What is its effect?
Glycogen is converted to glucose and released into the blood
Glucagon acts on the liver, causing glycogen to be broken down to glucose, which raises blood glucose.
A person with type 2 diabetes has a high blood glucose concentration even though their pancreas produces insulin. The most likely reason is:
Their kidneys reabsorb too much water
Their body cells no longer respond properly to insulin
Their liver makes too much glucagon
In type 2 diabetes body cells become resistant to insulin, so glucose is not taken up from the blood.
Which of these is a negative feedback loop involving blood glucose?
Low glucose, less glucagon, glucose stays low
High glucose, more insulin, glucose falls
High glucose, less insulin, glucose rises further
Low glucose, more insulin, glucose falls further
Negative feedback reverses a change: high glucose triggers insulin release, which lowers glucose back to normal.
Explain how blood glucose concentration is brought back to normal after a meal rich in carbohydrate in a healthy person. (3 marks)

Blood glucose rises after the meal and is detected by the pancreas; pancreas secretes insulin into the blood; insulin makes liver (and muscle) cells take up glucose and convert it to glycogen, so blood glucose falls back to normal.
A person with type 1 diabetes eats a large meal but does not inject insulin. Describe and explain what happens to their blood glucose concentration. (2 marks)
Blood glucose rises and stays high; the pancreas does not produce insulin so glucose is not taken up by cells or converted to glycogen in the liver.
Suggest why a person with type 1 diabetes may inject insulin before a meal but should not take too large a dose. (3 marks)

Insulin lowers blood glucose / prevents it rising too high after eating; too much insulin removes too much glucose from the blood; blood glucose becomes dangerously low (hypoglycaemia) so brain cells lack glucose/may cause confusion or collapse.
Why is type 2 diabetes often managed first with diet and exercise, whereas type 1 is not?
In type 1 the body still makes insulin but responds poorly; in type 2 no insulin is made
Type 2 is caused only by diet, while type 1 is caused only by a lack of exercise
In type 2 the body still makes insulin but responds poorly; in type 1 no insulin is made
Exercise produces insulin, which replaces the insulin missing in type 2 diabetes
Obesity is a major risk factor for type 2.
the-kidneys-and-osmoregulation: Which hormone controls the amount of water reabsorbed by the kidneys?
ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct.
Urea is produced in the liver from:
Deamination of excess amino acids produces ammonia, converted to urea.
Where does filtration (ultrafiltration) take place in a nephron?
High pressure forces small molecules out of the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule.
Which substance is completely reabsorbed in a healthy kidney?
All glucose is selectively reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule.
Explain what happens when blood water content is too low.
Detected by the hypothalamus; pituitary releases more ADH; collecting ducts become more permeable; more water reabsorbed into the blood; small volume of concentrated urine produced.
Which of these is the correct order of the path of urine out of the body?
Urine is made in the kidneys, passes down the ureters to the bladder and leaves via the urethra.
Which substance would you NOT expect to find in the filtrate in the Bowman's capsule of a healthy person?
Ultrafiltration forces small molecules out of the blood; large protein molecules and blood cells are too big to pass through.
A person runs a marathon on a hot day and sweats heavily. What happens to their urine?
Sweating lowers blood water content, so more ADH is released and more water is reabsorbed, giving small volumes of concentrated urine.
Which hormone is released by the pituitary gland and acts on the kidney tubules?
ADH (anti-diuretic hormone) is released by the pituitary gland and makes the kidney tubules more permeable to water.
Glucose is found in the filtrate but not in the urine of a healthy person. This is because glucose is:
All glucose is selectively reabsorbed (by active transport) from the nephron back into the blood.
Describe how the kidney produces urine from blood. (4 marks)

Blood is filtered under high pressure at the glomerulus/Bowman's capsule; small molecules (water, glucose, urea, ions) enter the filtrate; all glucose is reabsorbed (active transport) along with some ions and water; urea and excess water/ions pass out as urine.
A person drinks a large volume of water. Explain how negative feedback returns the water content of their blood to normal. (4 marks)

Blood water content rises and is detected by the hypothalamus; the pituitary gland releases less ADH; kidney tubules become less permeable to water so less water is reabsorbed; more dilute urine is produced and water content falls back to normal.
Explain why urea must be removed from the body. Where is it made? (2 marks)
Urea is toxic/harmful if it builds up in the blood; it is made in the liver from the breakdown of excess amino acids.
Glucose is normally absent from urine because:
Glucose molecules are too large to be filtered out of the blood in the glomerulus
The liver removes all the glucose from the blood before it reaches the kidneys
All the filtered glucose is selectively reabsorbed back into the blood in the nephron
ADH breaks down the glucose in the collecting duct before the urine is formed
treating-kidney-failure: kft-1
In dialysis, the dialysis fluid contains:
No glucose
The same glucose and ion concentrations as healthy blood plasma
Lots of urea
Pure water
This ensures urea diffuses out but useful substances aren't lost.
kft-2
A disadvantage of a kidney transplant is:
Must be repeated weekly
Risk of rejection, needing immunosuppressant drugs
Can't be done
It's temporary
The immune system may attack the donor kidney.
kft-3
Compare dialysis and transplants as treatments for kidney failure.

Dialysis: available, but time-consuming (several sessions a week), restricts diet and costs a lot over time. Transplant: long-term cure and freedom, but shortage of donors, surgery risks and lifelong immunosuppressants.
g15-tkf-1
During dialysis, urea moves from the patient's blood into the dialysis fluid by:
Osmosis
Filtration through the skin
Active transport
Diffusion
Urea is at a higher concentration in the blood than in the dialysis fluid, so it diffuses across the partially permeable membrane.
g15-tkf-2
Why is the dialysis fluid kept flowing past the membrane rather than left still?
To increase the pressure in the blood
To keep the fluid warm
To maintain a concentration gradient for urea
To stop blood clotting
Fresh fluid keeps the urea concentration low outside the blood, maintaining the diffusion gradient.
g15-tkf-3
Why might the dialysis fluid contain glucose at the same concentration as normal blood plasma?
To feed the patient
So that glucose does not diffuse out of the patient's blood
To make urea diffuse faster
To destroy bacteria
No concentration gradient for glucose means it is not lost from the blood, while waste urea still diffuses out.
g15-tkf-4
Which of these makes a kidney transplant less likely to be rejected?
A donor of a different species
Stopping all medication
Using a kidney from a much older donor only
A donor with a similar tissue type
A close tissue match (e.g. from a relative) means the recipient's antibodies are less likely to attack the new kidney.
g15-tkf-5
Patients with a transplanted kidney must take immunosuppressant drugs. A risk of this is that they:
Lose the ability to make ADH
Produce too much insulin
Become allergic to urea
Are more likely to catch infections
Immunosuppressants reduce the immune response, so patients are more vulnerable to infection.
g15-tkf-6
Explain why a patient with kidney failure needs dialysis. (3 marks)
Failed kidneys cannot filter blood / remove urea and excess ions and water; these would build up and become toxic; dialysis removes them from the blood.
g15-tkf-7
Give two advantages of a kidney transplant compared with long-term dialysis. (2 marks)
No need for regular, time-consuming dialysis sessions; fewer dietary restrictions / greater freedom; cheaper in the long term; kidney works continuously.
g15-tkf-8
Explain why a patient who receives a donor kidney is given immunosuppressant drugs. (3 marks)
The donor kidney has foreign antigens; the recipient's immune system recognises it as foreign and could attack it (rejection); immunosuppressants reduce this immune response so the kidney survives.
gcse-bio-treating-kidney-failure-c1
During dialysis, urea leaves the blood but glucose does not, because the dialysis fluid:
Has the same glucose concentration as normal blood but contains no urea
Contains more urea than blood, so urea leaves the blood by active transport
Contains no glucose, so glucose molecules cannot cross the membrane
Is pure water, which lets only urea molecules diffuse through it
There is a concentration gradient for urea but none for glucose.
exchange-surfaces-and-the-alveoli: alv-1
Which feature of alveoli does NOT help gas exchange?
Large surface area
Thin walls
Good blood supply
Thick mucus lining
Alveoli have a large surface area, one-cell-thick walls and many capillaries. A thick layer would slow diffusion.
alv-2
Which gas diffuses from the blood into the alveoli?
Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Nitrogen
Glucose
Carbon dioxide diffuses out of the blood into the alveoli to be breathed out. Oxygen moves the other way.
alv-3
Explain why large organisms need specialised exchange surfaces.
They have a small surface area to volume ratio and long diffusion distances, so diffusion across the body surface alone is too slow to meet their needs.
g15-alv-1
Which feature of the alveoli allows oxygen to diffuse into the blood quickly?
Very low blood flow
A thick layer of mucus
Walls that are many cells thick
A wall that is one cell thick
A very thin (one cell thick) wall gives a short diffusion distance.
g15-alv-2
Why is a good blood supply to the alveoli important for gas exchange?
It makes the air moist
It keeps the lungs warm
It maintains a steep concentration gradient by removing oxygen and bringing carbon dioxide
It increases the surface area
Constant blood flow carries oxygen away and brings carbon dioxide, keeping the concentration gradients steep.
g15-alv-3
Ventilation of the lungs helps gas exchange because it:
Makes the alveoli bigger
Brings fresh air in and removes carbon dioxide, maintaining concentration gradients
Pumps blood to the lungs
Pushes gases across by active transport
Breathing replaces the air in the alveoli, keeping oxygen high and carbon dioxide low inside them.
g15-alv-4
In which direction does carbon dioxide diffuse at the alveoli?
From the blood into the air in the alveoli
From the air into the red blood cells
It does not move
From the air into the blood
Blood arriving at the lungs has a high carbon dioxide concentration, so it diffuses into the alveolar air and is breathed out.
g15-alv-5
Compared with a single large sphere of the same total volume, many small alveoli give the lungs:
A thicker exchange surface
Less oxygen uptake
Smaller surface area
A larger surface area to volume ratio
Many small air sacs greatly increase the total surface area for the same volume, so gas exchange is faster.
g15-alv-6
Describe four ways the alveoli are adapted for efficient gas exchange. (4 marks)

Large surface area (millions of alveoli); thin walls (one cell thick) so short diffusion distance; rich blood supply with capillaries; moist lining so gases dissolve; ventilation maintains concentration gradient.
g15-alv-7
Explain how the diffusion of oxygen across the alveolar wall is affected by emphysema, where alveolar walls break down. (3 marks)
Alveoli walls break down so surface area is reduced; less oxygen can diffuse into the blood; the patient is breathless/less oxygen reaches respiring cells.
g15-alv-8
Explain why a person exercising breathes faster and more deeply, in terms of the concentration gradients at the alveoli. (3 marks)

Muscles respire faster so more carbon dioxide is produced and more oxygen is needed; faster, deeper breathing brings fresh air to alveoli and removes carbon dioxide; this keeps the concentration gradients steep so diffusion is faster.
gcse-bio-exchange-surfaces-and-the-alveoli-c1
Emphysema destroys alveolar walls. The main effect is that:
The alveoli become larger, so oxygen diffuses into the blood more quickly
Surface area for gas exchange falls, so less oxygen diffuses into the blood
More carbon dioxide diffuses from the air in the alveoli into the blood
The diffusion distance decreases, because the alveolar walls are thinner
Alveoli are adapted with a large surface area, thin walls and a good blood supply.
blood-and-its-components: Which part of the blood carries oxygen?
Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which binds oxygen.
Why do red blood cells have no nucleus?
To make more room for haemoglobin
No nucleus leaves more space for haemoglobin, so each cell carries more oxygen.
What is the role of platelets?
Platelets are cell fragments that help form clots at wounds.
Name three substances transported in blood plasma.
Any three: glucose, amino acids, carbon dioxide, urea, hormones, antibodies, mineral ions.
Which component of blood is a fragment of a cell rather than a whole cell?
Platelets are small fragments of cells that have no nucleus and help blood to clot.
Which statement correctly describes the shape of a red blood cell and why it is useful?
Long and thin, to carry nerve impulses
Biconcave disc, to give a large surface area for absorbing oxygen
The biconcave shape gives a large surface area to volume ratio, so oxygen diffuses in and out quickly.
What is the main function of white blood cells?
White blood cells ingest pathogens (phagocytes) or make antibodies and antitoxins (lymphocytes).
Which pair correctly matches a blood component with a substance it transports?
Plasma carries urea from the liver to the kidneys. Red cells carry oxygen, not hormones.
Oxygen binds to haemoglobin in the lungs to form which substance?
Haemoglobin + oxygen → oxyhaemoglobin. This releases oxygen again in tissues where oxygen concentration is low.
Describe how platelets help prevent pathogens entering the body after a cut. (3 marks)
Platelets collect at the wound; they trigger formation of a network of fibres (fibrin); this traps red blood cells to form a clot/scab that seals the wound.
Describe two ways in which red blood cells are adapted for transporting oxygen. (2 marks)
They contain haemoglobin, which binds to oxygen; no nucleus, so more room for haemoglobin; biconcave shape gives a large surface area for diffusion (any two).
Explain the difference between the role of phagocytes and the role of lymphocytes. (3 marks)
Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies; that bind to specific antigens on pathogens (and also produce antitoxins).
Red blood cells have no nucleus. The advantage is:
They can divide faster to replace cells lost in bleeding
More space for haemoglobin, so more oxygen can be carried
They can make antibodies against pathogens in the blood
They can squeeze through capillary walls into the tissues
Their biconcave shape also increases surface area.
blood-vessels: Which blood vessel has valves to stop backflow?
Veins carry blood at low pressure, so they have valves to keep it flowing towards the heart.
Why do arteries have thick, muscular, elastic walls?
To withstand high pressure from the heart
To carry blood to the heart
Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. Elastic fibres stretch and recoil.
Explain how capillaries are adapted for exchange.
Walls are one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance; they are narrow and form large networks, giving a large surface area close to cells.
Which blood vessel carries blood at the highest pressure?
Arteries carry blood straight from the ventricles, so it is at the highest pressure.
Why do veins have a wider lumen than arteries?
To reduce resistance to the low-pressure blood flow
Blood in veins is at low pressure, so a wide lumen lowers resistance to flow.
A capillary wall is only one cell thick. What is the main benefit of this?
It allows the vessel to contract
It gives a short diffusion distance
A thin wall means substances diffuse a short distance between blood and cells.
Which blood vessel carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart?
The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs into the left atrium.
Which vessel supplies the heart muscle itself with oxygenated blood?
Coronary arteries branch from the aorta and supply the cardiac muscle with oxygen and glucose.
Explain why arteries have a thick layer of elastic fibres in their walls. (2 marks)
The walls stretch as blood is forced out by the heart at high pressure; then recoil, which helps smooth and maintain blood flow/pressure.
Explain why veins have valves but arteries do not. (3 marks)
Blood in veins is at low pressure; so it could flow backwards; valves close to prevent backflow, whereas arteries have high pressure from the heart so backflow is not a problem.
A blocked coronary artery can cause a heart attack. Explain why. (3 marks)
Heart muscle receives less oxygen and glucose; so cardiac muscle cells cannot respire aerobically/release enough energy; so the muscle cannot contract and cells may die.
Veins have valves but arteries do not because:
Arteries carry less blood, so backflow cannot happen in them
Veins carry oxygenated blood, which needs valves to keep moving
Blood in veins is at low pressure, so valves prevent backflow
Valves raise the blood pressure in veins to match the arteries
Arteries have thick, elastic walls to withstand high pressure.
the-heart: hrt-1
Which chamber of the heart pumps blood to the body?
Right atrium
Right ventricle
Left atrium
Left ventricle
The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and around the body.
hrt-2
Which blood vessel carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs?
Pulmonary vein
Pulmonary artery
Vena cava
Aorta
The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
hrt-3
Explain why the left ventricle wall is thicker than the right ventricle wall.
The left ventricle pumps blood all around the body, so needs more muscle to produce higher pressure. The right only pumps to the nearby lungs.
g16-hrt-1
Which chamber of the heart receives deoxygenated blood from the body?
Left ventricle
Right ventricle
Left atrium
Right atrium
The vena cava brings deoxygenated blood from the body into the right atrium.
g16-hrt-2
What is the function of the valves in the heart?
To make the walls thicker
To pump blood
To stop blood flowing backwards
To supply the heart with oxygen
Valves open one way only, ensuring blood flows in the correct direction.
g16-hrt-3
Which sequence shows the correct path of blood through the heart, starting at the vena cava?
Right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle
Right atrium, right ventricle, lungs, left atrium, left ventricle
Left atrium, left ventricle, lungs, right atrium, right ventricle
Right ventricle, right atrium, lungs, left ventricle, left atrium
Blood goes right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery to lungs, pulmonary vein, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta.
g16-hrt-4
Which structure in the right atrium acts as the natural pacemaker?
Aorta
Coronary artery
Septum
Sinoatrial node
Pacemaker cells in the right atrium control the resting heart rate. An artificial pacemaker can correct irregularities.
g16-hrt-5
What is the role of the septum in the heart?
It stores blood
It supplies the heart muscle with blood
It separates oxygenated and deoxygenated blood
It pumps blood to the lungs
The septum separates the left and right sides so the two types of blood do not mix.
g16-hrt-6
Explain why humans are described as having a double circulatory system. (3 marks)

Blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit; the right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body; this keeps blood at high pressure for fast delivery.
g16-hrt-7
Describe how the heart muscle contracts to pump blood from the atria to the ventricles to the arteries. (3 marks)
Atria contract, pushing blood through open valves into the ventricles; ventricles then contract; atrioventricular valves close and blood is forced out through the semilunar valves into the arteries.
g16-hrt-8
Explain why the pulmonary artery has a lower pressure than the aorta. (2 marks)
The right ventricle has a thinner muscular wall than the left; the pulmonary artery only carries blood a short distance to the lungs, whereas the aorta carries blood around the whole body.
gcse-bio-the-heart-c1
Which is the correct order of blood flow from the body back to the body?
Vena cava → left atrium → left ventricle → pulmonary vein → lungs → pulmonary artery → right atrium → right ventricle → aorta
Pulmonary vein → right atrium → right ventricle → aorta → body → vena cava → left atrium → left ventricle → pulmonary artery
Vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary vein → lungs → pulmonary artery → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta
Vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta
This is a double circulation: blood passes through the heart twice per circuit.
aerobic-and-anaerobic-respiration: What are the products of aerobic respiration?
Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (energy released).
What is produced by anaerobic respiration in human muscle?
Anaerobic respiration in animals produces lactic acid only.
Why is respiration described as exothermic?
It transfers energy to the surroundings
Respiration releases energy, some of it as heat to the surroundings.
Explain why breathing rate stays high for a while after exercise.
To repay the oxygen debt: extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid that built up during anaerobic respiration.
Which is the correct word equation for aerobic respiration?
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose, releasing carbon dioxide and water.
Which organisms produce ethanol and carbon dioxide during anaerobic respiration?
Yeast carries out fermentation: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.
Why does anaerobic respiration release less energy than aerobic respiration?
Glucose is not fully broken down
Without oxygen, glucose is only partially oxidised, so less energy is released per glucose molecule.
Where in a cell do most of the reactions of aerobic respiration take place?
Mitochondria contain the enzymes needed for the aerobic stages of respiration.
During vigorous exercise, why does the heart rate increase?
To deliver more oxygen and glucose to muscles and remove carbon dioxide
To slow the removal of lactic acid
To lower the body temperature to zero
Muscles respire faster, so blood must supply more oxygen and glucose and remove carbon dioxide.
Give two uses of the energy released by respiration in the human body. (2 marks)
Any two: muscle contraction/movement; keeping warm/maintaining body temperature; building larger molecules (e.g. proteins) from smaller ones; active transport.
Write the word equation for anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells and explain why it can cause muscle fatigue. (3 marks)
Glucose → lactic acid; lactic acid builds up in the muscles; this causes fatigue/cramp and the muscles stop contracting efficiently.
Explain how the oxygen debt is repaid after exercise. (3 marks)

Breathing rate and heart rate stay high after exercise to take in extra oxygen; this oxygen reacts with/breaks down the lactic acid (to carbon dioxide and water); lactic acid is carried in the blood from the muscles to the liver (where some is converted back to glucose).
Why does a person keep breathing fast after hard exercise has stopped?
The muscles are still contracting hard and need oxygen for anaerobic respiration
Carbon dioxide is no longer produced, so breathing must remove the extra oxygen
Extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid that built up (the oxygen debt)
Anaerobic respiration keeps producing oxygen, which must be breathed out
Anaerobic respiration in muscles produces lactic acid.
cardiac-output: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate
Cardiac output = heart rate ÷ stroke volume
Stroke volume = cardiac output × heart rate
Heart rate = stroke volume × cardiac output
Cardiac output (cm³/min) = stroke volume (cm³) × heart rate (beats/min).
Stroke volume is 70 cm³ and heart rate is 80 bpm. What is the cardiac output?
Cardiac output is 6000 cm³/min and heart rate is 75 bpm. Calculate stroke volume.
What are the units of cardiac output?
Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute, so cm³/min.
A person has a heart rate of 72 beats/min and a stroke volume of 75 cm³. What is their cardiac output?
Volume of blood pumped out of the ventricle in one beat
Volume of blood pumped per minute
Volume of blood in the whole body
Stroke volume is the volume of blood ejected from the ventricle with each beat.
During vigorous exercise, which change helps cardiac output increase?
Heart rate and stroke volume both increase
Only the number of red blood cells changes
Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate, so increasing either or both raises it, supplying more oxygen and glucose to muscles.
Regular endurance training often lowers a person's resting heart rate. What is the most likely reason?
Stroke volume increases, so the same cardiac output needs fewer beats
A stronger heart pumps more blood per beat, so fewer beats per minute give the same cardiac output.
A person's resting cardiac output is 5100 cm³/min and their heart rate is 68 beats/min. Calculate their stroke volume. (2 marks)
Stroke volume = cardiac output ÷ heart rate; 5100 ÷ 68 = 75 cm³.
Explain why cardiac output increases during exercise. (3 marks)

Muscles respire faster and need more oxygen and glucose; heart rate increases and stroke volume increases; so more blood is pumped per minute (cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate), delivering oxygen and removing carbon dioxide faster.

Athlete A and person B both have a cardiac output of 5000 cm³/min at rest. A has a heart rate of 50 beats/min and B has 80 beats/min. Calculate the stroke volume of each and suggest why they differ. (4 marks)
A: 5000 ÷ 50 = 100 cm³; B: 5000 ÷ 80 = 62.5 cm³; the athlete's heart is stronger/larger due to training; so pumps more blood per beat.
An athlete's cardiac output at rest is 5.0 L/min and their heart rate is 50 beats/min. Calculate their stroke volume, and explain why it is larger than an untrained person's.
100 mL (0.10 L) per beat; training strengthens the heart muscle, so more blood is pumped per beat.
Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate, so SV = 5000 mL ÷ 50 = 100 mL.
ecosystems-and-levels-of-organisation: All the populations of different species in a habitat
A community and its abiotic environment
An ecosystem is the interaction of a community with non-living parts of its environment.
All organisms of one species in a habitat
A population is a group of the same species living in the same area.
Put these in order from smallest to largest: ecosystem, individual, community, population.
A pond contains frogs, fish, algae, water, sunlight and dissolved oxygen. This whole system is a(n):
An ecosystem is the community of organisms together with the non-living parts of their environment.
All the frogs living in the pond make up a:
A population is all the organisms of one species in a habitat.
The place where an organism lives
All the organisms in an area
A habitat is the place where an organism lives, such as a pond or woodland floor.
Which list shows the levels of organisation in an ecosystem from smallest to largest?
Why can an ecosystem be described as self-sustaining?
It recycles materials such as carbon and nitrogen, with energy from the Sun
Materials are cycled between living things and the environment, and sunlight provides the energy input for producers.
Distinguish between a population and a community. (2 marks)
A population is all the organisms of one species in an area; a community is all the populations of different species living together in an area.
A student studies a woodland. Give one example each of an organism, a population and a community in the woodland. (3 marks)
Organism: e.g. one oak tree / one fox; population: e.g. all the foxes / all the oak trees in the wood; community: all the plants and animals living in the wood.
Explain why the producers are essential to an ecosystem. (3 marks)
Producers (green plants/algae) photosynthesise; they convert light energy into chemical energy in glucose/biomass; this is the source of energy and biomass for all other organisms in the food chain.
All the populations of different species living in one habitat make up:
An ecosystem is the community plus the abiotic environment.
abiotic-and-biotic-factors: Abiotic factors are non-living: light, temperature, water, pollutants.
Biotic factors are living: food, predators, pathogens, competition.
If a new predator arrives, the prey population will most likely:
Explain how a drop in temperature could affect a population of lizards.
Lizards are ectotherms, so their metabolism and enzyme activity slow; they may be less active, find less food, reproduce less, or die, so the population decreases.
Which of these is an abiotic factor affecting a woodland community?
Light intensity is non-living; the others involve living organisms.
Biotic factors involve living organisms, such as predators, competition, disease and food availability.
A new species of pathogen kills many individuals in a population of rabbits. This is an example of a change in a:
Why might a decrease in the mean temperature reduce the number of insects in a habitat?
Enzyme activity and metabolism slow, reducing activity, feeding and reproduction
Insects maintain a constant body temperature
Insects are ectotherms; lower temperatures slow enzyme-controlled reactions so they feed and breed less.
Which pair of factors would most directly limit the rate of photosynthesis of plants growing under a dense tree canopy?
The canopy reduces light intensity; light and CO₂ are abiotic factors that limit photosynthesis.
Name three abiotic factors that can affect the distribution of organisms. (3 marks)

Any three from: light intensity; temperature; moisture/water availability; soil pH; mineral ions in soil; wind intensity and direction; carbon dioxide concentration (plants); oxygen concentration (aquatic animals).
Explain how a new, more aggressive competitor could affect a population of a native species. (3 marks)
Competitor uses more of the shared resources (food, light, space, water); less resources are available for the native species; so fewer survive and reproduce and the population decreases.
A farmer notices fewer earthworms in compacted, dry soil. Suggest two abiotic reasons. (2 marks)
Less moisture so earthworms dry out/cannot move or breathe through skin; less oxygen in compacted soil / harder to burrow.
Which is a biotic factor affecting a population of rabbits?
A change in the pH of the soil in their habitat
A rise in the average temperature of the area
A fall in light intensity under the woodland
A new disease spreading through the population
Biotic factors are living: predators, competition, disease and food.
interdependence: One benefits and one is harmed
E.g. bees pollinating flowers while getting nectar.
Lives on or in a host and harms it
In a predator–prey cycle, the predator population peak usually:
Predator numbers rise after prey increases, then fall as prey decreases.
Explain what is meant by interdependence.
Organisms in a community depend on each other for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal etc. A change in one population affects others.
A tick feeds on the blood of a dog and the dog is harmed. This relationship is:
In parasitism, the parasite benefits and the host is harmed.
Which is an example of mutualism?
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules of legumes
A tapeworm in a human gut
Bacteria get sugars and the legume gets nitrate-containing compounds, so both benefit.
In a stable community, a sudden rise in the number of aphids is most likely to cause the number of ladybirds (which eat aphids) to:
More food allows predators to reproduce and survive, so predator numbers rise after a time lag.
A food web shows that owls and foxes both eat voles. If all foxes are removed, what is the most likely short-term effect on voles?
Voles decrease because of fewer predators
Voles increase because there is less predation
Less predation means more voles survive, though owl predation may limit the rise.
Which statement best describes a stable community?
Population sizes fluctuate around a roughly constant level and processes such as material cycling balance
In a stable community, species and environmental factors are in balance, with small fluctuations.
Explain what is meant by interdependence in a community, using an example. (3 marks)
Organisms depend on others for food, shelter, pollination or seed dispersal; e.g. bees need nectar from flowers and flowers need bees for pollination; a change in one population affects others.
Describe the shape of a typical predator–prey graph and explain why the predator peak follows the prey peak. (3 marks)

Both populations rise and fall in repeating cycles; predator peak occurs slightly after the prey peak; more prey gives more food so predators increase; then more predators eat more prey, so prey fall, then predators fall due to lack of food.
Disease kills most of the trees in a woodland. Explain how this could affect the populations of insects that feed on the trees and the birds that feed on those insects. (4 marks)
Fewer trees means less food and habitat for insects; the insect population decreases; birds have less food so bird numbers decrease or birds move away; interdependence in the food web.
Clover and the nitrogen-fixing bacteria in its root nodules are an example of:
Both benefit: the bacteria get sugars; the plant gets nitrogen compounds.
sampling-with-quadrats: Why should quadrats be placed randomly?
Random placement gives a representative sample.
A belt transect is used to:
Estimate population of a whole field
Show how distribution changes along a gradient
Quadrats are placed at intervals along a line, e.g. from shore to land.
Mean of 4 daisies per 0.25 m² quadrat. Field is 100 m². Estimated population?
Give two ways to make quadrat sampling more reliable.
Use more quadrats / larger sample size; place randomly (e.g. random number generator); repeat and calculate a mean.
A student counts 12 plants in a 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrat. What is the density per m²?
Which is the best way to choose quadrat positions in a field?
Along the edge of a path
Using random coordinates from a random number generator
Random coordinates remove bias, so the sample represents the whole area.
A quadrat is used to measure percentage cover rather than counting individuals. This is most useful when:
Organisms are small, numerous or hard to count, such as grass
Percentage cover estimates how much of the quadrat is covered, which suits plants that cannot easily be counted individually.
Which piece of equipment is needed to carry out a belt transect from a hedge into an open field?
Measuring tape to lay a line and quadrat placed at regular intervals
A tape marks the transect line and quadrats are placed at fixed intervals along it.
Quadrat counts of dandelions in five places were 3, 5, 4, 8 and 0. What is the mean number per quadrat?
A field has an area of 600 m². A student places ten 1 m² quadrats at random and finds a total of 45 buttercups. Estimate the population in the field. (3 marks)
Mean per quadrat = 45 ÷ 10 = 4.5; per m² = 4.5; population = 4.5 × 600 = 2700 buttercups.
Describe how you would investigate whether the number of daisies changes with distance from a tree. (4 marks)

Lay a tape/transect line from the tree outwards; place a quadrat at regular intervals along the line; count daisies in each quadrat; repeat with several transects and calculate means for each distance; use the same size quadrat.
Explain why a larger number of quadrats gives a more reliable estimate of population size. (2 marks)
A larger sample is more likely to be representative of the whole area; reduces the effect of anomalies/chance (unusually dense or sparse patches) on the mean.
The mean number of daisies in a 0.25 m² quadrat is 3.5. The field is 200 m². Estimate the daisy population.
Density = 3.5 ÷ 0.25 = 14 per m²; 14 × 200 = 2800. Quadrats must be placed randomly.
energy-transfer-and-biomass-pyramids: ene-1
Approximately what percentage of energy is passed to the next trophic level?
About 10%. Most is lost through respiration, movement, heat, and undigested waste.
ene-2
A pyramid of biomass shows:
Number of organisms at each level
Mass of living material at each level
Speed of energy transfer
Number of species
Biomass pyramids are almost always pyramid-shaped.
ene-3
A producer stores 20 000 kJ and the primary consumer stores 2 000 kJ. Efficiency?
ene-4
Give two reasons why energy is lost between trophic levels.
Respiration releases energy used for movement/heat; not all of the organism is eaten (bones, roots); some is egested as faeces; urea excreted.
g18-ene-1
Which is NOT a reason why energy is lost between trophic levels?
Energy being created by photosynthesis in consumers
Parts of organisms not eaten, such as bones
Heat released during respiration
Faeces that are not digested
Consumers do not photosynthesise; the other options are all real losses.
g18-ene-2
Why are food chains rarely longer than four or five trophic levels?
Decomposers use all the energy first
Predators dislike small prey
So little energy remains at the higher levels
Plants cannot support herbivores
Only about 10% passes on at each stage, so very little is left for higher levels.
g18-ene-3
Grass stores 8000 kJ per m². A cow eats it and stores 800 kJ. The percentage efficiency of transfer is:
g18-ene-4
A pyramid of biomass is measured using dry mass because:
Dry mass is easier to see
Wet organisms are too heavy
It shows energy lost as heat
Water content varies and is not part of the organism's stored biomass
Water content varies between organisms, so dry mass gives a fairer comparison of biological material.
g18-ene-5
Why is eating plants more efficient than eating meat for supplying energy to people?
Animals contain no energy
Plants are always cheaper
Plants contain more protein
Fewer energy-transfer steps so less energy is lost
Eating producers directly avoids losses at an extra trophic level.
g18-ene-6
Calculate the percentage efficiency of energy transfer from a primary consumer storing 1500 kJ to a secondary consumer storing 120 kJ. (2 marks)
g18-ene-7
Explain why a pyramid of biomass is usually pyramid-shaped. (3 marks)
Biomass is lost between trophic levels; because energy is lost as heat from respiration, in waste and undigested material; so less biomass can be supported at each higher level.
g18-ene-8
Suggest two ways farmers can increase the efficiency of energy transfer to livestock. (2 marks)
Restrict movement of animals so less energy is lost in movement; keep them warm/indoors to reduce heat loss; control pests and disease; feed high-energy food.
gcse-bio-energy-transfer-and-biomass-pyramids-c1
Producers in a food chain contain 2000 kJ of energy and the primary consumers contain 120 kJ. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer, and give two reasons why energy is lost.
6%; energy is lost in respiration (as heat), in egested material and in parts not eaten.
human-impacts-on-biodiversity: Nitrates and phosphates cause algal blooms; decomposers use up oxygen, killing fish.
Out-compete native species and reduce biodiversity
Invasive species, e.g. grey squirrels, compete with natives.
Fish farms can harm the environment by:
Spreading disease and waste into wild populations
Waste, parasites and escaped fish affect wild ecosystems.
Explain how eutrophication leads to fish dying.
Fertilisers wash into water; algae grow rapidly and block light; plants below die; bacteria decompose dead material and use up oxygen through respiration; fish suffocate.
Which gas released by burning fossil fuels contributes most to global warming?
Carbon dioxide (and methane) are greenhouse gases that trap heat.
Peat bogs are drained for compost. One effect on the environment is:
Carbon dioxide is released as peat decomposes
Less carbon dioxide enters the air
Peat stores carbon; drying and use releases CO₂ and destroys habitats.
A rising global temperature may harm biodiversity because:
Species may have to migrate or die as their habitats change
Changes to climate alter habitats and can force migration of species or extinction.
Deforestation reduces biodiversity mainly because it:
Lowers the water table to zero
Removing trees removes the habitats and food of the species that depend on them.
Which is a reason people clear tropical rainforest?
To plant crops such as palm oil and for cattle grazing
Land is cleared for agriculture, biofuels and timber.
Explain how deforestation can increase the carbon dioxide concentration in the atmosphere. (3 marks)
Fewer trees to absorb CO₂ in photosynthesis; burning of trees releases CO₂; decomposition of the felled wood by microorganisms releases CO₂ through respiration.
Describe two ways humans pollute the environment and one effect of each. (4 marks)

Fertiliser run-off: eutrophication, killing aquatic life; smoke/sulfur dioxide from burning fuels: acid rain damaging trees; waste/chemicals in water or on land: poisoning organisms; plastics: harm to wildlife.
Suggest why human population growth has led to a reduction in biodiversity. (3 marks)
More land is needed for housing, farming and quarrying; this destroys habitats; more waste and pollution is produced; more resources are used and more carbon dioxide released.
Which is the correct order of events in eutrophication?
Fertiliser runoff → plants grow → algae die → decomposers release oxygen → fish die
Fertiliser runoff → algal bloom → light blocked, plants die → decomposers use up oxygen → fish die
Algal bloom → fertiliser runoff → plants die → oxygen levels rise → fish die
Fertiliser runoff → fish die → decomposers use up oxygen → algal bloom → plants die
Decomposers respiring aerobically remove dissolved oxygen.
conservation-and-biodiversity: Breed endangered species in zoos and may release them
Give two benefits of maintaining biodiversity.
Stable ecosystems; protects food sources; potential new medicines; ecotourism; cultural/aesthetic value; protects pollinators.
A seed bank helps conserve biodiversity by:
Storing seeds of rare plants so they can be grown later
Seeds can be stored cheaply for many years and used to restore plant populations.
Why is replanting hedgerows useful for conservation?
They provide habitats and food for wildlife
Hedgerows provide shelter, food and corridors for animals.
Protecting a natural habitat from development is an example of:
Reserves and protected areas preserve whole ecosystems.
Reducing deforestation and carbon dioxide emissions helps biodiversity because it:
Slows habitat loss and climate change
Both measures reduce pressure on habitats.
A challenge for conservation programmes is that:
People may need land and resources and conflict with conservation aims
Costs, farming needs and local livelihoods can conflict with protecting wildlife.
Explain why it is important to maintain biodiversity. (3 marks)
Species depend on each other so loss of one affects food webs; stable ecosystems provide food/materials/pollination; potential source of new medicines and crops; ecotourism and aesthetic value.
Describe two ways scientists or governments can help to conserve endangered species. (2 marks)
Captive breeding programmes and release; protected nature reserves/national parks; legal protection/ban on hunting or trade; seed banks; replanting hedgerows or habitats; setting fishing quotas.
Suggest why some farmers may not agree with creating areas of wildlife conservation. (2 marks)
Land would be taken out of food production so reducing income; conservation measures cost money and time; some protected animals may damage crops or livestock.
Why are seed banks useful for conservation?
They store genetic diversity of plant species that could be lost from the wild
They make stored plant species grow faster when they are replanted
They remove invasive plant species from habitats to protect native ones
They breed plants that are more tolerant of air pollution in cities
Captive breeding and reforestation are other strategies.
food-security: fsc-1
Food security means:
Locking food away
Having enough affordable, nutritious food for everyone
Growing GM crops only
Eating less
It's about reliable access to enough safe and nutritious food.
fsc-2
Which threatens food security?
Increasing population
Reduced meat eating
Better pest control
New crop varieties
Growing population, climate change, pests and diseases all threaten food security.
fsc-3
Give two ways biotechnology could improve food security.
GM crops with higher yield or pest/drought resistance; crops with added nutrients; mycoprotein grown in fermenters; biological control of pests.
g19-food-1
Which of the following is a biological factor that can reduce food security?
Selective breeding for higher yield
New strains of pest or pathogen that damage crops
Improved crop storage
Use of fertilisers
New pests and pathogens (for example a fungal disease of wheat) destroy crops and reduce the food available. The other options increase food supply.
g19-food-2
Rearing animals in small pens with restricted movement and a controlled temperature increases food production because:
Animals gain more energy from the sun
Less energy is lost through movement and keeping warm, so more is used for growth
Animals eat less food overall
Animals respire faster
Restricting movement and keeping animals warm reduces energy lost in respiration, so more energy goes into biomass. There are ethical objections to this.
g19-food-3
Why are fish stocks in some areas at risk of collapse?
Overfishing removes too many fish for the population to replace
Larger mesh nets let all fish escape
Fish eat too much plankton
Fish cannot reproduce in cold water
If fish are caught faster than they can breed, numbers fall and the stock may collapse. Maintaining stocks needs quotas and larger mesh sizes.
g19-food-4
Mycoprotein is produced by growing:
Algae in the sea
GM wheat in fields
Bacteria in soil
A fungus in a fermenter using glucose syrup
Mycoprotein comes from the fungus Fusarium grown in aerobic fermenters on glucose syrup, and is used as a meat substitute (Quorn).
g19-food-5
Why is eating plant crops directly usually more efficient for food security than feeding the crops to animals first?
Meat is always more expensive to store
Plants contain more protein than meat
Energy is lost at each trophic level, so less food energy is produced per hectare from animals
Animals cannot digest plants
Only about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level, so growing plants for people uses land more efficiently than raising animals.
g19-food-6
Give three biological factors that have made it difficult to feed the human population sustainably. (3 marks)

Any three from: rising birth rate / growing population; changing diets in developing countries increasing demand for meat; new pests and pathogens affecting farming; environmental changes such as drought or flooding affecting yields; cost of agricultural inputs (fertiliser, pesticide); conflicts affecting food availability.
g19-food-7
Explain how fish stocks in the oceans can be maintained at a sustainable level. (3 marks)

Fishing quotas limit the number or mass of fish that can be caught; nets with larger mesh sizes let young fish escape; so enough fish survive to breed and replace those caught; fishing banned in breeding areas or at breeding times.
g19-food-8
Describe how a GM crop could help to increase food security. (3 marks)

Genes can be transferred into crops to give resistance to pests or disease; or tolerance of drought/herbicides; or higher yield / added nutrients; so less of the crop is lost and more food is produced per hectare.
gcse-bio-food-security-c1
Increasing meat consumption reduces global food security mainly because:
Meat contains less protein than crops, so more food is needed to meet people's needs
Meat spoils faster than crops, so more of the food produced is wasted before it is eaten
Livestock farming uses less land than crops, so fewer farms are left growing food
Energy is lost at each trophic level, so more crops are needed to feed livestock than people
Population growth, pests and climate change also threaten food security.
the-carbon-cycle: Which process removes CO₂ from the atmosphere?
Plants and algae take in CO₂ to make glucose.
Decomposers return carbon to the air by:
Microorganisms respire as they break down dead material.
Combustion releases carbon locked away for millions of years.
Describe how carbon in a plant can end up in an animal and back in the atmosphere.
The animal eats the plant; carbon compounds become part of the animal's biomass; the animal respires releasing CO₂; when it dies decomposers respire, releasing more CO₂.
Which process transfers carbon from the atmosphere into the biomass of living organisms?
Photosynthesis uses CO₂ to make glucose, which is then converted into carbohydrates, proteins and fats in plant biomass.
Which of these returns carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide?
Respiration by plants, animals and microorganisms
All living organisms respire and release CO₂. Photosynthesis and fossil formation remove carbon from the atmosphere/active cycle.
Coal and oil formed from dead organisms because:
Conditions prevented decay, so carbon was locked up and compressed over millions of years
They were burned in forest fires
They were dissolved in the sea
Where decay is prevented (little oxygen), the carbon-rich remains are buried and compressed over millions of years into fossil fuels.
Compared with the burning of fossil fuels, what is the effect of respiration by decomposers on the carbon cycle?
It adds carbon that was locked up for millions of years
It releases carbon that was in recently living material
It removes carbon permanently from the cycle
Decomposers release carbon from dead plant and animal matter that was recently part of the cycle, whereas burning fossil fuels releases carbon locked away for millions of years.
Deforestation increases the concentration of atmospheric CO₂ because:
Fewer trees remove CO₂ by photosynthesis, and burning or rotting wood releases CO₂
Fewer trees means less CO₂ is absorbed, and the felled trees are burned or decay, releasing CO₂.
Describe how carbon in a dead leaf can return to the atmosphere. (3 marks)
Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) feed on the dead leaf; they break down carbon compounds and respire; releasing carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
Explain why the carbon cycle is described as a cycle with a balance between processes. (2 marks)
Carbon is removed from the air by photosynthesis and returned by respiration, combustion and decay; so the overall amount of CO₂ stays roughly constant when these are in balance.
Explain how human activities have disturbed the balance of the carbon cycle. (3 marks)
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon locked away for millions of years as CO₂; deforestation reduces photosynthesis; so more CO₂ is released than removed, and atmospheric CO₂ rises.
Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
the-water-cycle: Which process changes water vapour into liquid water in clouds?
It has low levels of dissolved substances and microbes.
Removing salt by distillation or reverse osmosis
Used in areas with little fresh water but expensive in energy.
Explain why desalination is not used widely.
It needs large amounts of energy, making it expensive; produces salty waste that can harm marine life.
Which process moves water from the leaves of plants into the atmosphere?
Transpiration is loss of water vapour from leaves, mainly through stomata.
What causes water to evaporate from the sea surface?
Heat from the Sun gives water molecules enough energy to become vapour.
Which stage of water treatment kills microorganisms?
Chlorine is added to sterilise the water and kill microbes. Filtration and sedimentation remove solids.
Water vapour in rising warm air forms clouds because:
The air cools, so water vapour condenses into droplets
As air rises it cools, and water vapour condenses into tiny liquid droplets that form clouds.
Which source of water needs the least treatment to make it potable?
Deep groundwater is naturally filtered and usually has few dissolved or suspended pollutants, so it needs only simple treatment.
Describe the main steps used to produce potable water from fresh water. (3 marks)
Choose a suitable source of fresh water; pass it through filter beds to remove solid particles; sterilise using chlorine (or ozone or ultraviolet light) to kill microbes.
Explain why rain is not considered potable water as soon as it falls, even though it is largely free of dissolved salts. (2 marks)
It may contain dissolved gases, dust or pollutants and microorganisms; potable water must have safe levels of dissolved substances and microbes.
Explain how cutting down large areas of forest could change the water cycle locally. (3 marks)
Fewer trees means less transpiration; so less water vapour enters the air and less rainfall may occur; more water runs off the soil, which may increase erosion/flooding.
In areas of drought, potable water can be produced from seawater by:
Desalination (for example by distillation or reverse osmosis)
Fermenting the seawater with yeast to remove the salt
Adding fertiliser so that algae absorb the dissolved salt
Freezing seawater and drinking the liquid that remains
the-nitrogen-cycle: Which bacteria convert nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds?
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in soil and root nodules of legumes.
They oxidise ammonium compounds to nitrites then nitrates.
Denitrifying bacteria are most active in:
They convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas in low-oxygen conditions.
Why do farmers rotate crops including legumes?
Legumes have nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules, adding nitrates to the soil, so less fertiliser is needed for the next crop.
