Why do plants need nitrates from the soil?
To make amino acids and then proteins
Plants combine nitrates with glucose to make amino acids, which are built into proteins for growth.
Which statement about nitrogen gas in the air is correct?
It must be converted into nitrogen compounds before most organisms can use it
It is produced only by lightning
Plants and animals can use it directly
Nitrogen gas is unreactive and cannot be used directly by plants or animals. Nitrogen fixation converts it into nitrates or ammonia.
What do decomposers release when they break down proteins and urea in dead matter?
Decomposers convert proteins and urea into ammonia, which nitrifying bacteria then convert into nitrates.
Where do nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as Rhizobium live?
Rhizobium lives in root nodules of legumes (peas, beans, clover) and supplies the plant with nitrogen compounds in exchange for sugars.
A farmer's field is waterlogged after heavy rain and the crop turns yellow with poor growth. Which explanation is most likely?
Denitrifying bacteria convert soil nitrates into nitrogen gas in oxygen-poor conditions
In waterlogged, anaerobic soil denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates to nitrogen gas, so the crop lacks nitrates and grows poorly.
Describe how nitrogen in a protein from a dead animal could become nitrogen in a plant protein. (4 marks)

Decomposers break down the protein / urea into ammonia; nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia into nitrates; plant roots absorb nitrates from the soil; plants combine nitrates with glucose to make amino acids and then proteins.
Give two ways in which nitrogen gas can be converted into nitrogen compounds that plants can absorb. (2 marks)

Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the soil or in root nodules; lightning (high temperatures cause nitrogen to react with oxygen, forming nitrogen oxides that dissolve in rain); also the Haber process to make fertilisers.
Explain why adding too much nitrate fertiliser to a field is harmful to a nearby lake. (3 marks)
Excess nitrates are washed into the lake (leaching/runoff); causing algal bloom; which blocks light so plants die; decomposers respire using up oxygen, so fish die (eutrophication).
Waterlogged soils often become less fertile because:
Anaerobic conditions favour denitrifying bacteria, which convert nitrates to nitrogen gas
Anaerobic conditions favour nitrifying bacteria, which convert nitrates into ammonium ions
Plants absorb too many nitrates from wet soil, so the soil quickly runs out of them
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria work faster in water, using up all of the soil's nitrates
Ploughing and drainage add oxygen, favouring nitrifying bacteria.
decomposition: Decomposers' enzymes work best when warm with water and oxygen.
Why does food last longer in a fridge?
Low temperature slows microbial growth and enzymes
Rate of decay: 20 g of mass lost over 10 days. Rate?
Explain why gardeners turn compost heaps.
Turning adds oxygen so decomposers can respire aerobically, speeding up decomposition.
Which organisms are mainly responsible for decomposition?
Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi secrete enzymes that break down dead plants and animals.
Decomposers release enzymes onto dead material. What is the main benefit of this to the ecosystem?
It increases the temperature of the soil
It returns mineral ions to the soil for plants to absorb
Breakdown of dead material releases minerals (e.g. nitrates) that producers take up, so nutrients are recycled.
Which change would speed up the rate of decay of leaf litter?
Keeping the litter warm and moist
Warmth, moisture and oxygen increase the activity and reproduction of decomposers.
Why does decay happen more slowly in a waterlogged bog than in a garden compost heap?
There is little oxygen, so fewer aerobic decomposers can respire
Waterlogging limits oxygen, and acidic, oxygen-poor conditions reduce decomposer activity.
A gardener makes compost. Which carbon compound is released into the air by the respiration of decomposers?
Aerobic respiration by decomposers releases CO₂, returning carbon to the atmosphere.
Explain why a compost heap decays faster in summer than in winter. (3 marks)
Higher temperature in summer; increases enzyme activity / rate of respiration and reproduction of decomposers; so dead material is broken down faster (enzymes work at a lower rate when cold).
Describe how decomposers help to maintain the carbon cycle and the mineral supply in a woodland. (3 marks)
Decomposers break down dead leaves and animals; respire and release carbon dioxide into the air for photosynthesis; release minerals/nitrates into the soil which plants absorb for growth.
A student sets up bottles of milk at 5 °C, 25 °C and 60 °C and records how long each takes to go sour. Predict the order of the fastest to slowest and explain. (3 marks)

25 °C fastest, then 5 °C, then 60 °C slowest (or 60 °C may be near zero); at 25 °C bacteria are near optimum so reproduce and respire quickly; at 5 °C enzyme activity is slow; at 60 °C bacterial enzymes denature / bacteria are killed.
A 50 g sample of leaf litter decomposes to 35 g in 30 days. Calculate the mean rate of decay, and give two conditions that would increase it.
0.5 g/day; warmer temperatures (up to the decomposers' optimum), more water and more oxygen.
indicator-species: Lichens are used to indicate levels of:
Many lichens can't survive in air with high SO₂.
Stonefly larvae in a river indicate:
They survive in low oxygen conditions.
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using indicator species instead of chemical tests.
Advantages: cheap; shows long-term effects. Disadvantages: less precise; doesn't identify the exact pollutant or its concentration.
A species that is always the largest in a habitat
A species whose presence or absence shows the level of an environmental factor
A species that feeds only on algae
A species that can survive anywhere
Indicator species are sensitive to a condition such as pollution, so they reflect environmental quality.
A stream contains only rat-tailed maggots and sludgeworms. What does this suggest?
The water is polluted with low oxygen
The water is clean and oxygen-rich
These species tolerate low oxygen, so their dominance indicates organic pollution.
Why do sewage and fertiliser run-off reduce oxygen levels in a river?
They make plants release more oxygen
Bacteria multiply and use up oxygen decomposing the material
Eutrophication and decay by aerobic microbes lower dissolved oxygen, killing sensitive species.
Which is a disadvantage of using indicator species rather than measuring dissolved oxygen directly?
It does not give an exact numerical value
Indicator species give a rough guide only; instruments give precise values at one moment.
Which would be found on trees in an area with very clean air?
Bushy and leafy lichens are sensitive to SO₂; crusty lichens tolerate more pollution.
A river is sampled upstream and downstream of a sewage outlet. Stonefly larvae are found upstream only. Explain this result. (3 marks)
Stonefly larvae need high oxygen levels; sewage causes bacterial growth that uses up oxygen downstream; so stoneflies cannot survive downstream (indicating pollution).
Explain why indicator species can give a better picture of pollution than a single chemical test. (2 marks)

Organisms are exposed to conditions over a long time / reflect average pollution over weeks or months; a chemical test only shows the level at the moment of sampling and pollution may be intermittent.
Describe how you could use lichens to compare air pollution at two sites. (3 marks)

Use a quadrat on tree trunks at each site; record the types of lichen present (crusty, leafy, bushy) and percentage cover; more leafy/bushy lichens means cleaner air; repeat on several trees and compare means.
A stream has many bloodworms and sludgeworms but no stonefly nymphs. This indicates that the water:
Is polluted, with low oxygen levels
Is too cold for any life
Stonefly nymphs and freshwater shrimp indicate clean water; lichens indicate clean air.
cp-using-a-light-microscope: Which objective lens should you start with when focusing?
Start low power to find the specimen, then increase.
Why are stains such as iodine added to slides?
When using a high-power lens you should only use the:
Coarse focus could crash the objective into the slide.
Describe how to prepare a slide of onion epidermis.
Peel a thin layer of epidermis; place on a slide in a drop of water/iodine; lower a coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles; view under the microscope.
A student uses a ×10 eyepiece and a ×40 objective lens. What is the total magnification?
Why is a coverslip placed over the specimen?
To hold the specimen flat and protect the objective lens
It flattens the specimen and keeps the lens from touching the liquid.
Why should the coverslip be lowered at an angle using a mounted needle?
Air bubbles can be mistaken for cells and obscure the specimen.
In a scientific drawing of cells, which is correct?
Use sharp, continuous pencil lines and label with ruled lines
Drawings need clear lines, no shading, and labels with straight lines that do not cross.
A cell image is 6 mm wide and the real cell is 30 µm wide. What is the magnification?
Describe how to focus a microscope on a specimen, starting from a prepared slide. (4 marks)

Place slide on the stage and clip it; select the lowest power objective; use the coarse focus to move the stage/lens until the image is roughly clear (viewing from the side first to avoid contact); use the fine focus to sharpen; change to higher power if needed and use fine focus only.
A cell appears 45 mm long in a drawing. The magnification is ×300. Calculate the real length in µm. (2 marks)
Real size = image size ÷ magnification; 45 mm = 45 000 µm; 45 000 ÷ 300 = 150 µm.
Explain why a thin specimen is needed to view cells with a light microscope. (2 marks)
Light must pass through the specimen; if it is too thick, light cannot pass through / layers overlap, so the image is dark or unclear.
Why should you start with the lowest-power objective lens?
It gives the highest magnification, so cells are easiest to find and focus on
It gives a wider field of view to find the specimen and reduces the risk of damaging the slide
It improves the resolution, so the smallest organelles can be seen clearly
It lets more light through, which stains the cells so they are easier to see
Then switch to a higher power and use only the fine focus.
cp-ph-and-amylase-activity: cpa-1

Benedict's
Iodine turning blue-black
Biuret
Limewater
When iodine stays orange-brown, starch has been digested.
cpa-2
What is the independent variable?
Temperature
pH
Time taken
Volume of amylase
pH is changed using buffer solutions.
cpa-3
Why use a water bath at a fixed temperature?
To control temperature as a variable
To heat the iodine
To change pH
To kill amylase
Temperature affects enzyme activity, so must be kept constant.
cpa-4
Describe how to time when starch is fully digested.
Put iodine drops on a spotting tile; every 10–30 s take a drop of the mixture and add to iodine; record when the iodine no longer turns blue-black.
g20-cpa-1
Why is a buffer solution added to the amylase and starch mixture?
To keep the pH at a set value
To speed up the reaction at all pH values
To change the colour of iodine
To provide energy
Buffers hold the pH constant at the value being tested.
g20-cpa-2
Amylase is added to starch at pH 2. After 10 minutes iodine still turns blue-black. What is the best conclusion?
Amylase works best at pH 2
Iodine is faulty
Starch has been fully digested
Amylase is denatured or inactive at pH 2
Blue-black means starch remains, because acidic pH denatures amylase's active site.
g20-cpa-3
Which is the dependent variable in this investigation?
Temperature of the water bath
pH of the buffer
Concentration of starch
Time taken for starch to disappear
The time taken (or rate) is what is measured in response to changing pH.
g20-cpa-4
Amylase was fastest at pH 7 (30 s) and slower at pH 5 (120 s). Which calculation gives the rate at pH 7?
Rate is proportional to 1 ÷ time, so 1000 ÷ 30 (s⁻¹ × 1000).
g20-cpa-5
Why is it important to mix the enzyme and substrate only after both have reached the water bath temperature?
To make the solution colourless
To increase the amount of enzyme
To lower the pH
So the reaction starts at the correct temperature
Otherwise the temperature varies at the start and the results are not valid.
g20-cpa-6
Describe how the effect of pH on the rate of amylase can be investigated. (4 marks)

Add starch solution and buffer of a set pH to a tube in a water bath at constant temperature; add amylase and start the timer; every 30 s remove a drop and add to iodine on a spotting tile; record time when iodine stays orange-brown; repeat at other pH values.
g20-cpa-7
Name two variables that must be controlled and explain why. (2 marks)
Temperature, volume/concentration of amylase or starch; these also affect the rate of reaction so would affect results / make the test unfair.
g20-cpa-8
Explain, using the shape of an enzyme, why amylase activity falls at very low or very high pH. (3 marks)
Extreme pH disrupts the bonds holding the enzyme's shape; the active site changes shape / enzyme denatures; the substrate (starch) can no longer fit so fewer reactions occur.
gcse-bio-cp-ph-and-amylase-activity-c1
Why are the amylase and starch solutions placed separately in the water bath before mixing?
So the iodine cannot react with the starch before timing starts
So the pH of each solution changes to the value being tested
So they reach the set temperature before the reaction begins
So the enzyme is partly denatured before it meets the starch
Temperature is a control variable when pH is the independent variable.

Why are potato pieces blotted dry before weighing?

To kill them
To add sugar
To speed osmosis

The starting masses differ, so percentages allow fair comparison
It's always positive

Percentage change allows comparison of different starting masses.

At which point on the graph is the sucrose concentration equal to the potato cell sap concentration?
Where the line crosses 0% change in mass
At the highest point
At 0 M sucrose
Where the line is steepest

cpo-4
A potato piece loses mass in 1.0 M sucrose solution. Explain why.
The sucrose solution is more concentrated than the cell sap, so water leaves the cells by osmosis.

Potato cylinders are cut with a cork borer rather than with a knife freehand. Why?
It removes the potato skin cells
It makes the cylinders sterile
It gives cylinders of the same diameter, so surface area is controlled
It stops osmosis happening during cutting
A cork borer gives equal-width cylinders, so surface area to volume ratio is a controlled variable.
g21-pot-2
A potato cylinder increases in mass in a solution. What does this show?
The solution is more concentrated than the cell sap
The solution is less concentrated than the cell sap
The solution has the same concentration as the cell sap
Water left the cells by active transport
Water moved into the cells by osmosis from a dilute solution (high water concentration), so mass increased.
g21-pot-3
In this investigation, which is the dependent variable?
Time in the solution
Percentage change in mass of the potato
Temperature of the room
Concentration of sucrose solution
The percentage change in mass is what is measured and depends on the sucrose concentration.
g21-pot-4
Potato cylinder A starts at 2.50 g and ends at 2.20 g. What is the percentage change in mass?

Why should the experiment include a potato piece in distilled water?

To act as a control showing the effect of pure water with no solute
To make the sucrose less concentrated
To kill bacteria on the potato

Describe how you would use a graph of percentage change in mass against sucrose concentration to estimate the concentration of the potato cell sap. (2 marks)

Find where the line of best fit crosses the x-axis / 0% change in mass; read the sucrose concentration at that point, which equals the concentration of the cell sap because there is no net movement of water.
g21-pot-7
Give three variables that should be controlled in the potato osmosis investigation. (3 marks)

Any three from: volume of solution; temperature; time left in solution; size / surface area / diameter of potato cylinders; type / same potato; method of blotting; same number of cylinders per beaker.
g21-pot-8
A student says the results are more reliable if repeated. Explain how the student could improve reliability and how they should process the repeats. (2 marks)
Use several cylinders (e.g. three) in each concentration / repeat the experiment; calculate a mean percentage change for each concentration; identify and ignore anomalies.
gcse-bio-cp-osmosis-in-potato-c1
Why are potato cylinders blotted dry before they are weighed?
To stop osmosis continuing while the cylinders are weighed
To kill the cells so that their mass no longer changes
To remove surface solution that would add to the mass
To remove the water from inside the cells before weighing
Inconsistent surface water would cause random error.
cp-food-tests: Which test needs heating in a water bath?
Benedict's reagent must be heated to detect reducing sugars.
The ethanol emulsion test for lipids gives:
Lipids form a milky emulsion when water is added.
Give one safety precaution for food tests.
Wear eye protection; keep ethanol away from flames; use a water bath not a direct flame to heat Benedict's.
Which result shows that starch is present in a food sample?
Cloudy emulsion with ethanol then water
Iodine solution changes from orange-brown to blue-black in the presence of starch.
A food sample is tested with Benedict's reagent and heated. The mixture stays blue. What can you conclude?
No sugar of any kind is present
Blue means no reducing sugar. Non-reducing sugars such as sucrose would not be detected.
What is the positive result for the biuret test for protein?
Biuret reagent turns from blue to purple (lilac) when protein is present.
In the emulsion test for lipids, why is the food first ground up and shaken with ethanol?
To dissolve any lipid in the ethanol
To turn the lipid into starch
Lipids dissolve in ethanol, and pouring this into water gives a cloudy emulsion as the lipid droplets come out of solution.
Which colour sequence is seen as the amount of reducing sugar increases in a Benedict's test?
Blue → green → yellow → orange → brick red
More reducing sugar gives a greater colour change, from blue through green, yellow and orange to brick red.
Describe how to test a liquid food sample for reducing sugars. (4 marks)

Add Benedict's reagent to the sample in a test tube; heat in a water bath (about 80 °C / hot water); for a few minutes; positive result is colour change from blue to green / yellow / orange / brick red.
A sample gives a blue-black colour with iodine and a purple colour with biuret reagent. What does it contain? (2 marks)
Explain why a water bath is used rather than a Bunsen flame to heat the Benedict's test, and why ethanol is a hazard in the lipid test. (2 marks)
A water bath heats more gently / evenly so the liquid does not spit out; ethanol is flammable so must be kept away from naked flames.
Benedict's test results ranked from the least to the most reducing sugar are:
Brick red, orange, yellow, green, blue
Blue, green, yellow, orange, brick red
The test is semi-quantitative; use the same volume of sample and reagent and heat in a water bath.
cp-calorimetry: Energy per gram of food is calculated by:
Energy transferred ÷ mass of food burned
Divide energy transferred (J) by the mass of food burned (g).
To make the result more accurate you could:
Insulate the tube to reduce heat loss
Less heat lost to the surroundings means a more accurate value.
A 0.5 g crisp heats 25 g of water by 12 °C. Calculate energy per gram (4.2 J/g/°C).
In a food calorimetry experiment, what is the energy transferred to the water calculated from?
Mass of water × specific heat capacity × temperature change
Energy = mass of water × specific heat capacity × change in temperature.
A food heats 20 g of water from 20 °C to 45 °C. What energy is transferred to the water? (4.2 J/g/°C)
Why is the energy value found in a school calorimetry experiment usually lower than the value on the food packet?
Some energy is lost to the surroundings and the food burns incompletely
The food gains energy from the air
Heat is lost to the air and apparatus, and burning may be incomplete, so less energy reaches the water.
Which change would improve the accuracy of the investigation?
Using a thermometer reading to the nearest 10 °C
Putting the boiling tube close to the food and using a draught shield
Heating a larger volume of water without measuring it
Holding the food 20 cm below the tube
Reducing heat loss to the surroundings means more energy is transferred to the water.
Which unit is commonly used to give the energy per gram of food on a packet?
Energy content on food labels is given in kJ (or kcal) per 100 g.
A 0.8 g peanut heats 30 g of water by 40 °C. Calculate the energy released per gram of peanut. (4.2 J/g/°C) (3 marks)
Give two variables that must be controlled when comparing the energy in different foods. (2 marks)
Any two from: volume / mass of water; starting temperature of water; distance between the food and the tube; mass of food; same apparatus / same type of tube.
Explain how the student could improve the reliability of the results when comparing two foods. (2 marks)
Repeat the experiment for each food and calculate a mean; ignore anomalous results / check repeats are close together.
Suggest two improvements to the boiling-tube calorimetry method that would make the energy values closer to the true values.
Insulate the tube (or use a lid) to reduce heat loss; place the burning food closer to the tube; make sure the food burns completely, relighting if needed; stir the water.
Most error comes from heat transferred to the surroundings rather than the water.
cp-antibiotics-and-bacterial-growth: Why are agar plates incubated at 25 °C in schools?
To reduce the chance of growing human pathogens
Higher temperatures could favour pathogens that grow at body temperature.
A larger clear zone around an antibiotic disc means:
Area of a circular clear zone with radius 5 mm (π = 3.14)?
Give two aseptic techniques used when culturing bacteria.
Sterilise the inoculating loop in a flame; tape the lid (not fully sealed); flame the neck of bottles; open lids minimally; sterilise equipment in an autoclave.
Why should the lid of a Petri dish be taped with only two or four short pieces and not sealed all around?
To allow oxygen in so harmful anaerobic bacteria do not grow
Sealing fully could create anaerobic conditions, favouring dangerous anaerobic pathogens.
A clear zone appears around an antibiotic disc on a bacterial lawn. What does this show?
The antibiotic is a source of food
The antibiotic prevented bacteria growing nearby
The bacteria are resistant to the antibiotic
Antibiotic diffuses into the agar and kills or inhibits bacteria, leaving a clear zone with no growth.
Why is a control disc soaked in sterile water often included on the plate?
To show that the paper disc itself does not stop bacterial growth
To increase the rate of diffusion
If no clear zone forms around the control, the clear zones around other discs are due to the antibiotic.
The diameter of a clear zone is 12 mm. What is its area? (π = 3.14)
Why are agar plates and culture media sterilised before use?
To kill unwanted microorganisms that would contaminate the culture
Heating (e.g. autoclaving) kills microorganisms already present, so only the bacteria being investigated grow.
Describe how you would use a sterile loop to transfer bacteria to a Petri dish safely. (3 marks)
Sterilise the loop by passing it through a flame; let it cool; remove lid only slightly / minimally and spread bacteria on the agar; replace lid and tape it.
Antibiotic A gives a clear zone of diameter 14 mm and antibiotic B a zone of diameter 8 mm. Which is more effective, and why? Calculate the area of A's zone (π = 3.14). (3 marks)
A is more effective; because it has a larger clear zone / killed more bacteria; area = 3.14 × 7² = 153.9 mm² (about 154 mm²).
Explain why cultures in schools are incubated at 25 °C or below, not at 37 °C. (2 marks)
37 °C is body temperature; it would encourage growth of human pathogens; 25 °C reduces the risk of harmful pathogens growing.
A clear zone around an antibiotic disc has a diameter of 14 mm. Calculate its area.
Area = πr² = π × 7² ≈ 154 mm². Use the radius, not the diameter.
cp-light-intensity-and-photosynthesis: In the pondweed experiment, rate is measured by:
Counting oxygen bubbles or volume of gas
Why is a beaker of water or LED lamp used?
To control temperature changes from the lamp
Lamps give off heat, which would be an uncontrolled variable.
Which change will decrease the number of bubbles per minute?
Suggest why counting bubbles is not very accurate.
Bubbles vary in size; fast bubbles are hard to count; some oxygen dissolves in water. Using a gas syringe to measure volume is better.
In the pondweed experiment, the independent variable is usually:
The distance between the lamp and the pondweed
The number of bubbles produced per minute
The distance from the lamp is the variable you deliberately change. Bubbles per minute is the dependent variable.
Which gas makes up the bubbles given off by pondweed in bright light?
Photosynthesis produces oxygen as a waste product, and this is released as bubbles.
Sodium hydrogencarbonate is added to the water in the pondweed experiment to:
Supply carbon dioxide so it is not limiting
Sodium hydrogencarbonate dissolves to release CO₂, so carbon dioxide does not limit the rate and light intensity can be investigated.
A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 20 cm from the pondweed. Light intensity is proportional to 1/d². How does light intensity change?
Doubling the distance gives 1/2² = 1/4 of the intensity.
At high light intensity the rate of photosynthesis stops increasing. This is because:
Light is no longer absorbed by leaves
Another factor, such as CO₂ concentration or temperature, is now limiting
The chlorophyll has been used up completely
Once light is no longer the limiting factor, another factor such as CO₂ or temperature limits the rate, so the graph plateaus.
Describe how you would use a gas syringe to find the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed. (4 marks)

Place a piece of pondweed in a beaker of water with sodium hydrogencarbonate (CO₂ source), connected to a gas syringe (or inverted funnel and syringe); place a lamp at a measured distance from the beaker; leave to adjust then record the volume of oxygen collected in a set time (e.g. 2 minutes); repeat at different distances, keeping temperature (e.g. use a water bath / heat shield) and pondweed the same; calculate volume per minute for each distance.
Pondweed produces 12 cm³ of oxygen in 4 minutes. Calculate the rate in cm³ per minute. (2 marks)
Rate = volume ÷ time; 12 ÷ 4 = 3 cm³ per minute.
Explain why the pondweed should be left for a few minutes after moving the lamp before counting bubbles. (2 marks)
To allow the pondweed to adjust / photosynthesis rate to settle at the new light intensity; so the bubbles counted are produced at that light intensity and not the previous one.
In the pondweed experiment, a beaker of water is placed between the lamp and the pondweed. Its purpose is to:
Supply extra carbon dioxide to the pondweed as it photosynthesises
Absorb heat from the lamp so that temperature does not change
Focus the light so that the pondweed receives a higher intensity
Collect the oxygen produced so that its volume can be measured
Temperature is a control variable; sodium hydrogencarbonate is added to supply CO₂.
cp-respiration-rate-in-small-organisms: What does soda lime do in a respirometer?
So the movement of the liquid shows oxygen uptake.
As organisms respire, the coloured liquid moves:
Oxygen is used and CO₂ absorbed, so pressure in the tube decreases.
What is the control in this experiment?
A tube with glass beads of the same mass instead of organisms
A tube at a higher temperature
This shows any change is due to the organisms.
Give one ethical consideration when using live organisms.
Handle carefully; don't leave them too long; avoid contact with soda lime; return them to their habitat afterwards.
Which organisms are suitable to use in a respirometer?
Small living, respiring organisms such as germinating seeds, woodlice or maggots are used. Dry seeds respire very slowly.
Why does the coloured liquid move towards the organisms in a respirometer?
CO₂ is released into the tube
The tube heats up and gas expands
Oxygen is used up and the CO₂ produced is absorbed, so the gas volume falls
Organisms take in O₂ and release CO₂, which soda lime absorbs. The net gas volume decreases and pressure falls, drawing the liquid towards the tube.
The liquid moves 24 mm in 8 minutes. What is the rate of movement?
To investigate the effect of temperature on respiration rate, the respirometer tubes should be placed in:
Water baths allow the temperature (independent variable) to be set and kept steady.
A student uses 5 g of woodlice in one tube and 10 g in another. What is the best way to compare their respiration rates?
Use the tube with more woodlice only
Compare only the total distance moved
Calculate the movement per minute per gram of woodlice
Dividing by mass allows fair comparison between different numbers or masses of organisms.
Explain why a control tube containing glass beads is set up. (2 marks)

The control shows whether changes in gas volume / liquid movement are due to the living organisms; glass beads do not respire, so any movement would be caused by other factors such as temperature or pressure changes.
Suggest why the organisms are kept on a mesh platform above the soda lime. (2 marks)
So the organisms do not touch the soda lime; as soda lime would harm / kill them (it is caustic); but the soda lime can still absorb the CO₂ produced from the air around them.
Describe how the results from a respirometer would change if the temperature was increased from 10 °C to 25 °C, and explain why. (3 marks)

The liquid would move faster / greater distance per minute at 25 °C; because respiration is controlled by enzymes and a higher temperature gives more kinetic energy and more frequent collisions, so respiration rate increases and oxygen is used up more quickly.
In a respirometer, soda lime absorbs carbon dioxide. As the organisms respire, the coloured liquid moves towards them because:
They release extra oxygen as they respire, which pushes the liquid towards them
They use up oxygen, and the CO₂ they release is absorbed, so the gas volume falls
Soda lime releases gas as it absorbs CO₂, which pulls the liquid towards them
Their respiration warms the air, which contracts and pulls the liquid towards them
The distance moved per minute measures the rate of oxygen uptake.
cp-sampling-with-quadrats: cpq-1
How can you place quadrats randomly in a field?
Throw over your shoulder
Use a grid and random number generator for coordinates
Place where there are most plants
Place in a line
Random coordinates avoid bias.
cpq-2
Percentage cover estimates:
The number of plants
The proportion of a quadrat's area covered by a species
The height of plants
Plant mass
Used when individual plants are hard to count, e.g. grass.
cpq-3
Describe how to investigate how plant distribution changes from a hedge into an open field.

Lay a tape measure as a transect from the hedge; place a quadrat at regular intervals; count/estimate % cover of each species; measure abiotic factors like light intensity at each point; repeat with more transects.
Why should many quadrats be used in a sampling investigation?
To make a random sample unnecessary
To damage fewer plants
To save time
To make the results more representative of the whole area
A larger sample reduces the effect of chance and anomalies, so it better represents the whole area.
A transect is used to study:
The total number of species in a pond
Random distribution only
Soil pH only
How distribution changes along a line, such as from a path into woodland
Placing quadrats at intervals along a line shows how species distribution changes with a gradient.
Five 1 m² quadrats contain 4, 6, 3, 7 and 5 daisies. A field has an area of 800 m². What is the estimated population?
Which is the best way to avoid bias when placing quadrats?
Place them only near the edge
Choose easy-to-reach places
Place them where there are most plants
Use random numbers as coordinates on a grid
Random coordinates ensure every part of the area has an equal chance of being sampled.
A quadrat has 100 squares. A species covers about 35 of them. What is its percentage cover?
Describe how to find the mean number of dandelions per m² in a field using 0.25 m² quadrats. (3 marks)

Place quadrats at random positions (e.g. using random coordinates from a grid laid over the field); count the dandelions in each quadrat; calculate the mean number per quadrat then multiply by 4 to give the number per m² (a 0.25 m² quadrat is a quarter of 1 m²).
Explain why a transect is better than random sampling to investigate the effect of shade on plants. (2 marks)

A transect samples along a line from sunny to shady areas; so changes in distribution can be linked to the change in light / the gradient, whereas random sampling would not show a pattern with distance from the shade.
Give two abiotic factors that could be measured alongside quadrat counts and name a piece of equipment for one. (3 marks)
Any two abiotic factors with equipment for one: light intensity (light meter); soil pH (pH probe / indicator); soil moisture (moisture meter); temperature (thermometer).
gcse-bio-cp-sampling-with-quadrats-c1
To study how plant distribution changes from a path into a field, the best method is to:
Place quadrats randomly across the field
Count plants only next to the path
Use one large quadrat
Place quadrats at regular intervals along a transect
Random sampling estimates abundance; a transect shows change across a gradient.
cp-temperature-and-decay: cpt-1
Bags of fresh grass clippings are kept at different temperatures. How can rate of decay be measured?
Measure the loss in mass over time
Count the bags
Measure the colour of the bag
Measure the light intensity
Decomposers respire, releasing CO₂ and water, so the mass of the clippings falls.
cpt-2
Why does decay slow at very high temperatures?
Decomposers' enzymes denature
There is more oxygen
Water is added
The grass grows
Enzymes in decomposers lose their shape, so microbes die or stop working.
cpt-3
State two variables that must be controlled.
Starting mass of grass; type/freshness of grass; moisture/water content; oxygen availability (bag type); time period.
Slightly alkaline milk containing universal indicator is purple. Which colour change shows that microorganisms are making acid as they decay the milk?
No change
Clear to green
Purple to yellow
Yellow to purple
Microorganisms produce acid as they break down milk, so the pH falls and the indicator changes from purple towards green / yellow. Faster change means faster decay.
At 0 °C decay is very slow because:
There is too much oxygen
The food is dry
Decomposers' enzymes work very slowly at low temperature
Decomposers are denatured
Low temperature means little kinetic energy, so enzyme-controlled reactions are very slow, though enzymes are not denatured.
What is the optimum temperature for decay likely to be?
Below −10 °C
Around 30–40 °C
Decomposers' enzymes work best at warm temperatures, usually around 30–40 °C.
Which variable must be kept the same when comparing decay at different temperatures?
The temperature
The time of day only
The volume and type of milk
The colour of the tubes only
Only the temperature should change; the amount and type of material must be controlled.
A student's results show decay is fastest at 35 °C and nearly zero at 70 °C. The best explanation for 70 °C is:
Oxygen runs out
Water evaporates only
Enzymes in decomposers are denatured and the microorganisms die
Enzymes are too cold to work
High temperatures denature enzymes and kill decomposers, stopping decay.
Describe a method to investigate the effect of temperature on the decay of milk. (4 marks)

Put equal volumes of milk (and same amount of indicator, e.g. universal indicator with a little alkali) in several test tubes; add the same amount of lipase / decomposer culture or microorganisms to each; place tubes in water baths at different temperatures (e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 °C); time how long the indicator takes to change colour (to show acidity); repeat for reliability.
Explain why rate of decay can be calculated as 1000 ÷ time taken for colour change. (2 marks)
Rate is proportional to 1 ÷ time because a shorter time means faster decay; multiplying by 1000 gives convenient whole numbers / allows rates at different temperatures to be compared.
Explain why gardeners use compost heaps in summer rather than leaving rubbish in a freezer to rot. (3 marks)

Warm summer temperatures are closer to the optimum for decomposers' enzymes, so decay is faster; in a freezer the low temperature makes enzymes work very slowly, so little decay happens; compost heaps also have oxygen and moisture, which decomposers need.
gcse-bio-cp-temperature-and-decay-c1
The rate of decay is fastest at 35 °C and slow at both 5 °C and 70 °C. The best explanation is that:
Decomposers are killed by cold and also by heat, so they only survive near 35 °C
Heat always speeds up decay, but water evaporates at 70 °C and this stops it
Decomposers stop feeding at 5 °C and form spores at 70 °C, so nothing is digested
Decomposer enzymes work slowly in the cold and are denatured at high temperatures
Microorganisms' respiration and enzyme activity depend on temperature.

Producers contain 10 000 kJ. If 10% of the energy passes to each level, how much reaches tertiary consumers?

Water enters both cells by osmosis. The plant cell swells until its membrane presses against the strong cellulose cell wall, which stops it bursting (it becomes turgid). The animal cell has no cell wall, so it swells and bursts.

If fertilisation does not happen, the uterus lining breaks down because:
Progesterone maintains the lining; when it falls, menstruation begins.

Another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, becomes the limiting factor, so extra light makes no difference to the rate.
The graph levels off where light is no longer limiting.
Explain how the over-use of antibiotics has led to the spread of MRSA.

Random mutations made some bacteria resistant. Antibiotics killed non-resistant bacteria, so resistant ones survived, reproduced and passed on the resistance allele. With repeated antibiotic use, resistant strains such as MRSA became common.
Use the steps of natural selection; the antibiotic does not cause the mutation.
